# Preliminary Remark.

[...recounts] of the impression which it made upon his spirit, and of the sublime idea which it awakened in his soul of these great men, of these illustrious heroes and defenders of Christianity <note>original: *Christenthumes*</note>. He hopes that by not taking the thoughts and judgments of others as his guiding principle, he has avoided the accusation of being a slavish copyist <note>original: *knechtischer Ausschreiber* — a common 18th-century critique of writers or translators who merely compiled others' work without adding original thought or style.</note> or a tedious echo; instead, he wished to provide something that would be interesting at least for its novelty, as may perhaps be seen from the following introduction. The author requests that the reader does not skip <note>original: *überschlagen*</note> this introduction, as he deems it necessary for a better overview of the work.

## of the Christian Defenders <note>original: *Schutzredner* — more commonly known to modern readers as the "Apologists," these writers specialized in making a formal legal and philosophical defense of the Christian faith to the Roman authorities.</note>,
### who appear in this work.

Saint **Justin, philosopher and martyr.** He was born in the year of Christ 103, and received the martyr's crown in the year 167 under the reign of Marcus Aurelius <note>original: *Mark = Aurel* — the Roman Emperor and Stoic philosopher who ruled from 161 to 180 AD.</note>. Page 49

**Tatian, Justin's student,** whose contemporary he was. He survived him by several years; but neither the year of his birth nor of his death can be specified. 78

**Athenagoras.** His defense <note>original: *Schutzschrift* — specifically his "Embassy for the Christians."</note> to the Emperor Marcus Aurelius clarifies for us the time when he lived; and that is also everything we know of him. 88

**Theophilus of Antioch.** In his third book to Autolycus <note>original: *Autolykus*</note> one finds a chronology reaching up to the sixteenth year of Marcus Aurelius's reign; from this, one can reliably conclude the time when he flourished. 105

**Clement of Alexandria.** It is commonly held that Clement died at a great age around the first years of the third century. He must therefore have been born quite early in the second century. 116

**Hermias.** All good critics place him in the second century. 129

**Origen.** The great Origen was born in the year 185 and died in the year 253. Consequently, he lived into his sixty-ninth year. 138

**Minutius Felix.** One does not know exactly at what time Minutius Felix lived. Saint Jerome <note>original: *Hieronymus*</note>

# Introduction.

### On the Character, Insights, and Works of those Ancient Philosophers, who were the first Apologists <note>original: *Schutzredner* — literally "defense-speakers." These were intellectuals who wrote formal, often legalistic defenses of Christianity against state persecution and philosophical attacks.</note> and Defenders of the Christian Religion.

Behold the most striking spectacle for both the unbelieving and the Christian world: those illustrious refugees who have crossed from the camp of <term>Idolatry <note>original: *Abgötterey* — This refers to the polytheistic worship of the Greco-Roman gods, which Christian writers viewed as the worship of false idols.</note></term> to the banner of Jesus Christ; those admirable men who, after distinguishing themselves among the pagans <note>original: *Heyden*</note> with the greatest fame through their extensive knowledge and deep insight, subsequently became the heroes, the protection, and the pride of the Christian name. In the midst of the darkness of pagan superstition into which they were born and raised—within the bosom of a religion that infinitely flattered the senses and favored all passions—a ray of an entirely new light struck their eyes. They perceived, as if through a mist, some traces of the holiness and truths of the Gospel teachings, and discovered in its followers <note>original: *Schülern* — literally "students" or "disciples."</note> sublime, heroic, almost inconceivable virtues. Struck by all these things, they reflected upon this phenomenon, and

# Introduction.

the more maturely they reflected, the more they became convinced that something superhuman must necessarily reside in the knowledge this religion imparted and in the courage it inspired. Since grace found in them a teachable heart and a sincere soul, they soon yielded and urgently desired to be accepted among the Christians.

While <term>Idolatry <note>original: *Abgötterey* — the worship of idols or false gods.</note></term> was initially horrified by this loss, it was later even more terrified by the attacks these illustrious refugees dared to make against it. They exposed, on one hand, the abominations and absurdities of <term>idol-worship <note>original: *Götzendienst*.</note></term>, and on the other, revealed the holiness, purity, and divinity of the new religion. An astonishing erudition in every field, a strength of reasoning <note>original: *Stärke im Schließen* — the ability to form logical conclusions or arguments.</note> that nothing could resist, a perfect knowledge of everything said, taught, and practiced in both religions, and a deep-seated knowledge of the laws—of both civil and natural law—formed the foundation of the victorious apologies <note>original: *Schutzreden* — formal defenses of the faith, from the Greek "apologia."</note> that these new defenders of Christianity brought to light. These defenses filled all the pagans with amazement; they opened the eyes of some, silenced others, and daily multiplied the most magnificent conquests of this religion.

And indeed, the contrast that emerged when comparing the two religions could not have been more striking. On one side was the most sublime, most majestic, and worthiest image of the Deity that could ever be imagined; on the other, however, the absurdities,

[th]at was monstrous and absurd in everything said about the gods and attributed to them. On one side, one ascended to the first origin of all things through a series of insights that satisfied reason, supported by a steadfast tradition whose traces were found among all nations; on the other, there was a swarm of fables without foundation or probability, which violated all reason, or one found oneself in the midst of a labyrinth of <term>philosophical systems <note>original: *philosophischer Lehrgebäude* — literally "philosophical teaching-buildings," referring to the complex, structured schools of thought in ancient philosophy.</note></term> that sounded even more absurd than the fables themselves. On one side, one discovered the infinite majesty, wisdom, and holiness of the Creator in the manner in which He governs His creatures, in the laws He gives them, and in the purpose for which He destines them. On the other, one saw nothing but humans who seemed to have been cast into the world at random, without knowledge of their origin, without social principles, without duties, without uniformity of customs and laws, and without certain concepts of what they were and what they were one day to become. On one side appeared the moving spectacle of the purest, most heroic virtue, which brings man as close to the Deity as possible; on the other, every eye was offended by the sight of the crudest vices and most shameful passions, which outraged all reason and degraded humanity to the level of beasts.

Among the pagans, there were people of every kind, just as there have always been and as there still are in the world today. Among them were found upright, honor-loving, enlightened [people]...

# Introduction.

<page-num>4</page-num>
<meta>Catchword: Al</meta>

[...persons whose] souls were receptive to truth, who lacked neither the insight to feel this truth, nor the courage to declare themselves for it, however great the sacrifice one had to make for it, and however great the danger might be that one ran in taking this step. On the other hand, there was among them the multitude who looked upon everything relating to religion with an indifferent eye, and in their conduct took the path marked out for them by a purely <term>human policy <note>original: *menschliche Politik* — in this context, it refers to worldly pragmatism or self-interest rather than government administration.</note></term>, which limits itself entirely to present goods and advantages: people who cared little for the duties of man toward God and for his relationship with the Supreme Being. Among these were many who did nothing but revel, piling vice upon vice, surrendering to the most shameful excesses, and were simply incapable of hearing the voice of reason, wisdom, and decency; excesses to which they surrendered without fear and without remorse, because the general tone—indeed, religion and the examples of the gods themselves—advocated for them. Finally, there was also a numerous class of people who called themselves philosophers and made it their duty to <term>rationalize <note>original: *vernünfteln* — a pejorative term for over-analyzing or using faulty logic to justify anything.</note></term> about everything and to dispute everything; who put presumption and pride in the place of reason and sound judgment, and in all their hatched-up systems of religion, <term>ethics <note>original: *Sittenlehren* — the study or teaching of moral conduct.</note></term>, politics, and government, brought nothing but absurd nonsense to the market. The description of this philosophical brood is found to be wonderfully and strikingly drawn in <term>Lucian’s <note>Lucian of Samosata (c. 125 – 180 AD) was a Syrian-Greek satirist known for poking fun at traditional mythology and the hypocrisy of philosophical schools.</note></term> dialogues and in most of the works of our Christian <term>apologists <note>original: *Schutzredner* — "defense-speakers"; early Christian writers who wrote formal defenses of their faith against Roman and Greek critics.</note></term>.

# Introduction.

Such was the state of the world when the Christian religion began to be proclaimed. This was the diverse mindset, these the customs of the nations and peoples that constituted the Roman Empire. Such were the temperaments of the people whom the preachers and defenders of the Christian religion had to contend with, instruct, and enlighten. From this, one can infer the boldness of the undertaking, the total transformation that had to be—and was intended to be—brought about in the world, the persecutions that were to be expected, and the obstacles of every kind that had to be overcome.

The first thing these new worshipers and disciples of Jesus Christ undertook was to tear away from the <term>pagans<note>original: *Heyden* — referring generally to the non-Christian, polytheistic inhabitants of the Roman Empire.</note></term> the unfortunate blindfold that veiled their eyes, and to hold before them that heavenly torch which illuminated the absurdities and the horrors of idolatry, as well as every insult offered to decency and nature by the licentiousness of their customs. Since they themselves had been born and raised in the pagan religion and were instructed in everything concerning idolatrous practices—possessing a full knowledge of <term>mythology<note>original: *Fabellehre* — literally "fable-lore," referring to the body of traditional stories regarding gods and heroes.</note></term> or pagan theology, knowing everything that occurred in the abominable <term>mysteries<note>original: *Geheimnissen* — refers to the "Mystery Cults" of antiquity (like those of Eleusis or Isis), which involved secret initiation rites.</note></term> of this religion into which they themselves had been initiated, and being familiar with all the excesses which these mysteries occasioned—they certainly had the advantage on their side in making the pagans feel how greatly reason was dishonored and humanity insulted by idolatry. How great was their superiority, since they borrowed from their own enemies the very weapons with which to combat them?

# Introduction.

<sig>A 4</sig>

<note>This page begins mid-word, completing "Ungereimtheit" from the previous page.</note> absurdity of the ridiculous fables upon which <term>paganism<note>original: *Heydenthum* — the polytheistic religious systems of the ancient world, particularly those of Greece and Rome.</note></term> is founded. We could cite a multitude of other writers who undertook the defense of the Christian religion. However, it is sufficient for us to have named a few whose primary intention was to clearly demonstrate to the pagans how greatly their principles and doctrines violated all reason and truth.

To this extensive and ever-victorious erudition and literacy, which astonished and dazzled the pagans, was added an invincible strength of <term>logical reasoning<note>original: *Vernunftschlüsse* — formal conclusions drawn through the application of logic.</note></term> against which nothing could be objected and which could not be resisted. <term>Tertullian’s Apology<note>original: *Tertullians Schutzschrift* — refers to the *Apologeticum* (c. 197 AD), one of the most famous defenses of Christianity, written to Roman governors to demand legal fairness for Christians.</note></term> can be regarded as an incomparable work, unique in its field. The writing style is concise, <term>vigorous<note>original: *nervig* — in this historical context, it means "sinewy" or "muscular," referring to a lean, powerful prose style.</note></term>, and powerful. The imagery within it is striking; often, a single expression creates a grand picture. It contains nearly as many thoughts as words, and as many vivid proofs as logical conclusions. The inner voice of conscience, the principles of true philosophy, and the judicial procedures prescribed by Roman law are the means used by Tertullian to tangibly prove to the Romans the shame of their errors and the injustice of their persecutions.

It is impossible to find a treatise written with more philosophy and order, or one that leads to conviction by such a natural path, than <term>Athenagoras’s<note>original: *Athenagoras* — a 2nd-century Christian philosopher from Athens who applied Platonism to Christian doctrine.</note></term> treatise on the resurrection of the

Justin, as is known, became a Christian around the thirtieth year of his life, and one is struck by the vast scope of his knowledge and his correct understanding of the prophetic books, even in those of his works which he published a short time after his conversion; such as, for example, his *Apology* addressed to the Emperor Antoninus, and his *Dialogue with Trypho the Jew*. A religion that came from heaven should be received with the deepest reverence and demanded the most perfect submission of the intellect. A religion that was to lead men to heaven and unite them with the deity required the greatest innocence of the soul and an untarnished purity of morals. One can judge this from the testimony which paganism gave them, albeit with entirely different intentions. **Pliny** <note>Pliny the Younger (c. 61–113 AD), a Roman governor whose correspondence with Emperor Trajan provides some of the earliest non-Christian accounts of the early Church.</note> in his letter to **Trajan** reports to this Emperor that, after the most precise and strictest investigations, it was found that the Christians vow in their assemblies to avoid all vices which run contrary to integrity and harmony, against good order, and peace in society, such as murder, adultery, faithlessness toward their commitments, slanders, and to fulfill every kind of duty precisely. Such was the concept formed in paganism of the moral purity and the virtues of the Christians.

And indeed, one can hardly imagine a more enchanting and striking spectacle than that which their entire conduct provided. Educated in the divine school of **Jesus Christ** <note>Original: J. This presentation of the Gospel principles by which the Christians lived, this beautiful portrait of their customs and virtues, was that very philosophy which our **apologists** <term>Schutzredner: literally "defense-speakers," referring to the early Christian writers who wrote "Apologies" to defend the faith against pagan accusations.</term> held up against pagan worldly wisdom. To this philosophy they invited the idolatrous world—a world blinded by its passions, its prejudices, and its religion. At their persuasion, people of all classes—great and small, rich and poor, learned and unlearned—accepted this philosophy. This beautiful century can rightly be called the century of enlightenment, of true wisdom, and reason. <note>The author is using "Enlightenment" (Aufklärung) here to describe the transformative power of early Christianity rather than the 18th-century intellectual movement.</note>

If the knowledge of the one true God was reserved for our times, should one really become jealous of that? Let us make use of the good that is offered to us. Would that one might set limits to superstition, abandon wicked idolatry, and embrace the true religion."

# Justin,

Despite his youth, he soon realized that this glittering exterior covered nothing but vanity and pride. For, when he questioned his teachers about the concept one should form of God, he soon discovered that they stammered over such an important question and knew nothing definite to say; indeed, in the end, they even dared to make the strange claim: "This knowledge is in no way necessary for man." His sincere soul and his natural reason revolted against this way of thinking and answering, and he made the resolution to take his leave of his first teachers and look around for those more enlightened.

The followers of *Aristotle*, or the *Peripatetics* <note>A school of philosophy characterized by the habit of walking about while lecturing or debating.</note>, had the reputation at that time of being the most perceptive of all philosophers. Among them, he chose a teacher who was meant to lead his thirst for truth onto the right path. But he was no luckier in his second choice than in his first. He soon discovered that this new teacher was nothing more than a great windbag and, moreover, the most self-interested creature, possessing none of those qualities that characterize a true philosopher. He therefore felt compelled to turn elsewhere to satisfy his needs.

At that time, there lived in Syria a follower of *Pythagoras* <note>A Greek philosopher famous for his theories on numbers, music, and the transmigration of souls.</note> who enjoyed a great reputation, and whose genius, science, and extensive knowledge were uncommonly praised. *Justin* paid him a visit and explained that his thirst for truth and his decided taste for genuine philosophy were the only motives for his visit, and that he would count himself happy if a man of such fame would accept him as a student. He was reasonably satisfied with his initial reception. Afterward, the philosopher asked him whether he was well-versed in geometry <note>Original: "Feldmeßkunst," literally the art of measuring fields.</note>, music, and astronomy: for these, he said,

# The Philosopher and Martyr.

...is absolutely necessary, in order to arrive at the knowledge of the Beautiful and the True, to raise the soul above sensible objects and make it receptive to grasping the beautiful ideal, and recognizing what true happiness consists of. He <note>Referring to the follower of Pythagoras mentioned on the previous page.</note> made a great deal of fuss about these various branches of knowledge and advised him to apply himself to them with all seriousness, promising to accept him among his disciples as soon as he had made the necessary progress. Justin did not find this proposal to his liking. The long time he would have had to devote to these sciences <note>The Pythagorean school required students to master music, astronomy, and geometry before they were permitted to study the nature of God.</note> deterred him, and he knew as little now as he did in the beginning what to hold to or what he should decide. But during this period of indecision, one of the most renowned philosophers from the school of **Plato** arrived in Naplouſe <note>Modern-day Nablus, the ancient city of Shechem.</note>.

Shortly after the arrival of this new teacher, Justin visited him. He was initially delighted by the concepts this man expressed regarding incorporeal, purely spiritual objects; he found pleasure in his company, listened untiringly to his teaching exercises, and even chose the teacher's house as his own residence. He flattered himself that he would soon attain true wisdom and the sublime knowledge of the Godhead; for that is the primary aim of **Platonic philosophy**.

With the intention of reaching this goal more quickly and pursuing his philosophical reflections more undisturbed, Justin decided, following his teacher's advice, to flee the bustle of social life and choose some wilderness for his residence, where nothing could distract his mind or hinder his meditation. He found such a place not far from the seashore which, it seemed to him, perfectly matched his intentions, plans, and taste; he describes it to us himself in his *Dialogue with Trypho* <note>original: "Unterredung mit Triphon." This refers to Justin's famous written work, *Dialogus cum Tryphone*, which recounts his search for truth and eventual conversion to Christianity.</note>.

### Justin,

One day, he says, when I was completely immersed in my favorite reflections, believing myself to be alone in my solitary retreat, and was thus wandering about at random, I saw a venerable old man <note>In his *Dialogue with Trypho*, Justin describes this encounter taking place by the sea, likely near Caesarea Maritima.</note> following me, whose gentle and serious facial expression betrayed the beauty of his soul and the true wisdom that sat enthroned in his heart. I turned around, stopped short, and fixed my gaze steadily upon him. Why do you look at me so attentively? the old man said to me; do you perhaps know me? No, was my answer; but it surprises me to see you in this place. I believed myself to be in a complete wilderness, and certainly did not expect to meet a human figure here. I am concerned about some friends, replied the old man, who have undertaken a journey together and whose return I await with longing: and with the intention of seeing whether I might discover anything that announces their return, I came here. But you, he continued, what are you doing in this desolate region? I enjoy wandering about in this solitude, I replied, where nothing disturbs me in my reflections, with which I nourish my spirit. These places, removed from all the world, are the most suitable residence for a man who earnestly wishes to develop his reason and perfect himself in the great art of thinking <note>The "art of thinking" or dialectics was a core discipline in ancient philosophy.</note>. You find, then, the old man interrupted, a primary taste for philosophy. But what is your main intention and your actual purpose therein? What goal have you chosen for yourself in this study? Do you perhaps pursue it more with the intention of shining before others through acuteness of mind and eloquence, than to better your own heart? Is it perhaps more important to you to have the ability to express yourself eloquently and appropriately on every subject, than to put into practice what the truth advises?

The old man pleased me: I found in his words something new, which was well-suited to arouse and sharpen the attention. What better thing can one do,

# The Philosopher and Martyr <note>The German term used here is *Blutzeuge*, which literally translates to "blood-witness," a poetic term for a martyr who testifies to their faith through death.</note>.

I replied that one seeks to prove that reason must be the only guide for man. With such a secure guide, one discovers without difficulty the errors of those who behave in a way that does not correspond to the intentions of the Supreme Being. There is found neither prudence nor wisdom in a man who is not a philosopher. True philosophy, which consists in the investigation and love of truth and virtue, is as essential to every human being as it is worthy of them. Everything else is lowly and contemptible, and every inclination that is not aroused and approved by philosophy is always reprehensible and constantly has unfortunate consequences.

"So philosophy, then, constitutes the happiness of man?" asked the old man. 

"Without a doubt," I returned immediately, "it alone can make us happy." 

Here, the clever old man piled question upon question. "What is this philosophy? What is the nature of that happiness to which it leads? What concepts do you form of the Deity?" 

"Philosophy," I answered, "is the science of being <note>original: *Wissenschaft des Wesens*. This refers to ontology, the philosophical study of the nature of existence or reality.</note> and the knowledge of truth. Happiness is the reward and the fruit of this science and knowledge. And God is the self-existent, immutable Being, and the primary cause of everything that exists outside of Him."

I soon noticed that the venerable old man found pleasure in my answers; but in order to lead me to the most perfect and sublime philosophy, he asked many more questions about the origin of humans, about the nature of the soul, about its immortality and freedom, about its fate after this life, and about the difference between humans and animals. I answered all these questions according to the principles I had found among the most esteemed philosophers, whom I deemed to be the most enlightened. Meanwhile, from time to time, I became troubled by his objections, and because of the questionable, unpleasant, and dangerous consequences that, as he pointed out, could be drawn from my answers,

## Representations, or Exhortation
## to the Greeks regarding the Investigation of Religion.

One of the first works that Justin composed was a very learned and pressing treatise, in which he undertakes the most important investigations into the pagan and Christian religions, and into those who can be considered the founders of these two religions.

After a very brief introduction, in which a soul reveals itself that is entirely feeling and love for the truth, Justin asks the pagans what kind of people they considered to be the founders of their religion? Whether it were the poets, or rather the philosophers: and then he depicts in the strongest colors all the inconsistencies, the horrors, and the abominations which the poets have displayed on this subject. He exposes the ridiculous nature of the theogony <term>theogony</term> <note>A term referring to the genealogical accounts of the origins and births of the gods, most famously those written by Hesiod.</note> of Homer and Hesiod, and makes sport of the mad fairy tales which the adventurous imagination of these two poets has hatched regarding the origin of the gods whom the Greeks and Romans worshiped. The fragments that he extracts from their poems are the clearest proofs of what he asserts. **For,** says Justin to the pagans, **if you believe what these two renowned poets have written, you must necessarily confess that either your gods are really constituted as these writers depict them, or they are no gods at all.** From this he concludes that a religion based on the authority of such teachers is absurd in the highest degree.

Afterward he comes to the philosophers, whose authority he invalidates in the same manner. He lets them all pass through review <note>The author uses the military term *Musterung* (inspection/review) to describe Justin's systematic critique of each philosophical school.</note>, from Thales the Milesian <note>Thales of Miletus (c. 624–546 BC), often regarded as the first philosopher in the Greek tradition.</note> to Empedocles. He shows that not a single one

But, if your poets and philosophers cannot teach you the true principles of religion, Justin continues, to whom must you then turn to receive the necessary instruction on such important matters? I say, to the prophets, whom the Deity itself immediately inspired and instructed. He then provides the most magnificent description of these men. He places Moses <note>original: Moyses</note> at their head and cites the testimony given to their admirable talents and insights by the greatest writers of paganism <term>paganism</term> <note>In this context, it refers to the non-Christian, polytheistic world of the Greeks and Romans.</note>. He shows that this Moses wrote long before the art of writing was even known among the Greeks; that his teaching was not foreign to the Egyptians; and that from these Egyptians, several Greek poets and philosophers borrowed a multitude of concepts which have much similarity with those found in the books of Moses. He cites several examples of this from Pythagoras, Plato, Orpheus, Sophocles, and even from Homer, the pagans' most esteemed poet.

Afterward, he shows that all the prophets after Moses taught exactly the same truths, presented the same principles, and bore witness to the same religion. In conclusion, he says to the pagans: No other choice remains for you but to confess that the only certain way to instruct yourselves, and to recognize the Supreme Being and the true religion with dignity, is through the writings of the prophets, these men inspired by God.

# The First Apology to the Emperor Marcus Aurelius.

If any work ever deserved to be regarded as a masterpiece of wisdom, strength, the art of demonstration, and the fearlessness to speak and defend the truth, it is surely Justin’s defense speech <note>Justin’s "First Apology" is one of the most important early Christian texts, written to explain and defend the faith to the Roman authorities.</note> to the Emperor Marcus Aurelius <note>original: Mark-Antonin</note>. This monarch was considered the wisest prince who ever sat upon a throne. He was a lord of the most blameless character and fulfilled all the duties of a regent with the most conscientious punctuality. He ruled through virtue alone, and it was this virtue which, during twenty-three full years of his reign, inspired all subjects of this immense monarchy with the most vivid feelings of admiration, obedience, gratitude, and love toward such a good master. Like Rome itself, foreign nations and kings also held the most unbounded respect for him; they often brought the disputes that arose among them before his throne and left them to his decision, so that every day of his reign was a day of peace, harmony, and tranquility for the whole world. This admirable virtue and goodness of heart earned him the surname *Pius* <note>While the text refers to Marcus Aurelius here, the title "Pius" specifically belonged to his predecessor, Antoninus Pius; Marcus was his adopted son and successor.</note>: for this Latin word denotes a person of a sensitive, tender, and good-natured soul.

Emperor Hadrian <note>original: Adrian</note>, his predecessor, being childless, initially adopted Lucius Ceionius <note>original: Leionius</note> Commodus Verus as a son, whom he also designated as his successor and had proclaimed as Caesar under the name Aelius <note>original: Oelius</note> Verus. But since this prince died shortly thereafter, he transferred all these privileges to Arrius Antoninus <note>Known to history as Antoninus Pius.</note>, on the condition that he adopt as children the son of the deceased prince, Lucius Annius Verus, and Marcus Aurelius Antoninus, who also called himself *Verissimus* <note>A play on his name "Verus," meaning "most true" or "most genuine."</note> and had married Faustina <note>original: Faustine</note>, Antoninus’s daughter...

This is what you are praised for throughout the entire empire, as you yourselves know. But is the pure truth actually spoken in this regard? The outcome must prove it. We do not appear before you in the spirit of flattery, nor to beg for your favor; rather, we demand of you that you speak in our cause according to the dictates of unbiased reason. We wish to prevent you from being carried away—whether by the prejudices of courtiers, or by a desire to please superstitious people, or by haste, or by the fanatical outcry that has been heard for a long time—into passing a judgment that would make you yourselves punishable. You can indeed kill us, but you cannot harm us. We speak to you in this way with good reason. We implore your love of equity to conduct judicial investigations. If the vices of which the Christians are accused can be proven, then fine, let us be punished with all severity; but if no proof can be produced, how can you allow innocence to be murdered without becoming criminals yourselves and dishonoring yourselves?

To speak in such a tone to the masters of the entire world testifies to a greatness of soul that can never be admired enough, and to which religion alone can elevate a person.

## Second Apology

### of the Christian Religion to Rome's Senate and the Roman People.

First of all, we believe we must inform the reader about the occasion of this <term>apology (German: Schutzschrift)</term>, <note>In this context, an "apology" is not an admission of guilt, but a formal legal defense of one's faith.</note> for which purpose we set down here what Justin himself reports about it. A pagan lady had for a long time led a more dissolute life. She followed the example of her husband, who was himself a great profligate. After a Christian priest named Ptolemaeus converted her and drew her away from her excesses, she attempted to play the apostle to her husband and bring him also to better ways. When she did not succeed, she insisted on the right granted to her by Roman law and wished to be divorced. But the man accused her of her faith in court, and also denounced the one who had converted her, thereby instigating a kind of persecution in which several Christians were martyred. — This apology of Saint Justin begins thus:

> What has just happened in Rome under the Prefect Urbicius, and happens daily throughout the entire empire, places me under the necessity of stepping forward with this apology for the rescue of innocent people, who run the risk daily of experiencing a similar fate, although they are human beings like you; which you, however, blinded by new rank and your positions of honor, will hardly admit—indeed, to all appearances, do not want to know.

He then relates in detail the whole incident with the converted lady, and the many death sentences that resulted from it.

This entire writing is mainly concerned with the refutation of two accusations with which the pagans <term>heathens (German: Heyden)</term> were constantly taunting the conduct, the doctrines, and the customs of the Christians. First, they said: "If you are so eager for union with your God, why do you not take your own lives and leave us in peace?" Second: "If you were truly dear and precious to your God, and if he protected you as you want to make us believe, then he could not look on so calmly as you are mangled, tortured, and killed every day."

To answer the first fallacy, Justin shows that the worshipful providence <note>original: "anbethungswürdige Fügung"</note> of the Creator, the order and wisdom of foresight, and even the benefits of the persecutors do not allow Christians to lay hands on themselves. He deals with this point briefly, but with all fire and emphasis.

The answer to the second accusation turned out to be much more extensive. First, Justin explains how the Creator of this world created everything for the sake of man and subjected it to his power. Afterwards, he says, God appointed the angels as guardian spirits <term>protective spirits (German: Schutzgeister)</term> for mankind and for most of the creatures that are under the heavens. Then he explains how a portion of these angels had slipped from the path that the Creator had prescribed for them before the fall of man. He expresses himself quite correctly on this according to the principles of faith and appropriately cites what the ancient poets and philosophers said about good and evil geniuses <note>In this historical context, "geniuses" refers to "genii," or intermediary spirits between gods and humans.</note> and spirits, in which partly consists the basis of the mythologies <term>teachings of the gods (German: Götterlehren)</term> and the pagan edifice of faith. ## Treatise
### on the Unity of God, or on Monarchy.

## D i a l o g u e
### of Saint Justin with the Jew Tryphon.

The title of this work is not based merely on an arbitrary idea or the choice of the author, but on an actual fact and those conversations which Saint Justin held for two consecutive days with several Jews, at whose head was Tryphon, the leader of the synagogue of Antioch. This writing is the strongest, most illuminating, and most deeply reasoned proof that has perhaps ever been offered for the accomplished arrival of the Messiah, for the divinity of his religion, and the fulfillment of the prophecies in the person of J.C. <note>An abbreviation for Jesus Christ.</note>. Everything is decided by the authority of the holy books, because this was the only means of conviction that could be used against the Jews. The head of the synagogue was an honor-loving, insightful, and rational man, though extremely prejudiced against the Christians. C.* <note>Jesus Christ</note> brought from heaven to earth. This passage is followed by a touching portrait of the new Church and the rejection of the Synagogue <note>In this context, "Synagogue" refers to the established Jewish religious community of the time</note>.

When Justin mentions the appearances of the Lord <note>These divine appearances are often called "theophanies" in theology.</note> with which Abraham, Jacob, Moses, Joshua, and others were favored, he adopts as a fundamental principle in most cases that the one who is designated in these passages by the name of the Lord was the Word <note>The *Logos* or the pre-existent Christ.</note>, the eternal Wisdom, the Son of God. # The Philosopher and Martyr.

the way the Passover lamb was treated is the most striking prototype <note>In theology, a "type" or prototype is an Old Testament event or object seen as prefiguring something in the life of Christ.</note> of the position of <term>J. C. <note>Jesus Christ</note></term>, this true divine Lamb, on the cross. For, when it was roasted, the hind legs had to be stretched out next to each other, like on the body of a hanging person; the front legs, however, were stretched out like the arms of a crucified man, and in this position on a small roasting spit, which ran across the large one horizontally, just as the cross-bar on a cross runs across the main beam. This anecdote must be dear and precious to Christians.

III. The Jew Tryphon said to Justin: Everything that the Christians believed regarding Jesus’s miraculous birth and resurrection could well be placed in the same category as the myths that the heathen poets presented about **Perseus**, **Bacchus**, **Aesculapius** <note>Perseus was a hero of Greek myth; Bacchus (Dionysus) was the god of wine; Aesculapius was the god of medicine. Tryphon is suggesting Christian stories are just more Greco-Roman mythology.</note>, and so forth. Justin answers this objection with a triumphant superiority. First, he shows him that everything the Christians say on this subject was already announced in the divine Scripture and foretold by the prophets. Then he asserts that the devils—those enemies of God and man—recognized much of what was prophesied through the prophets and, in order to deceive men and weaken the deep impression that the mysteries of a divine Redeemer were bound to make, they spread a multitude of lies which bore some similarity to these adorable mysteries. This proof is not exactly self-evident; but it has much probability and credibility, and fits perfectly well with what the holy books tell us about the cunning of the devil.

IV. From the beginning of this conversation to the end, that distinctive character stands out among the Jews which they have maintained ever since the death of Jesus: 1) Resorting to noise, mockery, and malicious attacks when they enter the arena of debate against Christians. 2) An irreconcilable hatred and an abhorrence of them—

For him, nothing in the mysteries seems hidden or dark. ### Tatian.

Even if we were to judge Tatian solely by the single work that antiquity has preserved for us, we would nonetheless classify him among the finest minds of the second century without hesitation. A strong and fiery imagination, a penetrating spirit that searched tirelessly and tracked down the truth, and immense erudition—these are the merits perceived in his *Address to the Greeks* <note>original: "Rede an die Griechen," historically known by its Latin title, *Oratio ad Graecos*</note>, in which he exposes the absurdities, indecency, and ridicule of the worship they offer to their alleged deities. 

His discourse is composed in a concise writing style, richly layered with bold thoughts that occasionally border on the bombastic, yet remain charming and significant, and are sometimes seasoned with biting wit. It contains depictions of characters, portrayals of manners, and such powerful expressions that they do honor to the author's spirit. Since he had stuffed his head with all the systems of the Greek philosophers in his youth, it should not surprise us that he goes astray when he ventures to explain the nature of the soul. Aside from this, his introductory discourse to the Greeks is very beautiful and instructive.

This great writer was born in Assyria around the beginning of the second century. Since he had been born into paganism, he restricted himself to the study of purely pagan sciences. He dedicated himself entirely to philosophy and the fine arts, and indeed with such success that he was appointed as a teacher of <term>eloquence <note>The art of persuasive speaking and writing, a core subject of classical education known as rhetoric.</note></term> while still very young. In this—

In this position, his talents showed themselves in the most advantageous light, as Eusebius of Caesarea <note>A 4th-century scholar often called the "Father of Church History" for his records of the early Christian era.</note> vouches for, and all of Asia admired him. After he had held this post for several years, he traveled—as he himself reports—through a large part of the inhabited world, without his zeal for the sciences and fine arts cooling; he loved these subjects passionately and practiced them even during his travels, until he finally arrived in the capital of the world <note>Rome</note>.

Since he possessed a steady and resolute character that sought nothing but the truth, and since his sensibilities—which were tuned only toward greatness—were revolted by everything that was hollow and groundless, he soon became aware of the pride that prevailed among the Romans and grew to loathe it. Thereupon he engaged with the philosophers: but when he saw that they were nothing more than cold word-mongers <note>The German "Wortkrämer" suggests someone who haggles over words without regard for their meaning or truth.</note> who could never agree on anything, he abandoned these unbearable people as well, and finally made the acquaintance of Saint Justin, who was indeed also a philosopher, but at the same time a Christian. Charmed by the gentleness of his manners, the wisdom of his principles, and the scope of his insights, he attached himself to him with his whole soul.

It did not cost Saint Justin much effort to make the absurdity of idolatry <note>The worship of physical idols or pagan deities.</note> understandable to the new pupil. He initially showed him the full wisdom of the moral teachings and the complete sublimity of the tenets of the Gospel, and advised him to instruct himself and to read the Holy Scriptures thoughtfully. "I read them, these divine books," Tatian says to the Greeks and other pagan nations, "with all zeal and an insatiable desire; and I soon recognized that they are much older than anything the Greeks ever wrote, and are incomparably more venerable and sublime when one notices all the errors with which the writings of the Greeks teem. Some time after Justin's death, Tatian moved to Asia, where he wrote several works that have not come down to us. It seems he lost much through the death of his teacher: for after that time, he fell into many errors and became the head of the Encratites, or the "Abstinent," <note>The Encratites were an early Christian ascetic sect that practiced "encraty" (self-control), which involved renouncing marriage and abstaining from meat and wine.</note> which heretics pushed the evangelical counsels <term>Evangelical counsels: In Christian tradition, these are the "counsels of perfection"—poverty, chastity, and obedience—which are recommended for spiritual growth but not strictly commanded as laws for all believers.</term> to an immoderate severity, and wished to bind all people to their observation as if they were commandments. The impetuous heat of an all too inquisitive and presumptuous genius has been the cliff upon which the finest talents have run aground. The time of his death is not precisely known. The structure of our work requires us to provide a short extract of his *Address to the Greeks*, from which one will be able to judge his genius.

## Tatian’s Oration

### to the Greeks regarding Religion.

<margin>Nonnotte’s *The Philosophers*.</margin> <note>original: "Nonnottens Philosophen." Likely a reference to the work of Claude-Adrien Nonnotte, a French Jesuit who wrote critiques of Enlightenment philosophy and early church history.</note>
In this oration, Tatian intends to show the Greeks—that is, all idolaters—how far the Christian religion surpasses all of theirs: 1. because of the antiquity of the documents <note>Tatian argued that Moses and the prophets were much older than the Greek philosophers and poets like Homer.</note> upon which it is founded; 2. because of the sublime concepts it provides concerning the Deity; 3. because of the purity of the moral teachings it preaches and teaches its students to practice. The manner in which he treats his subject is fiery, the contrast between Christianity and paganism is striking, and the style of writing is lively, concise, and very often seasoned with biting salt <note>A rhetorical term (akin to "Attic salt") referring to sharp, refined wit or sarcasm used to expose folly.</note>. One can clearly see from the work that the orator does not anxiously hunt for words and expressions, but rather occupies himself entirely with the subject matter, without this negligence harming the power of the presentation.

# Tatian.

Without the rhetorical flourishes of a methodical introduction and delivery, he immediately takes his subject in hand. You express, he says, nothing but aversion toward those you call *Barbarians*; and yet you are jealous of all their inventions. Is that fair? Have you not drawn all your knowledge from these people? The *Babylonians* also taught astronomy, the *Persians* the science of hidden natural forces, the *Phoenicians* writing, *Orpheus* music, and so forth. In the name of heaven! Cease at last to pass yourselves off as the inventors of the arts, which you have merely borrowed from others. You are proud of your melodious and harmonious language. You praise yourselves without waiting to see if perhaps foreigners might wish to take this trouble upon themselves, as would be fitting if you were wise. Then he takes on the most famous philosophers of the *Greeks*, and deals each his small share of criticism <note>original: "Scherfchen." Literally a "mite" or small coin; here used idiomatically to mean he gives each philosopher a small, cutting piece of his mind.</note>. He censures without mercy either the missteps of their conduct or the errors of their writings, and draws the conclusion that they are all worthless and deserve all the less consideration because they agree with each other in no point, but are always jealous of one another, and reveal pride and vanity on every occasion.

Now he prepares to show the great superiority of the Christian religion over Paganism.
> “*Greeks*! (he says) why are you so ill-disposed toward our principles? Why do you persecute us if we do not accept yours, as if we were the most godless villains? We observe every social duty; we fear and worship the only God, and if one were to force me to renounce Him, I would never obey, and would rather choose death than make myself guilty of faithlessness and ingratitude toward Him.”

After this courageous declaration, he establishes the most sublime concept of the Christian God. He describes Him as the Creator of this world and the Judge of all men

# Tatian.

...after the resurrection. You mock the resurrection, he writes, but on what do you base your mockery? I knew nothing of myself before my birth: for I was nothing, and belonged merely among the possibilities <note>original: "möglichen Dinge," referring to the philosophical concept of things that have the potential to exist but do not yet have being</note>. But now I, who once was not, know through my very existence that I am now. After my death, I shall once again be no more; but I shall receive my existence again in due time and appear anew. And though fire may have destroyed this body of mine, or water dissolved it, or worms consumed it, the matter still exists, scattered and dispersed throughout the world: the Almighty shall come, and—even if the godless refuse to believe this truth—He shall restore it.

The judgment, which he proclaims on behalf of the Creator following the resurrection, he bases on the concept we form of God’s justice and of human freedom. The Divine Word <term>Logos: the Word or Reason of God, which Tatian identifies as the intermediary in creation and the source of moral law</term>, Tatian writes when he comes to speak of freedom, knows everything that occurs among His creatures—not according to the determination of blind fate, nor out of the compulsion of some necessity, but what they will do out of free choice. This Divine Word has forbidden vice to them and held out the glorious reward of virtue. On this occasion, he mocks the foolish doctrine of fate, which rules over both men and gods with its iron scepter. From this, he takes the opportunity to season his jokes about these gods with as much salt <note>A reference to "Attic salt," a common term for sharp, refined wit or satire</note> as the whimsical Lucian <note>Lucian of Samosata, a contemporary 2nd-century Greek satirist known for his biting humor and skepticism toward traditional religion</note> ever used in his dialogues, in order to prove that nothing so outrages reason and common sense as these absurd doctrines. Our own evil will, he says, is the cause of our ruin; the works of God are good; the human heart has hatched vice.

A philosophical reference to 'possibilia'—things that have the potential to exist but do not yet have being.</note>. Now, however, I know—I who once was not—through my existence itself, that I am now. After my death I will again not be; but I will receive my existence back in its time and appear anew. And though fire may have destroyed this body of mine, or water dissolved it, or worms consumed it, the matter still remains scattered and dispersed throughout the world: the Almighty will come and—even if the godless refuse to believe this truth—restore it.

The judgment, which he proclaims from the perspective of the Creator after the resurrection, he bases on the concepts we form of God's justice and of human freedom. The divine Word <note>The "Logos."</note>, Tatian writes, when he comes to speak of freedom, knows everything that happens among His creatures, or what they will do—not by the determination of blind fate, nor out of the compulsion of any necessity, but out of free choice. This divine Word has forbidden them vice and held out the glorious reward of virtue. On this occasion, he mocks the stupid system of Fate, which rules over men and gods with its iron scepter. 

From this he takes the opportunity to season his jesting about these gods with as much salt <note>original: "mit so viel Salz zu würzen." This refers to "Attic salt," a classical term for refined, sharp wit.</note> as the moody Lucian <note>Lucian of Samosata (c. 125 – 180 AD), a contemporary of Tatian and a famous satirist who ridiculed traditional religion and philosophy.</note> ever used in his dialogues, in order to prove that nothing so outrages reason and common sense as these absurd systems. Our own evil will, he says, is the cause of our ruin; the works of God are good; the human heart has hatched the vice.

### Tatian. 84

But how did the seed of vice enter the human heart? Through the malice and envy of the devils <note>Tatian refers to these as demons—beings who were originally created good but fell from grace.</note>, who rebelled against God out of pride. They were cast out of heaven, and since that time, they have sought in every way to draw humanity into their rebellion. The manner in which Tatian explains the influence of the devils on human senses is quite ingenious, although the principle upon which he builds his doctrine—or the idea he gives regarding the nature of the devil and the human soul—is not acceptable <note>The author likely finds Tatian's Gnostic-leaning or overly-ascetic views on the soul to be heterodox or illogical by the standards of the 18th century.</note>.

Tatian identifies this influence of the devils upon man as the source of all the disorders and errors into which the human race has fallen. Consequently, he presents the most vivid picture of the slippery and debauched theatrical plays of the heathens; he mocks the eternal bickering and mutual contradictions of their philosophers—whom they nevertheless held to be their infallible teachers and arbiters—and he palpably exposes the ridiculousness of the adventurous tales they tell of their gods.

# Athenagoras.

It might seem very striking at first glance that not a single ancient record provides us with information about Athenagoras, this great man; but this will soon no longer surprise us if we take into account the irreplaceable loss that the Church suffered to its most precious historical records through the persecutions, and later through the invasions of barbarian peoples into every land of the Roman Empire. We therefore have no knowledge of Athenagoras other than what the titles of his works provide us. By means of these, we know that he was a native of Athens and was a Christian philosopher who lived in the second century.

We can, therefore, provide no historical account of him. However, in his *Defense of the Christians* <note>original: "Schutzschrift." This refers to his *Legatio pro Christianis* (Embassy for the Christians), a formal appeal for justice.</note> addressed to the Emperor Marcus Aurelius <note>Marcus Aurelius (reigned 161–180 AD) was a Stoic philosopher and Roman Emperor; Athenagoras addressed him as a fellow philosopher to argue for the legal rights of Christians.</note>, and in his treatise *On the Resurrection of the Dead*, one finds the most unmistakable features of a truly beautiful and great soul. These writings of his are the most undeniable proof of the vast extent of his knowledge and insights, his immense reading, brilliant eloquence, sharp-witted mind, and a wealth of the most fortunate talents. But we do not wish to get ahead of our readers; rather, we shall let them judge for themselves from the brief excerpt we are about to provide from these two excellent writings.

To the accusation made against the Christians—that they refuse to worship those gods to whom sacrifices are offered in various cities of the empire—he responds in a way that is as simple as it is decisive. He shows that these cities themselves do not worship all the gods of other places, without this omission being held against them as a crime, and he goes into quite entertaining detail on this point. In regard to the most famous statues, of which the pagans <note>original: "Heyden"</note> made the most fuss, he boldly says that they have no other merit than that which the artist's skillful chisel has given them. But just as the material worked by the sculptor is far inferior to the sculptor himself, so too is the Creator of this universe infinitely exalted above the creatures He has drawn forth from nothing, and consequently, our worship is infinitely more worthy. Finally: how long have these gods and statues even existed? Look up *Herodotus* <note>An ancient Greek historian known as the "Father of History."</note>; he will tell you that this era falls within the times of *Homer* and *Hesiod* <note>The most famous epic poets of ancient Greece.</note>, who lived barely four hundred years before *Herodotus*.

To further pursue the errors of idolatry <note>original: "Abgötterey," the worship of idols.</note>, *Athenagoras* cleverly cites everything that mythology says about the birth of the gods, and thereby makes the indecency and absurdity of this religious structure even more palpable. ## Treatise
### on the Resurrection of the Dead.

In no philosophical writing does one find as much order and method, nor such clear and indisputable principles, as in Athenagoras’s treatise <note>original: "Traktate"</note> on the resurrection of the dead. He establishes such propositions and truths as their foundation that one cannot refuse them one's approval; he then draws conclusions which follow visibly from these propositions:

flow from one another; and thus he proceeds from conclusion to conclusion, until he finally arrives at demonstrations <note>In this context, these are logical proofs that aim for mathematical certainty.</note> against which neither the profligate nor the unbeliever can find further objection.

After he has described, with a rare clarity and precision, the path one must choose to present the truth and win its approval—as well as that disposition of the heart and mind which might hinder truth’s victory—he sets out to prove, first: that the resurrection of the dead is not an impossible thing; and to this end, he removes all difficulties that might be raised against it. Second: “that even the concepts we form of the wisdom and justice of God, and our knowledge of human nature, compel our assent to this truth.”

“To demonstrate the impossibility of the resurrection,” speaks Athenagoras, “one would have to show that the Creator lacks either the will or the power to restore, one day, a body that has been destroyed and dissolved into its component parts. If this cannot be proven, then one must necessarily renounce an opinion that would be nothing more than a sign of godless unbelief or a hateful blasphemy. Now, however, one will certainly not be able to provide sufficient grounds for either of these propositions.

For firstly, the Creator does not lack the necessary power to reawaken dissolved and destroyed bodies. For this inability could only stem from a lack of insight—that He did not know how the matter was to be approached—or from a deficiency of power, such that He could not effect what He knows. To be certain that God does not will a thing, one would have to show that such a thing is either unjust by its nature or unworthy of God. Let us examine these two points in regard to the resurrection.

Should any injustice be involved in it, it could only affect the one being awakened, or those who are incapable of being awakened—a class consisting of pure spirits <note>referring to angels or celestial beings</note> and irrational animals. Regarding the former, no injustice takes place because the resurrection of humans has no bearing on their status or their happiness. The animals, however, vanish and are completely destroyed after their death. Just as little can an injustice against the resurrected human be found, as neither the rights of the soul nor those of the body are violated by the resurrection. Not the rights of the soul; for if they are not currently violated through union with a **corruptible** <term>verweslich; subject to decay or rot</term> body, then an impairment is even less conceivable once this body has become **incorruptible**. And what has the body to complain about, which through the resurrection participates in the immortality of the soul?

The concept of resurrection, therefore, includes no injustice within itself, and just as little does it contain anything that would be unworthy of God. For if God was able to produce corruptible and mortal creatures without violating His honor, He will be all the more able to make them immortal and incorruptible without detriment to that honor.

In conclusion, he says that everything we see in nature—elements, plants, and animals—each has its own specific and particular end purpose <term>Endzweck: The final cause or "teleological" goal for which a thing is created.</term>. Man, equipped with reason and understanding, was created for a noble and perfect purpose. This purpose, as we have proven, cannot be reached: it does not exist even after the separation of the soul from the body, because man then no longer exists <note>Athenagoras emphasizes that a "human" is strictly the union of body and soul; a soul without a body is not a complete human being.</note>. Consequently, these two parts must be reunited again; and

Thus, the resurrection is a necessary consequence of the wisdom of the Creator.

The resurrection, accordingly, enlightens us regarding the true final purpose <term>Endzweck: The ultimate goal or destiny for which humanity was created</term> of man. This final purpose is to adhere unswervingly to what uncorrupted reason prescribes, to occupy ourselves with the knowledge of the Supreme Being, to obey the laws which His divine wisdom has given us, and to comfort ourselves with the reward which He has promised us and reserved for eternity. Carried away by a taste for the present <note>original: "dem Geschmacke für das Gegenwärtige" — referring to a preference for temporal, worldly affairs over spiritual ones.</note>, most people find no pleasure in this sublime knowledge. But the error of a blind multitude does not nullify these sacred duties: for evil as well as good works must be examined and, in a subsequent judgment, punished or rewarded. Thus, the doctrine of the resurrection of the dead is a clearly proven truth.

# Theophilus of Antioch.

Theophilus of Antioch was born approximately one hundred years after the death of Jesus. This becomes clear from one of his final works, which contains a chronology <term>Zeitrechnung: A system or record for calculating and ordering historical events in time</term> extending to the final years of the reign of Marcus Aurelius <note>Marcus Aurelius was Roman Emperor from 161 to 180 AD; this suggests Theophilus was writing in the late 2nd century.</note>. Without doubt, he was a pagan by birth; for he himself confesses that the doctrine of the resurrection of the dead did not appeal to him for a long time, until he was finally convinced of this truth through the books of the Prophets <note>original: "Propheten"—referring to the Old Testament scriptures.</note>. It appears he was exceptionally well-versed in chronology, history, the writings of the poets, and the philosophical systems, whose contradictions he frequently critiques. He composed a great work on chronology and later published an excerpt of it, as he himself reports to us in his books to Autolycus. His style of writing is clear and distinct, his method of presenting evidence is triumphant, and the descriptions with which he seasons his writings are lively and striking. Of all his works—the list of which can be found in Eusebius of Caesarea <note>Eusebius (c. 260–339 AD) was a historian who recorded the titles of many early Christian writings that are now lost.</note>—none have come down to us except for the three books addressed to Autolycus. This Autolycus was a learned pagan and a bosom friend of Theophilus, who lived constantly in libraries and among books; yet, he was extremely prejudiced against the Christian religion.

The work which Theophilus dedicated to him is an examination of Christian and pagan religions—or better stated, a comparison of both—and consists of three books.

# Theophilus of Antioch.

In the first book, Theophilus demonstrates how noble and sublime the concepts are which the Christians maintain concerning the Godhead, and how far their value outweighs those notions that the heathens <note>original: "Heyden"—referring to practitioners of traditional Roman and Greek religion.</note> form of their own gods.

In the second, he quite tangibly exposes all the absurd and contradictory nonsense that the poets and philosophers have dreamed up regarding the origin of the world and the genealogy of the gods; whereupon he reveals the Creator, who, through the power of His essence-rich Word <note>original: "wesenreichen Wortes"—referring to the *Logos*, the divine reason or Word of God through which the world was created.</note>, commanded nothingness to bring forth life. His portrayal of creation is most magnificent and charming, and after he has depicted the omnipotence of the Lord in the work of the six days, he describes His wisdom in the religion He has revealed to humanity.

In the third book, he explains to Autolycus that his decided preference for fables and his relentless focus on reading the poets and philosophers are the greatest obstacles to his recognition of the truth. Indeed, for this very reason, says Theophilus, Autolycus himself considers the books of the Christians to be mere fantasies and tales which had only spread within the last few centuries. To open his friend's eyes, he repeats—in a brief, lively, and pithy overview—everything contained in the first two books. He depicts the errors, the instability, the contradictions, and the squabbles <note>original: "Balgereyen"—implying undignified fighting or petty brawling among various philosophical schools.</note> of the philosophers, contrasting them with the consistency of Moses, the prophets, and other holy writers, the purity and holiness of their moral teachings, their grand and worthy concepts of the Godhead, and their venerable and undeniable antiquity <note>original: "Alterthum"—a key argument in early Christian apologetics was that the Hebrew scriptures predated Greek philosophy and were therefore more authoritative.</note>.

I will not analyze these three books more minutely, but merely highlight a few passages and thoughts,

### Summary of the First Book.

After a very brief introduction, Theophilus says to his friend: “You are quite proud and high-minded regarding the gods you worship, looking down pityingly on me for being a Christian—indeed, for even boasting of being a Christian—and you say mockingly to me: 'So let me see your God for once; show me what He looks like.' And I say to you: Show first by your character and morals <note>original: "Gesinnungen und Sitten"—referring to one's internal disposition and external behavior.</note> that you are a human being; and immediately you shall see what my God is. Are the eyes of your spirit <note>original: "Geistes"—in this context, it refers to the mind or the intellectual soul capable of perceiving divine truth.</note> capable of seeing? Are the ears of your heart capable of hearing? God reveals Himself only to those who have the eyes of the spirit open. All people indeed have eyes; but in some, they are so weak and corrupt that they cannot even see the sun. Must the blind man blame the lack of sight on the rays of this celestial body, or rather on his own blindness? One must take care that the excesses of the heart do not blind the soul. You demand that I show you the God whom I worship. Strive first for the knowledge of Him yourself. I must first know whether you are not a slave to gluttony <term>Schwelgerey: excessive indulgence in food and drink</term>, to injustice, to lust, to pride, to envy <term>Scheelsucht: an archaic term literally meaning "squint-sickness," referring to jealousy or looking askance at the success of others</term>, or to greed: I must know whether you are not, as so many others are, violent, slanderous, and wicked. If these passions blind you, then you cannot see God: diseased eyes cannot endure the brilliance of this light, and a heart which is a servant to malice and godlessness cannot recognize God.”

"But you," Autolycus replies, "you certainly recognize Him; tell me then, who and what He is."

Now Theophilus presents the most magnificent and sublime concepts of God. He describes all divine perfections in a truly admirable manner; his entire discourse is richly interspersed with wise observations, ingenious thoughts, and evocative imagery. "This is how my God is constituted," he says, "this is the appearance of the Creator of this universe." Through Him you live, through Him you breathe; He grants you intellect and speech, and if you do not know Him, you must attribute it to the blindness of your mind and the excesses of your heart.

Since the great attributes of God are purely spiritual, Theophilus takes the most natural and clever approach to make them somewhat tangible. "Is not the soul within our body also invisible?" he asks; yet we recognize its existence through the activity it imparts to the body. In the same way, while God cannot be seen with physical eyes, one discovers Him in the greatness and splendor of His works, and in the wisdom and omnipotence with which He governs this world. He illustrates and develops this beautiful idea through a variety of appropriate and striking analogies <note>original: "Gleichnisse"—referring here to parables or illustrative comparisons used to explain the divine.</note>.

Following the magnificent portrait he has painted of God's glorious attributes, another follows—though shorter, it stands out distinctly. He paints "in miniature," yet with the most vivid colors, the stories told about the gods of paganism <note>original: "Heydenthumes"—Heathenism or Paganism.</note>; he exposes the total indecency and absurdity of these fables, showing how greatly they offend both modesty and reason. "Under such circumstances," Theophilus continues, "I would rather honor the Emperor than your gods; but as for worshipping him as you do—no, I would never do that. I worship only God, whom I alone adore."

# Excerpt of the Third Book.

## Theophilus’s Greeting to Autolycus.

You still maintain, despite everything that has been said in our previous conversations, that those venerable truths with which I entertained you are nothing but tall tales <note>original: "Aufschneidereyen," implying boastful exaggerations or fabrications.</note>, and that the books whose antiquity we praised are nothing more than modern inventions. To completely rid you of this delusion, I wish to enlighten you regarding the time when they were composed. From this, you will be able to judge their age for yourself and see how little stock one should put in the writings of your philosophers and poets, of whom you make such a great fuss. But first, allow me to express my astonishment that a man like you—of unbounded curiosity, to whom every branch of knowledge is welcome, and who keeps watch through entire nights in libraries—shows nothing but frosty indifference toward our writings.

Always maintaining the tone of respect that a man of such extensive knowledge deserves, Theophilus asks his friend what he actually thinks of all the nonsense that the poets and philosophers have written concerning the deity, religion, and morality. With great emphasis and precision, he exposes the various errors into which they have fallen, and contrasts them with the holiness and purity of Christian doctrines. "We, for our part," he says, "recognize a single God and Creator of the world; we acknowledge a Providence <note>original: "Vorsicht," a common eighteenth-century German term for Divine Providence or "Providentia."</note> and profess a holy law which God Himself has given." Thereupon, he cites the Ten Commandments, just as the Lord handed them over to Moses and as Moses communicated them to the Hebrews; he provides an excerpt of the history of this people and the diverse instruction they received from the prophets, and concludes with the most sublime and perfect teaching, which the Son of God Himself presented to mankind.

## Clement of Alexandria.

**Titus Flavius Clemens** was an Athenian. He was called **Clement of Alexandria** because he resided in that city for a long time, composed all his writings there, and was, moreover, the head of a renowned school established in that place. He himself reports in the book of his collections — <term>Miscellanies: original: *Stromata*, a Greek title meaning "patchwork" or "tapestry," used to describe a work of diverse subject matter</term> — that he was a student of the most skilled teachers in **Greece** and in that part of **Italy** known as **Magna Graecia** <note>original: "das große Griechenland," referring to the coastal areas of Southern Italy settled by Greek colonists</note>, and that he had heard the best among them in the **East**, in **Egypt**, and **Assyria**. Finally, he found a teacher of rare merit in **Palestine**, and this determined him to settle in **Egypt**. This great master was likely the famous **Pantaenus**, the head of the **Alexandrian school**, who was subsequently sent to **India** to preach the Gospel; from those countries, he brought back a copy of the **Gospel of Saint Matthew**, as **Eusebius of Caesarea** <note>an early 4th-century historian often called the "Father of Church History"</note> confirms.

Judging the holy **Clement** by his writings, he must have possessed the most extensive knowledge of everything concerning the humanities and philosophy, and at the same time, the most gifted memory that any man ever possessed. The **Holy Scriptures**, the poets, and all the philosophers among the **Greeks** and <term>barbarians: in the ancient context, this refers to non-Greeks, particularly those from the Near East or Egypt</term> appear in his work so naturally and so effortlessly that one would believe he could recite them all from memory and always had them laid out before him. Regarding his intellect, he thought with uncommon correctness, was fertile in ideas, and possessed an admir-

...worthy ease in tracking down the truth, explaining it, and making it felt. His style of writing is clear, but at times long-winded, and one not infrequently misses that precision and that fire which is so pleasing in the works of some other writers.

It is not known exactly at what time Saint *Clement* became a Christian. But in his *Exhortation to the Greeks*, he clearly gives it to be understood that he was long a pagan, and was perfectly well-versed in everything concerning that religion.

The high regard held for his merit, his talents, and his virtue was the reason that, after the death of *Pantaenus*, he was appointed head of the <term>Alexandrian school: a major center of Christian scholarship in the early centuries, famous for its allegorical interpretation of Scripture</term>. The pupil of this great man subsequently became the teacher of one even greater: the famous *Origen*. The many duties of this important office did not prevent him from producing many writings in the meantime, of which, however, nothing has come down to us except his *Exhortation to the Greeks* (that is, the pagans), his *Pedagogue*, and his collections, or *Stromata* <note>original: "Sammlungen, oder *Stromata*"; the Greek title *Stromata* means "miscellanies" or "tapestries"</note>.

His speech to the Greeks is the most effective work for exposing the origin and the fantastical nature of idolatry, and the excess of error and debauchery to which it leads. One finds therein quite singular investigations, and the author always speaks in a resolute and confident tone because he is certain of his cause and well knows that people will forever owe him an answer to his objections. We will insert an analysis of this speech further below.

Now we wish to analyze his speech to the Greeks, or to those peoples who professed the pagan religion.

### Speech, or Presentation
## to the Greeks regarding Idolatry.

# Hermias.

I do not believe that one will find in any library a work that combines as much clarity and precision, as much life and fire, as much wit and elegance, as this whimsical writing by Hermias about the pagan sages <note>original: *Heydnischen Weltweisen*. Referring to the pre-Christian Greek philosophers.</note> titled: **The Ridiculed Philosophers.** Often a well-chosen epithet or a single expression describes a philosopher and his system quite accurately, and the whole is seasoned with the finest and most biting wit <note>original: *Salze*. Literally "salt," a classical term for sharp, intellectual satire.</note>. The variety, the truth, and the abundance of the depictions please, illuminate, and carry the reader along. When one prepares to read it, it is almost like children being shown toys which they then want to see all at once; and it was precisely this variety and precision that prevented us from making a mere summary of this writing, and we felt compelled to look over it in its entirety. — We have no record from which one could know for certain who this Hermias was. However, it is clear from this short work of his that he must have been one of the most ingenious and significant minds in the world, and a zealous Christian. It is generally held that he lived in the second century.
