# Hermias.

### 135

<meta>catchword: I,</meta>

...but the soul of the world permeates everything, and we ourselves are animated by a small part of this soul. <note>This refers to the Stoic belief in the *pneuma* or world-soul that binds the cosmos together.</note> — But over there, a legion of African philosophers <note>Hermias likely refers to the Skeptics or perhaps the Cyrenaics; the term "African" here likely points to the school of Cyrene or the later Alexandrian thinkers who emphasized the limits of human knowledge.</note> advances, bringing forth principles quite different from what has been served to us so far. They reject all systems of doctrine across the board, asserting that everything is incomprehensible and impenetrable to the weak insights of man, and that here on earth, truth is always mixed with falsehood. Would it really be worth the effort to study systems of doctrine for so long, only to have to renounce them in the end?

One more word about the old horde of the first Pythagoreans with the muzzle <note>original: "Mundklemme" — a satirical reference to the *akousmatikoi*, the novice disciples of Pythagoras who were sworn to absolute silence for five years.</note>. They honor us with a philosophy as dark as the mysteries of Ceres <note>Ceres is the Roman name for Demeter; the reference is to the Eleusinian Mysteries, which were famously shrouded in secrecy.</note>. Their hobby-horse is: *The Teacher has said it.* <note>original: "Der Lehrer hats gesagt" — a translation of the famous Pythagorean formula *Ipse dixit* (He himself said it), used to stifle any further argument or questioning.</note> If one is fortunate enough to loosen their gag, they explain themselves thus: The primary cause of everything is the <term>Monad</term> <note>From the Greek *monas*, meaning "unity" or "one." In Pythagoreanism, it represents the first thing that came into existence.</note>, that is, Unity; and the different figures, or the different numbers of Unity, are the elements. Through these elements, the Pythagoreans explain nature, form, and measure, as they precisely determine how many right-angled and isosceles triangles each element is composed of. They assure us that every particle of fire has the shape of a pyramid [tetrahedron], air consists of eight-sided [octahedron], earth of cubical, and water of solid parts with twenty faces [icosahedron]. Thus Pythagoras lays out the structure of the world and measures the entire creation.

Now at last, it has succeeded. The divine Pythagoras has enlightened me. Lucky me! How I shall use his instruction! What insights, what knowledge I shall gather! Fatherland, wife, children, farewell! Once I have my measuring chain and the rest of the gear together and packed, I will soar into the air and begin by measuring the fire. Jupiter shall not be the only one to have knowledge of the heavens henceforth. I myself, I, great spirit—

# Hermias.

“Sublime, penetrating, insatiable spirit! How much further do you wish to go? Are you sufficiently convinced that in this world there is nothing but ignorance, darkness, weak concepts, blindness, error, and infinite deception? And yet you want to provide an account of everything? Do you still wish to investigate how great the number of atoms is, from which these infinite worlds are composed? <note>A direct jab at Epicurean physics, which claimed the universe was made of indivisible atoms and that multiple worlds existed.</note> Is there perhaps no more useful, no more necessary knowledge?”

“Philosophers, rationalizers! <note>The original term "Vernünftler" is a derogatory word for those who over-apply logic to trivial or unknowable things.</note> To you this insignificant work, this small collection of your ‘successful’ efforts, your opinions, and <term>systems of thought</term> <note>original: "Lehrgebäude" — literally "teaching-buildings," referring to the rigid, structured schools of philosophy like Stoicism or Platonism.</note> is dedicated, in order to show you their own absurdity and contradictions. It is meant to compel a confession regarding the errors of the investigations you dare to undertake, without ever finding a place where you might set a firm foot. If only you would confess that nothing is more incomprehensible, nothing more useless, than your philosophical systems, which are grounded neither in the certainty of the senses nor in reason!”

# Origen.

This great man was born in Alexandria around the end of the second century. His father was Saint Leonidas, who had shed his blood in defense of the faith during the persecution of Severus <note>Septimius Severus, Roman Emperor from 193 to 211 AD, whose reign saw localized persecutions of Christians.</note>. When the estates of the holy martyrs were confiscated, Origen, along with his mother and his six brothers, fell into the most extreme poverty. However, by this time he had already completed his studies in Alexandria and Athens, and had made the most astonishing progress in all branches of science and scholarship. Greece, so fertile in beautiful minds, could point to no one who could have rivaled him. It was seen with amazement how a youth of this age possessed complete mastery of everything brilliant, sharp, and profound in logic <term>Vernunftlehr: the study of rational thought or logic</term>, physics, astronomy, geometry <term>Meßkunst: literally the "art of measuring," referring to mathematics and geometry</term>, and rhetoric. He knew what had been taught in the schools of the various philosophers and had made himself familiar with all their systems and opinions. He had read all the poets and historians, and united within himself all the insights and talents which one would often seek in vain, even individually, among many of the most enlightened men. But it is even more to be admired that, in his case, virtues went hand in hand with talents. One has perhaps never seen a more modest man: his morals and his character were blameless and raised above all reproach, and during the persecution of Decius <note>Trajan Decius, Roman Emperor from 249 to 251 AD, who initiated the first empire-wide persecution of Christians.</note> he endured chains, torture, and martyrdom with invincible courage.

He was no more than eighteen years old when he was placed at the head of the school of Alexandria <note>The Catechetical School of Alexandria, the oldest center of Christian theological learning.</note>, which at that time was considered the most prestigious and famous in the entire Christian world. Pantaenus, Ammonius, and Clement had been his predecessors in this teaching chair: but it was not long before they were forgotten, and homage was paid to the fame of their successor. ces <note>The word is split here: "Wissenschaf-ten" (sciences).</note>

Instead of urging his return to resume his teaching office, he made a most violent and vehement resolution. After he had studied the systems of all the Greek philosophers from the ground up, read all the works of the most famous poets, informed himself of everything important and interesting contained in history, and set aside the prejudice that the Greeks held against "barbaric" <note>The Greeks used the term "barbaric" to describe any language or culture that was not Greek. Already at eighteen years of age, as the head of the Alexandrian school, he never neglected to give lectures on religion and the interpretation of the Holy Scripture; and alongside these, he also lectured on philosophy, mathematics, eloquence, and natural science to an indescribable crowd of inquisitive listeners from all walks of life.

# Origen.

One of the most important and laborious works is the collection of all the different editions and translations of the Holy Scriptures with characteristic notes, in which the variations of one translation from another regarding specific expressions are indicated. This great work appeared initially in six columns, which is called the **Hexapla**, and afterwards in eight columns, which is called the **Octapla**. Shortly thereafter, he published his treatises and homilies on the first four books of Moses, and also on many other books of the Old and New Testaments. He also composed a great number of writings against heretics and pagan philosophers. To enable all nations and people, of whatever rank or religion they might be, to judge Christianity for themselves, he brought to light his books on the fundamental principles of the Christian faith, which are known by the Greek title, *Peri Archon* <note>original: "περι αρχων", which translates to "On First Principles." This was one of the first systematic attempts to explain Christian theology.</note>. Saint Jerome <note>Hieronymus</note> assures us that the works of Origen reach nearly six thousand volumes or booklets; he says that Origen himself had seven scribes and six girls who wrote with such a swift hand that they recorded everything with the same speed as he dictated it. A certain nobleman at the court of the Emperor, named Ambrose <note>Ambros</note>, provided the necessary funds required for this. At the request of this gentleman, Origen set to work on that beautiful work against Celsus <note>Celsus was a 2nd-century Greek philosopher and opponent of Early Christianity; Origen's "Against Celsus" is considered one of the most important defenses of the faith.</note>; and it is believed that this was the last writing he composed.

This great man, who was the admiration even of the pagan world, was not spared from persecution despite all the high esteem in which he was held. He had terrible enemies, but also zealous and powerful defenders; and if one reads his works as they currently exist, one cannot help but confess that he often gave legitimate cause for the accusations of his enemies. If he had published them exactly as we have them today, his illustrious defenders would have had little reason to support him with such zeal <note>The author suggests that Origen's original writings may have been altered by later hands, either making them seem more radical to his enemies or more "safe" to his friends, leading to the long-standing controversies over his orthodoxy.</note>. One can therefore agree with these judicial verdicts without prejudice to the high esteem held for Origen.

And certainly, if one examines the matter not according to the prestige of the second church council <note>The Second Council of Constantinople (553 AD), which posthumously declared Origen a heretic.</note>, but according to the qualities and character of those who acted as defenders and accusers, then the victory of this great man is entirely assured. # Origen’s Answer
## to the Philosopher Celsus.

Origen says at the beginning of this book that our divine Savior and Lord Jesus Christ <note>The original uses the abbreviation "J. C."</note> offered nothing but his silence to the accusations of the Jews at the time of his passion; because all their slanders had already been sufficiently refuted by the radiance of his holiness and his virtues. In the same way, the shimmer of holiness and the blameless conduct of the true disciples of Jesus Christ have already sufficiently weakened all the blasphemies of Celsus against the Christian religion. Afterwards, he says: A Christian thoroughly instructed in his faith will likely never be led astray by such a meager <note>original: "kahle"; literally "bald" or "threadbare," implying the work lacks substance or intellectual weight.</note> writing as that of the philosopher Celsus; and he would not form a very favorable opinion of any believer upon whom it managed to make an impression. Nevertheless, he continues, because you so desire it, illustrious Ambrose <note>Ambrose of Alexandria, Origen’s friend and patron who encouraged and financed his writings.</note>, I shall respond regardless; but it would always be much better if such a response were not needed at all, and if such writings were never deemed worthy of a glance—writings toward which an upright Christian should express nothing but contempt. — This latter thought of Origen’s well deserves to be taken to heart in a century <note>Likely referring to the 18th century, the era of the Enlightenment, when the author was writing.</note> where, on the one hand, people write so boldly against religion, and on the other, take the liberty of reading everything written against religion. And how many are there not in every station of life who might well apply this passage to themselves!

Celsus begins his work with general reproaches against religion and with the crudest and most grisly blasphemies against the adorable person of Jesus Christ, which he places in the mouth of a Jew. The response to these two subjects constitutes the content of the first book.

->§. I.<-

The Christians, says Celsus, hold secret meetings in defiance of the laws, which must arouse justified suspicion and can be viewed as conspiracies against the state. Furthermore, their religion is based on dogmas which they have borrowed from barbarians <note>In the Greco-Roman world, "Barbarian" referred to anyone who did not speak Greek or follow Roman customs; here it specifically targets the Jewish origins of Christianity.</note>, and which deserve nothing but contempt. By the word "barbarians," Celsus refers to the Jews.

But, Origen answers, if people were found among the Scythians <note>The Scythians were an ancient nomadic people from the Eurasian steppes, often cited by ancient writers as the ultimate example of a "barbaric" and lawless society.</note>, whose laws, as we know, are so inhuman—and these people, living among these monsters from whose hands they could not escape, wished to hear of no other law than that which reason and justice approve: could one really say that these people violated the laws of the land and are rebelling against the state? And see, that is exactly the case of the Christians in the Empire. The Imperial laws command that one should worship statues, idols, and demons <note>original: "Teufel"; Origen frequently argued that pagan gods were actually malevolent spiritual entities or demons.</note>. Are these decrees not even more unjust than those of the Scythians? Should one become a criminal or deserve blame for disobeying these commands? We applaud those, Origen continues, who unite against a tyrant who has forced his way in, against an enemy of public liberty: therefore, one must also applaud the Christians when they hold their sacred assemblies despite the laws that the devil has inspired, which are more unjust than all the decrees of tyrants.

Regarding the accusation of Celsus, which he levels against the Christians for having borrowed their religion from the barbarians; he does not notice, says Origen, his own words nor the wound he inflicts upon himself. At the beginning of his work, he gives the barbarians the most splendid praise. He lauds them as the origi... <note>original: "Urhe-"; likely the beginning of "Urheber," meaning originators or creators.</note>

...of healthy *maxims*, and uncorrupted principles. How shortsighted is this man, who censures and condemns in us what he deemed worthy of his high esteem and approval only a few moments ago!

### II.

Only in secret, *Celsus* <note>Celsus was a 2nd-century Greek philosopher and the first major intellectual critic of Christianity; his work "The True Word" is only known through Origen's rebuttal.</note> adds, do the Christians teach, instruct, and carry out everything they wish; and they have their good reasons for it. They fear that the same fate might befall them which met certain philosophers, and among others, *Socrates* <note>The Athenian philosopher Socrates was executed in 399 BCE on charges of impiety and corrupting the youth, a fate early Christians often compared to their own persecution.</note>. Meanwhile, their religion contains nothing great and nothing new: regarding its moral teachings <note>original: "Sittenlehre"</note>, it is merely rehashed ideas <note>original: "aufgewärmter Kohl," literally "warmed-over cabbage," a German idiom for old ideas presented as new.</note> which the ancient philosophers have already set forth.

No sooner, says *Origen*, had the Athenians executed *Socrates*, than they regretted it and paid homage to the virtue of this man. For a full century, the Senate, the Emperors, the armies, and the people have conspired against Christianity, and yet with their combined strength, they cannot eradicate it. They should therefore recognize that it is supported by a power higher than any human authority. But do they recognize it?

As for the moral teachings and the judgments of God mentioned by *Celsus*, God has had all of this announced through His prophets. He has placed the seeds of all these truths into every heart: why should it surprise us if some philosophers had knowledge of them and spoke on these matters? Will not this very fact deprive the guilty man of any excuse when he must one day appear before God’s judgment seat?

### III.

One must admit, Celsus continues, that there are capable sorcerers among the Christians who know how to make the devils <note>In the 3rd-century context, "devils" or "demons" referred to spiritual entities believed to influence human affairs.</note> obedient to them.

### IV.

Here are several other objections from Celsus, which our modern philosophical street-vendors <note>original: "Garköche" — literally "cook-shop owners," a derogatory metaphor for thinkers who serve up unoriginal or "reheated" ideas.</note> constantly serve up to the public until they are sick of it. These people are mostly villains and rogues who foist whatever they want upon the simple folk. So too do the Christians. Never will they give you an account of what they believe. They always tell you: "Believe; faith makes one blessed." Worldly wisdom is a bad thing, and folly is better than it.

On this occasion, Origen always carries away the victory with great glory, and his modesty further enhances the brilliance of his triumph. ### VII.

With the intention of further disparaging the Christian religion, which recognizes the writings of Moses as divine books, Celsus writes: A horde of shepherds and cattle-herders, who had allowed themselves to be deluded by the stupid boastings of a certain Moses, believed that there was no more than one God. One might call him *Jupiter*, as the Greeks do, or give him another Indian, Persian, or Egyptian name; it will likely all be the same.

Where do names originate? asks Origen. Is their meaning arbitrary, based on convention, as Aristotle says? Or are they drawn from the nature of the thing itself, as the Stoics <note>A school of Hellenistic philosophy that believed language had a natural, rather than purely social, origin.</note> maintain? Or are they nothing more than sounds, as they happened to cross human lips at random, as Epicurus thinks? This would require a deeper investigation. It is beyond all doubt that among the sages of Egypt, among the Persian Magi, and among the Brahmans <note>The priestly class of India.</note> of India, there were words that possessed a certain power, which was called <term>magic</term> <note>In this context, Origen refers to the ancient belief that certain sacred names or sounds have inherent spiritual efficacy and are not merely symbols.</note>. ### VIII.

Another reproach that **Celsus** makes against the Hebrews concerns the angels, whom he claims they worship, and all sorts of sorceries to which they devote themselves.

If you have read these books, it cannot be unknown to you under what heavy penalties this outrage is forbidden therein. You truly have cause to brag about your omniscience!

->Origen.<-

Hear the victorious response with which Origen dismisses this blasphemous babbler. "You describe Jesus to us," he says to this Jew <note>As noted on the previous page, Celsus uses a fictional Jewish character to voice contemporary criticisms of Jesus's origins.</note>, "as the most contemptible impostor <note>original: "Blendling" — a derogatory term for someone of mixed or deceptive origins.</note> and the dregs of the rabble; and from that very fact I conclude irrefutably that he is truly the Son of God." In order to become a famous man, the power and wealth of the parents from whom one was born, an excellent education that one enjoyed, along with the means to develop one’s natural talents, have always been a great necessity. If one, without having a single one of these advantages on his side, fills the earth with the fame of his name, wins all hearts, and sets the whole world in motion, then surely, by everyone’s own admission, the greatest, most perfect, and most divine soul is required for such an end.

Or, how could a man born in poverty, who grew up without studying, without masters, and without any knowledge of the liberal arts <note>original: "schönen Künste" — here referring to the classical "artes liberales" or the education expected of a philosopher.</note>, master all hearts through his eloquence and introduce a new doctrine of faith that the whole world marveled at and still marvels at today? A doctrine that has toppled Jewish worship and shaken all the religious customs and ceremonies of the Greeks and other nations? How was he able to speak in such a wonderful way of divine judgment, of the reward of virtue, and the punishment of vice, that he convinced not only the common man and uneducated people, but also a great number of the most enlightened minds? These were surely people capable of examining for themselves a doctrine that, at first glance, seemed to have so much against it. How did he succeed, through the boldness and the most successful outcome of his undertakings, in surpassing the fame of all the great men celebrated in the history of former times? Afterward, Origen cites the opinions of the greatest philosophers of Greece, such as Plato, Pythagoras, and Empedocles, and says to Celsus: You know how these great men thought regarding the transmigration of souls <note>original: "Seelenwanderung" — also known as metempsychosis, the ancient Greek philosophical belief that the soul is reborn in different bodies based on its past actions.</note>. Souls are assigned their dwellings in various bodies according to their merit and the conduct they maintained during their former stay in other bodies. Those who allowed themselves to fall into great crimes must now migrate into the bodies of the most contemptible animals; for those who are less punishable, their lot is also less humiliating. But the most beautiful souls receive the most beautiful and perfect bodies: this is the reward for praiseworthy actions and practiced virtues. Now, could a soul that was one day to set the whole world in astonishment through the most incomprehensible wonders be united with a body that had been fathered in the most base and contemptible manner? Should a soul, which was meant to instill a love for the most beautiful virtues, be ordained to animate a body formed by the most loathsome vice? Must it not, on the contrary, have its residence assigned in a body that was, in its own way, entirely wonderful and divine?

# Origen.

He then returns to Jacob's prophecy, which places the birth of this Messiah at the time when the scepter—that is, the supreme sovereign power—shall be taken away from the tribe of Judah <note>Refers to Genesis 49:10, a passage traditionally interpreted by Christians as predicting that the Messiah would come when Jewish self-rule ended.</note>. Then he comes to Isaiah, who depicts this Messiah as the light of all nations and the object of their hope and most fervent desires. With this same prophet, he also presents him as a man of sorrows who walks among mortals, dies on the cross, and redeems the human race at the cost of his blood <note>Isaiah 53 is a cornerstone of Christian messianic interpretation, describing a "Suffering Servant."</note>. Finally, he portrays him through David as the invincible victor who reigns in triumph over all nations. All these passages are written in an exceedingly magnificent, instructive, and urgent manner.

### XIII.

Celsus has his fanatical Jew say to the Christians: "What advantage does your Jesus, who called himself the Son of God, have over so many others who claimed this same title for themselves?"

And Origen, for his part, asks Celsus's Jew: "And who then are these others who gave themselves out to be the Son of God? Will you perhaps cite those two or three sorcerers or rebels? One of them, named Theudas, appeared shortly before Jesus's arrival; another, called Judas, a few years before his birth; and the third, Dositheus the Samaritan, shortly after his death. And you wish to compare these scoundrels with Jesus, who is currently worshiped in all parts of the world and recognized as the true Son of God?"

## XIV.

The star that appeared to the three Wise Men and the flight of Jesus into Egypt provide the Jew <note>The fictional character created by Celsus to voice anti-Christian arguments</note> with material to mock the Christians. "This Jesus," he says, "boasted that Chaldeans <note>A term often used for the Magi or astrologers from the East</note> came to the manger to worship him. He claimed these Chaldeans revealed the purpose of their journey to Herod, who consequently had all the little boys in the area around Bethlehem killed; he, however, supposedly thwarted the bloodthirsty intentions of the king by his flight."

"Herod," says the mocker to Jesus, "wanted to kill you out of fear that you might seize his throne; so why did you not dare to take this step at a more mature age? Is fleeing, fearing, and hiding not an eternal disgrace for a Son of God? Upon my word, this was neither a great nor a courageous way to act."

Origen responds to this last outburst from the Jew with two points. Can it be found inglorious, faint-hearted, and unworthy of the divine Son to avoid death in order to be useful to the human race—to be able to enlighten and instruct them until the appointed moment arrives to be slaughtered for them and to complete his sacrifice? But first, he explains the conduct and methods of the Wise Men. This explanation is written entirely in the style of the Greeks, who acknowledged both good and evil spirits <term>genii: guardian spirits or supernatural influences in Greco-Roman belief</term>. Assuming that the Wise Men had some knowledge of Balaam’s prophecy <note>A biblical prophecy in Numbers 24:17 stating "a star shall come out of Jacob," which early Christians interpreted as predicting the birth of Christ</note>, Origen shows that their conduct was very wise and most fitting for men who sincerely sought the truth.

Can all of them together compete with the single *Jesus*? To say nothing of the innumerable conversions he has effected, his name even today heals the insane, drives out demons, dispels diseases, works a moral improvement <term>Sittenbesserung: a systematic reformation of one’s character and social behavior</term>, and tunes the soul to gentleness, to benevolence, to harmony, and to peace. This is evident in all those who have devoted themselves to the proclamation of the Gospel and of a future judgment.

# Origen.

...he ventured into those divine books, the interpretation of which presented the greatest difficulty; and everywhere the man reveals extensive knowledge and an unlimited insight. Saint Jerome <note>Hieronymus (c. 342–420 AD), a Latin scholar and Doctor of the Church, known for translating the Bible into the Vulgate.</note> translated his commentary on the *Song of Songs* <note>original: "hohe Lied." One of the most poetic and allegorical books of the Old Testament.</note>, and sent this work of his to the holy Pope Damasus, stating in his letter:

With astonishment, one discovers in his various interpretations of the holy books an admirable ease in explaining Scripture through Scripture itself. A dark passage suddenly becomes light and clear through other passages against which he holds it, just as an extinguished torch catches fire again as soon as it is brought near one that is lit. He discovers in matters that might not particularly strike anyone else the richest material for a multitude of remarks, instruction for all virtues, unexpected thoughts and intentions; delicacy, purity, and tenderness of sentiment, and the most beautiful and sublime spiritual sense.

His dialogues on the true faith in God are a masterpiece, in which one discovers all the erudition, all the acumen, all the presence, and liveliness of spirit of which a mortal is capable. Origen seems in them to be not a man, but an angel. These conversations were held before a massive crowd of people of all religions, some of whom were Catholics <note>In this context, "Catholic" refers to the "universal" or "orthodox" mainstream Christian church of the 3rd century, as opposed to sectarian groups.</note>, others heretics and pagans. His critique regarding the truth of the story of Susanna <note>Susanna is a figure in a narrative often included as Chapter 13 of the Book of Daniel, though its status as scripture was debated in the early Church.</note>, which is mentioned in Daniel’s book, is very interesting. The learned chronologist, Julius Africanus <note>A Christian traveler and historian of the 3rd century, often considered the father of Christian chronography.</note>, had expressed in a letter to Origen that he considered this story to be a forged work which had crept into Daniel’s book. At the same time, he presented him with eight objections that had occurred to him during his reading. Origen, acting as the oracle of his time, answered all of Julius’s difficulties and placed the truth of this historical record beyond all doubt.

One can judge the general high esteem in which Origen stood, and especially the value that Saint Gregory of Nazianzus and Basil <note>Gregory of Nazianzus (c. 329–390) and Basil the Great (330–379) were influential Greek bishops and theologians who shaped early Christian doctrine.</note> had for his books, from the treatise found at the end of his works under the title: *On the Love of the Beautiful* <note>original: "Von der Liebe des Schönen." This is the German translation of the Greek title *Philokalia*, a famous anthology of Origen's texts compiled by Gregory and Basil.</note>. This treatise is an excerpt, written with great intelligence and in the finest order, of the most instructive, magnificent, and striking passages contained in Origen's writings. These two great men never tired of studying Origen and selecting those passages which had particularly moved them. They gave the whole a proper order, and thus this treatise came into being, as is clear from the letter of Saint Gregory to the Bishop of Tyre, to whom he sent it.

From this, one can judge the immeasurable benefit that theologians and other scholars would draw from Origen's books if they were to read them with the same zeal as these two illustrious men.

## Minucius Felix.

Cicero’s *On the Nature of the Gods* <note>original: "Gespräche über die Natur der Götter" (Latin: *De Natura Deorum*). Marcus Tullius Cicero was a Roman statesman whose philosophical dialogues served as a primary model for later Latin writers.</note> can be regarded as one of the most beautiful works to have flowed from the pen of this great man. Each of the participating characters says everything that can possibly be said to the advantage of the opinion they have undertaken to defend; throughout, one finds a combination of thoroughness in proof, grace in writing style, and the varied richness of a rare erudition—everything one could possibly desire. Alongside this beautiful work, one can without hesitation place the writing of Minucius Felix <note>Marcus Minucius Felix (active c. 200–240 CE) was one of the earliest Latin-speaking Christian apologists in Rome.</note>, which he composed for the benefit of the Christian religion. This is not only because one finds therein almost the same progression and manner of treating a subject, but also because a great similarity prevails on both sides regarding the beauty of the concepts and thoughts, the purity of the language, and the strength of the expressions. We know nothing more of Minucius Felix than that he was a born pagan and, under Emperor Severus <note>Septimius Severus (reigned 193–211 CE).</note>, was one of Rome’s most famous orators, advocates, and legal scholars, and that after becoming a Christian, he wrote in defense of his religion.

The only work of his that time has spared is his dialogue on religion, which is composed entirely in Cicero’s style in *On the Nature of the Gods*. <note>This work is known as the *Octavius*. Cicero’s Cotta and Minucius’s Caecilius venture the very same attacks; and the Balbus of the former, and the Octavius of the latter, defend themselves in the same manner—yet with the difference that Octavius’s defense is much more striking and attractive because of the sublime subjects he treats and the illuminating proofs with which he supports his cause. Finally, both writers conclude and deliver their judgment in almost the same words and sentiments. "When the conversation came to an end, we went our separate ways," says Cicero; "Velleius gave the preference to Cotta’s speech, but it seemed to me that Balbus came closer to the truth." <note>original: "Als die Unterredung zu Ende war, giengen wir auseinander... Vellejus gab des Cotta's Rede den Vorzug; mich aber dünkte, Balbus komme der Wahrheit näher." This refers to the closing lines of Cicero's *De Natura Deorum*.</note> And Minucius Felix writes: "After this conversation, we went our separate ways very satisfied; Caecilius, that he was now convinced and instructed; Octavius, that he had gained the upper hand; and I, that the one had accepted the faith and the other had conquered idolatry." <note>original: "Nach diesem Gespräche giengen wir sehr zufrieden auseinander; Cäzil, daß er nun überzeugt und unterrichtet war; Oktavius, daß er die Oberhand gewonnen; ich aber, daß der Eine den Glauben angenommen, und der andere die Abgötterey besieget hatte." This is the conclusion of the *Octavius*.</note>

We believe our readers will be grateful if we acquaint them more closely with the interlocutors before we undertake the analysis of the dialogue itself. Minucius Felix, Octavius, and Caecilius were bosom friends; all three were born pagans and learned men who played an important role in court as advocates <note>original: "Sachwalter". These were legal experts or lawyers; the legal background of these early Latin Christians heavily influenced their logical and persuasive writing styles.</note>, so that one could say three advocates won this victory for religion. First, Octavius converted to Christianity; Minucius followed some time later, and Caecilius’s conversion was the fruit of this dialogue. Some are of the opinion...

These three friends left Rome during the harvest and vintage holidays, and betook themselves to the seashore at Ostia, a very charming retreat at that time. As they were walking out of the city together one day, their path took them past the Temple of Serapis. <note>Serapis was a Graeco-Egyptian deity whose cult was widely popular across the Roman Empire.</note> Caecilius, still a pagan, followed the custom of his religion by moving his hand to his mouth and reverently greeting the temple of the idol. <note>In antiquity, "kissing the hand" toward a statue or temple was a common gesture of adoration (from the Latin *adorare*, "to pray to").</note> "What are you thinking, brother?" the fiery Octavius now said to Minucius. "Can you calmly look on while your bosom friend, who is always with you, blindly abandons himself to an error that is the lot of the ignorant rabble; and before your very eyes worships unfeeling marble, which the sculptor's chisel has transformed into a god, and which is now sprinkled with sacrificial wine and adorned with flowers? Does the shame of this delusion not reflect back from him onto you?"

Caecilius was startled by these words, became more serious, and remained darkly silent until they reached the place where the company came to a halt. "What is the matter with you?" Minucius said to him; "where is your usual cheerfulness? You seem to me to be a completely different person." "Octavius's speech struck me," answered Caecilius, "in which he, quite indirectly, blames you for lightheadedness and a lack of wisdom, and me for gross ignorance. It is with him, then, that I have to deal; against him I must defend myself." And so the conversation began, which Caecilius opened. We set down here in summary the reasons he brought forward in defense of paganism and against the Christian religion, and the answers with which Octavius refuted these reasons and objections.

"Brother," said Caecilius, turning to Minucius, "you are familiar with both religions: for after you lived in the one for a long time, you preferred the other. You will therefore be able to act as the arbiter <term>Schiedrichter: an impartial judge or referee chosen to settle a dispute</term> between me and Octavius without falling into embarrassment. I therefore request that you, as judge, do not hold the scales lopsided, but look closely to equity <note>original: "Billigkeit" — in this context, it refers to fairness and natural justice rather than just the strict letter of the law</note>, so that your judgment may be a result of the arguments I shall bring forward, and not a consequence of your own private opinions."

Uncertainty, doubt, and darkness are the lot of those investigations which one dares to undertake regarding the things of this world; and even if one occasionally succeeds in catching a ray of probability, one will surely never find the truth. One must not even argue over this proposition. For this reason, there are people who, in order to avoid the effort and frustration that are inevitable in the search for truth, prefer to cling at random to the next best doctrinal system rather than seeking truth with such great difficulty and enduring diligence. Is it not therefore an annoying sight that a certain class of people <note>Caecilius is referring to the early Christians, who were often from the lower social classes and lacked formal Greek philosophical training</note>, mostly without science or learning, who follow the most contemptible trades, boldly pass judgment on things in which the philosophical schools of all centuries have not yet dared to decide anything? Is this cautious restraint of the philosophers not wise, since the human spirit is not at all equal to these subjects—which it is impossible for it to understand and which it may not track down—and it must suffice for man’s happiness, according to the decree of the Wise Man, that he knows himself? <note>This is a reference to the famous Socratic maxim "Know thyself," which Caecilius uses here to argue that humans should focus on their own limits rather than claiming to know the mind of God or the secrets of the universe.</note>

After this introduction, he prepared to prove that one can know nothing about the origin of the world. Is it eternal? ...an intelligent being? Or is everything rather a constant flux; so that whatever has existed is continually reborn, and that which is no more returns exactly as it once was? Afterward, he addresses the mixture of good and evil found in the world, believing he can demonstrate clearly from this that no divine providence <term>Vorsicht: here used in the sense of divine foresight or providence, from the Latin *providentia*</term> exists. Since truth is shrouded in impenetrable darkness, the most rational course of action would be to adhere to what our ancestors thought regarding the gods, who in the earliest ages of the world were kings or benefactors of the human race. Every distinct nation had its own gods, and Rome acquired its world dominion precisely because it worshiped all these various deities.

From the origin of the gods, Caecilius moves on to the soothsayers <note>These were the augurs and haruspices, Roman officials who observed natural signs to determine the will of the gods</note>, who predicted future events from the flight or the cries of birds. He remarks that he would rather believe the pronouncements of these men and share in the errors of antiquity than criticize and reject them on the pretext that the origin and logic of their art cannot be explained. He adopts this same approach regarding temple consecrations and the other customs and ceremonies of Roman worship <note>original: "Götzendienstes" — literally "idolatry," though here the text refers to the established Roman state religion</note>.

He goes on to say that if the Athenians once banished Protagoras <note>Protagoras (c. 490–420 BC) was a Greek philosopher whose books were burned in Athens because he claimed he could not know whether the gods existed or not</note> and burned all his writings for denying the existence of the gods, then the Christians certainly deserve to be banished for even more compelling reasons. He then depicts them in the most horrific colors, accusing them of the most unnatural vices, and charging them with high treason, incestuous abominations, and the murder of children <note>It was a common Roman misconception that the Christian Eucharist involved literal cannibalism and that their "agape" or love-feasts were orgies</note>. <meta>This page continues the speech of Caecilius from the previous page, where he defended traditional Roman religion and dismissed the validity of individual reason in theological matters. ->Minutius Felix.<-

...their worship, with their ceremonies, so shyly "behind the mountain" <note>The German idiom "hinter dem Berge halten" means to keep something secret or to be evasive.</note>? If one acts honestly, one has no hesitation in acting before the eyes of the whole world: only what is shameful is withdrawn from the gaze of others. Why do they have no temples, no altars, no statues, and no representations? Because, clearly, their entire religion amounts to shame and vice.

After these accusations, Caecilius comes to speak of the God whom the Christians worship. Who, he asks, is this single, solitary, abandoned God, unknown to all free nations, to all kingdoms, even to the Romans themselves? This God of an "ungarlanded" curiosity <note>original: "unbekränzten Vorwitze" — referring to the lack of ceremonial wreaths or honors used in Roman religious rites</note>, who pries into <note>original: "durchstänkeret" — a derogatory term implying prying or sniffing around</note> all hearts, is present everywhere, and wants to be an eyewitness to every trifle? What is one to make of that figment of the imagination <note>original: "Hirngespinste"</note> regarding the resurrection, with which you flatter yourselves, and for which you wait with such burning longing, while you now struggle with hunger and deprivation, and gallows and wooden stakes <note>A reference to the various methods of execution and martyrdom faced by early Christians in the Roman Empire.</note> threaten you in all places? And that God, who has intended a fullness of goods for you after your death—as you spin your tales—does he not lift a finger for your rescue during this life?

After all these arguments, he advises the Christians not to concern themselves so much with what happens in heaven, but instead to better utilize those goods which the earth offers, and to say with the wise Socrates: "What is above us is not for us down here" <note>The Latin maxim *Quod supra nos, nihil ad nos* ("What is above us is nothing to us").</note>. This is what true philosophy says; thus thought Arcesilaus, Carneades, Simonides, and the entire Academic school <note>The Academic Skeptics were a school of philosophers in Ancient Greece who maintained that knowledge of the truth is impossible.</note>; and so I think as well. What is doubtful may, for all I care, always remain doubtful; and where so many great men hold back their judgment, we too must not wish to decide boldly and presumptuously: for by doing so, one would either overturn all religion or open the gates to all superstition.

<note>The text begins by concluding the thought from the previous page: just as a house has one master, the world has one God.</note> Remus, then Caesar and Pompey. On this occasion, Octavius speaks in the most magnificent and sublime terms about the Unity of God, and testifies that even in ordinary and natural language, one recognizes this unity; that all great philosophers, although they express themselves differently, ultimately return to the Unity of God; so that one can say these philosophers were already Christians, or that today's Christians are true philosophers.

But what are your gods, of whom antiquity knew nothing, and against whom reason rebels? I will say nothing of your ridiculous fables, which serve as nothing more than material for nurse's tales; nothing of your absurd transformations; once again, what are these gods, whom our light-headed and simple ancestors accepted without investigation? They paid homage to their kings, were biased toward them, and wished to have their likeness with them even after their death; they celebrated their memory, and what they did at the beginning out of gratitude and to soothe the pain of their loss, became in time a religious worship. Read Euhemerus <note>Euhemerus (4th century BCE) was a Greek mythographer who argued that the gods were originally historical kings or heroes deified by their people.</note>, read the writings of the Stoics; there you will find news of the birth, the fatherland, the death, and the burial place of those whom you now worship as gods. One can imagine nothing more ridiculous than the Egyptian ceremonies, and the Romans have also introduced this folderol among themselves. And the Eleusinian <note>The Eleusinian Mysteries were secret religious rites for Demeter and Persephone; they were among the most famous of the ancient Greek spiritual traditions.</note> ceremonies, how simple-minded they are! <meta>This page continues the dialogue *Octavius* by Marcus Minutius Felix. On the previous page, Octavius was critiquing the absurdity of Egyptian animal worship and the historical origins of pagan gods as mere deified men. He now turns his attention to the Roman claim that their piety led to their imperial success.</meta>

->Minutius Felix.<-

...history teemed with stories of the gods, and depicted the entire horror of idolatry <note>original: *Götzendienstes*</note>.

Caecilius had claimed that the zeal of the Romans in worshipping the gods of every nation had earned them the reward of world dominion, and that they had distinguished themselves no less by their virtues than by their religion.

"Oh, indeed!" Octavius replies, "the Romans have certainly recommended themselves most particularly through their virtues. Who were the first Romans? Scoundrels, highwaymen, a rabble of thieves, and assassins. Their leader, Romulus, in order to harden them for acts of vice, provides the 'fine' example of fratricide <note>Romulus murdered his twin brother, Remus, during the founding of Rome.</note>. They drive their neighbors from their estates, destroy cities, temples, and altars, and violate women and girls. Consequently, Rome owes its power to its vices, and not to its religion. Their crimes remained unpunished because no one had strength enough to punish them. Look at how they have become great: Rome worships those very gods it has overcome and thrown into chains. Is that honoring them, or rather mocking them? And how did it happen that these gods—who were too weak to defend their own peoples—could so powerfully support the Romans? But who are Rome's native deities? A Romulus, a Picus <note>In Roman mythology, Picus was an early king of Italy and a son of Saturn.</note>, and a pair of harlots <note>original: *Metzen*</note> such as Laurentia and Flora were. And the morals of the Romans—of what nature were they? Less filth is practiced in their brothels than in their temples."

And what is the source of these hideous excesses? It is the unclean spirits, the demons, who—as Plato, the magicians, and the philosophers say—hide themselves in the statues, inhabit the idols, and give themselves the appearance of being deities who have chosen these places for their residence. # Tertullian.

All ancient writers seem to vie with one another in offering the loftiest praise for the talents, genius, and erudition of Tertullian, as well as for his works and their success; he was equally skilled whether defending Christianity or combating idolatry, heresy, and every form of unbelief. What astonishing wide-reading! What insights into everything concerning the divine and human sciences! Philosophy <note>original: Weltweisheit; literally "world-wisdom"</note>, philosophical systems and sects, history, and every branch of learning; his wonderful genius was a match for them all, and he knew how to unite everything within himself. He was a truly powerful spirit, who in his writings contested nothing that he did not crush through the force of his reasoning, or scatter through his shrewdness. # Tertullian.

...mies, whose blasphemies he thundered down through his victorious writings.” Thus speaks of **Tertullian** the learned monk and Abbot of **Lérins** <note>Vincent of Lérins (died c. 445 AD), a monk and theologian famous for his "Commonitory," which established guidelines for Christian doctrine</note>. I shall further cite what history has preserved for us concerning this great man.

He was born in **Carthage** <note>A major ancient city in modern-day Tunisia, then a Roman province</note> into a proconsular family <note>A high-ranking family belonging to the class of Roman provincial governors</note>. His name was **Quintus Septimus Florens Tertullianus**. The time of his birth occurred toward the end of **Marcus Aurelius’s** reign. While still a boy, he lost his father, who was a pagan <note>original: Heyde; a term used historically for non-Christians or polytheists</note> and an officer in the Roman army. His mother had him educated with all the care that his social standing and his excellent natural talents required. The school of **Carthage** was very flourishing at that time, and **Tertullian** developed himself under the guidance of the most famous teachers in the fine arts, philosophy, and history. He also studied law and jurisprudence, and it is believed he distinguished himself particularly in forensic eloquence <note>The art of legal oratory and argumentation used in courts</note>, because this was then the surest way to work one's way up to honorary offices. The exact time when he abandoned idolatry and turned to Christianity cannot be specified. This alone is known: that he was already a Christian and married when he arrived in **Rome** from **Africa** during the first years of **Severus’s** <note>Septimius Severus, Roman emperor from 193 to 211 AD</note> reign. Because of his fine intellect and the broad scope of his knowledge, as well as the brilliance of his virtue—which was already well known—he was elevated to the priestly dignity, and he undertook every labor with tireless industry for the benefit of religion.

During the first years of his reign, **Severus** was reasonably well-disposed toward the Christians; indeed, there were several of them at his court whom he knew, loved, and protected. But despite these favorable prospects, a persecution soon broke out against them. # Tertullian.

...the Emperor <note>Septimius Severus</note> entrusted the administration of the empire to **Plautian**, the Praetorian Prefect <note>The commander of the Praetorian Guard and a high-ranking administrative official in the Roman Empire</note>, who immediately declared himself against the Christians following the Emperor’s departure. This **Plautian** was the father-in-law of the imperial prince **Antonin Caracalla**, and his persecution prompted **Tertullian’s** finest work—that *Apology* <note>original: Schutzschrift; a formal legal and theological defense of the Christian faith</note> for the Christian religion, which was then the admiration of **Rome** and **Greece**, and has since become so for the entire world and across all centuries.

This *Apology* is not addressed to the Emperor, who was already in the East at that time, but to those who held the highest power in the empire at that same time, and specifically to **Plautian**. Shortly thereafter, his book *On the Testimony of the Soul* <note>original: Zeugniß der Seele; Latin title: De testimonio animae</note> was also published for the benefit of the Christian religion.

After the publication of these two works, he left **Rome** and returned again to **Africa**, where the persecution was raging fiercely. Here too, he presented a serious petition to **Tertullus Scapula**, the Proconsul of **Africa**, for the benefit of the Christians. In this work, he speaks emphatically on the duties of magistrates, the injustice of the persecution, and the tragic end of many persecutors. As he was not himself entangled in the persecution, he occupied himself solely with works for the benefit of the religion. To his fiery zeal, we owe a multitude of clear and important treatises in which the excesses of idolatry, the blindness of the **Jews**, the errors of the **heretics**, and the heroic courage of Christian virtues are dealt with using that strength and emphasis through which **Tertullian’s** way of thinking distinguishes itself so remarkably.

# Tertullian.

...path to the Christian religion through his piety and the most heroic virtues, <note>The text refers here to Montanus, the founder of the Montanist movement</note> initially greatly edified the Church. The people looked upon him with wonder; they followed him and believed he was filled with the Holy Spirit. This applause tickled his ambition, and he began to play the teacher of faith; and as he had always found a taste for overstrained virtues, he condemned second marriage, doubled fasting and mortification, and maintained that fornicators, adulterers, and those who had fallen from the faith during a persecution should never again be admitted to penance and reconciliation. Finally, he taught that the promise of the sending of the Holy Spirit had only partially taken place in the days of the Apostles; only in his own time, he claimed, had it come to reality in its full abundance. As a consequence of this teaching, he made no difficulty of calling himself the Comforter <note>original: "Tröster"; referring to the Paraclete or Holy Spirit</note>.

**Montanus’s** moral teachings harmonized too well with **Tertullian’s** taste and character for him not to have accepted them. Naturally hard, strict, and generally inclined toward the excessive under the pretext of greater perfection, these moral teachings were welcome to him. And when **Montanus** was condemned by the holy **Pope Zephyrinus**, **Tertullian** rebelled against this judgment and wrote with the greatest heat and bitterness against the Church. Because he had previously condemned **Montanus’s** tenets in his fine book *On Prescriptions* <note>original: "Verjährungen"; Latin: *De Praescriptione Haereticorum*</note>, he now took every effort to justify this fickleness in his writing *On Chastity* <note>original: "Ehrbarkeit"; Latin: *De Pudicitia*</note>.

# Outline
# of the Works of Tertullian.

Tertullian's works stand out particularly through the power and precision of his writing style, the irresistible strength of his logical conclusions, and an all-encompassing erudition. The Greeks, although they do not usually think favorably of the Westerners <note>original: "Abendländern"; referring to the Latin-speaking Western Church</note>, esteemed him very highly, as is clear from the writings of Eusebius of Caesarea <note>Eusebius (c. 260–339 AD) was a landmark Greek historian of the early Church.</note>. We intend to present an abstract of some of his works here.

## Tertullian’s Apology.

To make the full injustice of this hatred truly palpable, he shows that one has never persecuted a vice in the Christians, but always merely their name. He proves this from the testimony of the pagans <note>original: "Heyden"</note> themselves, who, when they see an upright man who leaves paganism and converts to Christianity, are accustomed to saying: “Lucius, or Gaius <note>Standard Roman names used here as placeholders for any individual</note>, was a virtuous man; it is always a pity that he has become a Christian.” He dwells on Trajan’s decision <note>Tertullian is famously critiquing Emperor Trajan’s letter to Pliny the Younger, which instructed that Christians should not be sought out, but punished if they were denounced and refused to recant.</note>, who, because he forbade the seeking out of Christians, thereby declared them innocent; and yet he decreed that they should be punished if they were reported, as if they were indeed guilty. He exposes before all eyes the full malice of the judges, who stretch evildoers—such as assassins, poisoners, or those who commit incest—on the rack <note>original: "Folter"</note> just as they do the Christians; the former to force a confession of their vices, and the latter to compel them to renounce their name. Thus, nothing is persecuted but the name, and not any actual crime. One need only read the legal sentences passed against them. In these, there is no mention of incest, assassination, or any other vice. Their name is their only crime.

He concludes with these emphatic words: “See, Romans, your judicial proceedings with us! You do not dare to conduct an investigation into our conduct, for fear of finding no proof for the accusations brought against us. Meanwhile, we are stretched upon the rack when we...”

Following these observations, the author adopts a more sublime tone. His language and reasons are triumphant when he justifies the Christians against the accusation of godlessness <note>original: "Gottlosigkeit"; in the Roman context, this was the charge of "atheism," meaning the refusal to recognize the state-sanctioned gods</note>. We worship, he says, the sole God, who, in order to reveal Himself, created the immense *mass* of all beings out of *nothing*. His *Word* commanded, His omnipotence executed the command, His wisdom ordered everything; His greatness makes Him known to man, and yet He remains unknown to man. Man's greatest vice consists in not recognizing Him, who does not allow Himself to be misunderstood. After this magnificent announcement of what that God is whom the Christians worship, he presents the most illuminating proofs of all that the holy books teach us about God, whose antiquity, authenticity, and majesty he demonstrates.

The Christians were also accused of high treason <term>Hochverrath; the legal charge of 'maiestas' or offending the dignity of the Roman state</term>, because they did not participate in the sacrifices offered for the Emperors, would not swear by their geniuses <note>The 'Genius' was the protective spirit or divine spark of the Emperor; swearing by it was a required act of political loyalty</note>, and would not call them gods. ## On the Testimony of the Soul.

In his *Apology* <note>original: "Schutzschrift"</note>, when he comes to speak of the unity of God, Tertullian exclaims with his usual fire: "O mighty testimony of the soul, which is Christian by nature!" <note>This refers to the famous Latin phrase "O testimonium animae naturaliter christianae." Tertullian argues that even people who aren't Christian often speak in ways that acknowledge one supreme God.</note> This very thought, which is carried out in an extremely ingenious manner, provided the material for the present small work. The author engages with a soul that is illuminated by the light of reason alone, which knows nothing of the many systems of teaching and the quarrels of the philosophers, and expresses itself entirely according to the impulse of dear, simple nature. He questions this soul on what it thinks about the important article of faith regarding the unity of God, and takes this opportunity to cite all the turns of phrase that were in vogue among the heathens <note>original: "Heyden"</note> and serve as proof of this truth.

The worshippers of the gods, says the author, do not speak well of us because we proclaim a single God, the Creator and uncrowned Arbiter <term>Schiedrichter; a supreme judge or referee who governs the universe</term> of all things. Have the kindness, and tell us, sincere, unbiased soul, your thoughts on this subject. Do we not hear you speak every day? "God has granted this to me." "If God wills," and so forth. Do you not thereby make a confession of a single God? How often do you say: "How good is God, who heaps benefits upon us?" Do you not pray to God for his blessing in the same way the Christian prays? What is more common than the words: "God sees everything"; "I leave that to God’s will"; "God will repay this"; "God will judge between me and you"? How is it that you express yourselves just as we do, though you are not Christians? Even in your temples, in the midst of your idols, before the statues of Jupiter, Aesculapius <note>original: "Aeskulap"; the Greek and Roman god of healing</note>, Isis, and Minerva, in the midst of the devils, the

# Treatise
## Against Hermogenes, or on the Eternity of Matter.

Never, perhaps, has the absurd opinion of the eternity of matter been contested with more successful results than <note>Hermogenes was a late 2nd-century artist and philosopher who argued that God created the world out of pre-existing, eternal matter, rather than out of nothing (ex nihilo). Tertullian viewed this as a threat to God's sovereignty.</note>

->Tertullian.<-

...r, as Tertullian does in this little work. <note>This sentence completes the thought from the previous page: "Against Hermogenes, or on the Eternity of Matter."</note> Hermogenes had renounced Christianity and had himself recruited into the sect of philosophers. He left the Church, the Academy <note>The school of philosophy founded by Plato</note>, and the Porticus <note>The "Porch" or Stoa, where Stoic philosophy was taught</note>, and joined the Stoics, who said that matter has always existed, and is without beginning or end, and that God made use of it when He gave our world its current form.

> "God," they said, "since He created all things, has
> "either drawn them from Himself—that is, from His nature—or
> "created them out of nothing; or He used something for
> "that purpose which already had its existence beforehand. Now, He
> "could not draw things from His nature, because it is
> "simple, immutable, and indivisible. Just as little
> "can He have created them from nothing: for since He is good,
> "indeed infinitely good, He cannot and will not bring
> "forth anything that does not correspond to His goodness and wisdom.
> "However, much evil is found in His works: how
> "does that happen? It cannot come from the will and choice of God;
> "it must therefore come from the matter which God
> "used to shape this world. Consequently, matter is eternal."

Tertullian's answers could not be more correct, precise, or ingenious.

The first attribute of the Godhead, he writes, is the eternity of His existence. But it would no longer be an attribute of God if matter were also eternal. The truth, which compels us to admit a single God, also forces us to confess that everything that belongs to Him must be so uniquely His that it can be found nowhere else but in Him. How then shall matter be eternal?

In vain does Hermogenes tell us, in order to save the rights of the Godhead, that God is indeed unique, the First, the Highest, and the source of everything that ever is. But, Origen <note>original: "Origenes"; a Greek scholar and early Christian theologian (c. 185–253 AD)</note> responds, is not also the

### Tertullian.

...is matter, alongside God, the first of all things and the origin of everything? If he <note>Hermogenes</note> says that matter cannot be compared with God because it stands beneath God and is less than He is, Origen <note>original: "Origenes." While the chapter focuses on Tertullian, the author here likely references Origen's similarly famous refutations of the eternity of matter to bolster the argument.</note> replies: What is eternal and uncreated is incapable of any change and cannot sink to a lower level. God and matter are therefore equal to each other: matter, just like He, can say: "I am the first; I am before all; through me everything exists and persists." Who would dare to place me below God, since both of us, He and I, are without beginning, without end, and without origin? Finally, Hermogenes suggests that God would not be omnipotent without matter, because without it He would have been unable to create anything. In this, he merely parrots the idle dreams of the philosophers, who are the "patriarchs of all heretics." <note>original: "Patriarchen aller Ketzer." This is a famous Tertullian quote—*philosophis, patriarchis hereticorum*—expressing his view that Greek philosophy was the source of all theological error.</note>

Will Hermogenes perhaps say: God uses matter as an artist uses the materials that belong to him? But how can He claim a right over matter, which is independent of Him regarding its very existence? One can have no right over a thing except by title of ownership, by grace <note>In this legalistic sense, "grace" refers to a favor or permission granted by an equal.</note>, or by force. God does not have the right of ownership for the reasons already stated; and the other two titles would run contrary to the majesty and holiness of God, who can neither accept a favor from another nor exercise mere violence.

Matter, says Hermogenes, is the origin of evil. But, Tertullian counters, how can matter be evil, and become the origin of evil? How can that which is eternal, independent, and unchangeable be evil? And if it were evil, how could it be overcome? And if it were invincible, how could one defend oneself against it? How could God punish those who allowed themselves to be defeated?

<meta>This page continues the logical refutation of Hermogenes' philosophy. The previous page ended by questioning God's "right" over matter if it were co-eternal with Him. ### Tertullian.

N 5

Moreover; insofar as this matter is evil: how could God have made something good using this evil matter? If one were to say that it contains the seeds of both good and evil, then one could no longer attribute the good to God as its author. Both good and evil would instead be credited to the account of matter, as it would be the substance that provided the material for both. From such a proposition, the most horrific and—for the Divinity—the most shameful consequences could be drawn.

But if someone were to say, along with Hermogenes, that matter in itself contains nothing good, but rather that whatever is good in creatures was placed into them by God through His omnipotence: then one could turn his own objections against him.

For if matter contains nothing good, then good could not have been extracted from matter either. If it could not be extracted from matter, then it must have come from God. If, however—as Hermogenes believed he had proven from his own principles—it cannot come from the immutable and indivisible <note>original: "unwandel: und untheilbaren"</note> God, then it must surely have been summoned or created out of nothing. And if good could be created out of nothing, why should evil not be able to have one and the same origin? Why not rather admit that God created everything out of nothing <note>This refers to the doctrine of *creatio ex nihilo*, which Tertullian was one of the first major Christian theologians to formalize in response to Gnostic and Platonic ideas.</note>? — One hesitates to let evil come from nothing out of fear that, in this way, God Himself would be made the author of evil. But if one makes matter the source of evil, is the holiness of God truly saved by this detour? One could still always say that the evil which now exists is either a consequence of His will (if He could have prevented it and did not) or a consequence of His inability (if He would have liked to prevent it but was unable to do so). One must read this treatise <note>original: "Schrift." Referring to Tertullian's work *Adversus Hermogenem* (Against Hermogenes).</note> oneself to see how the author lays out the sequence of his logical arguments.

->Tertullian.<-

Hermogenes may twist and turn as he likes, yet in the end he must confess that God becomes the <term>author</term> <note>German: "Urheber." In this context, it refers to the primary source or creator responsible for a thing's existence.</note> of evil as soon as he allows evil to spring from <term>matter</term> <note>In this philosophical debate, "matter" refers to the physical substance that Hermogenes argued was eternal and co-existent with God, rather than created by Him.</note>. This is because he who created evil things is the author of evil, and matter is also the author of evil because evil arose from its very essence. Hermogenes thus entangles himself in absurdities from which he cannot escape, unless he confesses that God created everything from nothing.

The unshakable <term>article of faith</term> <note>German: "Glaubenssatz." A fundamental dogma that cannot be compromised.</note> states: God is unique because He is alone; and He is alone only for the reason that nothing was with Him, and everything first came into being through His omnipotence. Thus, He created everything from nothing. Reason tells us this; the holy books teach us this. Upon these proofs follows a very ingenious interpretation of the beginning of the Book of Genesis and the first chapter of the Gospel of John, where Tertullian clearly exposes the absurdity of Hermogenes and all those doctrinal systems that allow for an eternal matter.

# Treatise
## on the Prescriptions.

The treatise on <term>prescriptions</term> <note>The Latin title is "De Praescriptione Haereticorum." In Roman law, a "praescriptio" was a legal objection that could end a case before it even began. It consists of two parts. The first is a preliminary instruction, or as Tertullian himself calls it, a preface, in which he shows what heresies and heretics are. In the second part, he proves from irrefutable grounds that one should not engage in a word-battle with heretics, nor examine the disputed points with them according to the Scriptures; rather, one must simply present them with the <term>inherited doctrine</term> <note>German: "Erblehre." This refers to the Apostolic Tradition—the teachings passed down directly from the Apostles to the bishops of the Church.</note> and the authority of the Church. He has given this treatise the title: Prescrip-

I know some <term>heretics</term> <note>From the Greek 'hairesis' meaning 'choice'; here referring to groups whose doctrines deviated from the established apostolic tradition.</note> boast that they can ascend with their teaching without difficulty all the way back to the Apostles. Fine! Then let them show us the origin of their church; let them point out the succession of their bishops to us, such that the first of them was an Apostle, or a disciple trained in their school who remained steadfast in the faith of the Apostles. We indeed have churches which were founded later and do not reach back to the times of the Apostles; however, they have received instruction and faith from the apostolic churches, and through their union they form with the original and apostolic church only one and the same Church. Let the heretics show us something significant among themselves. But how should they be able to do this, since the apostolic churches do not admit them to communion?

Let us go even further. Already the Apostles condemned all heresies which have arisen up to our times. Here *Tertullian* shows that the heresies of *Simon* <note>Simon Magus, often called the "father of all heresies."</note>, *Ebion* <note>The Ebionites, a group that emphasized Jewish law and denied the divinity of Christ.</note>, *Valentinus* <note>A prominent Gnostic teacher in the 2nd century.</note>, *Marcion* <note>A teacher who rejected the Old Testament and the God of the Jews, claiming the Father of Jesus was a different deity.</note>, and others still—though they are more cleverly devised and better disguised—have nevertheless already been branded in the letters and writings of the Apostles. And, he adds, should some heresies not be contained in this condemnation, they are no less condemned for the sake of their novelty <note>In the early Church, "novelty" or "newness" was considered a hallmark of error, as truth was believed to be that which was handed down from the beginning.</note>, and because they were announced beforehand. We, he says, we yield the rank to no one; we are the first of all; we go back to the source: consequently, the truth is on our side.

Nothing is more comforting and touching than the picture he paints of the apostolic churches. Do you wish

Afterward, he proves that heresy, just like idolatry, has the devil as its founder. His portrait of heresy is striking, yet so aptly designed that one recognizes in it the features of all heresies...

## Treatise on Baptism.

Tertullian proves within it its necessity and its effects. He begins by rebuking the absurdity of a certain woman, Quintilla by name, who belonged to the sect of the Cainites <note>The Cainites were an early Gnostic sect; Tertullian's work *De Baptismo* is the earliest surviving work on the theology of baptism.</note>, played the role of a teacher of the faith, and claimed that baptism was not necessary. "I pray you," he writes at the end of this tract, "remember in your prayers Tertullian the sinner."

## A Book Against the Valentinians.

Valentinus was a Platonist who had recast the history of the Old and New Covenants to fit the teachings of Platonic philosophy. In his refutation of this heretic, Tertullian chose a humorous tone, which is heavily seasoned with salt. <note>original: *mit Salze gewürzet*—this refers to "Attic salt," a classical term for sophisticated, sharp wit or satire.</note>

# Cyprian.

With good reason, the great Bishop of Carthage, Saint Cyprian, is counted among the most honorable and amiable men of the human race, both in regard to the rare beauty of his character and the grace of his spirit, the wise administration of his church, and the bright-shining splendor of his virtues. He was born in Carthage around the beginning of the third century and was named Thascius Cyprianus. Saint Gregory of Nazianzus <note>A 4th-century Archbishop of Constantinople known as "The Theologian" for his influential defense of the Trinity.</note> informs us that he came from one of the most noble families and held a significant position of dignity in the council of that great city. To acquire everything that Rome and Greece offered in knowledge for the cultivation of the mind and heart was the occupation of his early youth, after which, according to the custom of the young nobility, he dedicated himself to the realm of scholarship. In this career, he soon earned such distinguished fame that he had to yield to the wishes of the entire city and accept the position of a teacher of eloquence <note>original: "Lehrer der Beredsamkeit"—in the Roman world, a professor of rhetoric was a prestigious public intellectual.</note>.

In this post, he distinguished himself so advantageously that his fame grew with each passing day; at the same time, through the innocence of his morals, the charms of his character, the gentleness and grace of his social interactions, and the brilliance of his virtues, he compelled the whole world to hold him in high esteem and love.

While he taught eloquence with such great applause, the first concepts and feelings began to develop in his soul, which brought him closer to Christianity—

J."</note>: for this reason, he added the name Caecilius to the other names he had received from his family.

His companion at baptism was Donatus, his bosom friend, who had rivaled him for fame in eloquence and now, alongside him, paid homage to the Gospel. These two godly friends congratulated each other on their rebirth in Jesus Christ. At the beginning of our Saint's works, there is a wonderful letter to Donatus concerning the change that the grace of baptism had wrought in his soul. We will later have the opportunity to extract some passages from this letter, from which one will be able to judge the spirit, the writing style, and the refined taste of the author.

This transformation of which we speak was so great that—to use the words of his first deacon, Pontius <note>Pontius the Deacon wrote *The Life and Passion of Cyprian*, which is considered one of the earliest examples of Christian biography.</note>, who described the history of his life—he soared to the highest level of Christian perfection before he even had time to be fully instructed in it.
