# Cyprian.

<sig>O 4</sig>

He vowed eternal chastity to God, sold his estates, distributed the proceeds among the poor, and kept nothing for himself except for his gardens located at some distance outside of Carthage <note>A major Roman city in North Africa, near modern-day Tunis, which was a central hub for early Latin Christianity.</note>. He now restricted his entire course of study to the Holy Books <note>Referring here to the Christian Bible.</note>, and practiced every work of mercy, so that he became the refuge, the support, and the comfort of all who turned to him in their affairs. Because of this, as soon as he had been incorporated into the community of the faithful, all eyes were fixed upon him. He was the object of admiration and love for both the people and the clergy, who raised him to the priestly dignity, and shortly thereafter to the bishopric <note>The office of a bishop.</note>. His humility initially resisted this pious insistence; but the faithful occupied all the gates of his house, and since all paths of escape were cut off, he finally had to submit to accepting the pastoral office <term>pastoral office: the role of a "shepherd" or leader of a Christian congregation</term>; and thus, shortly after joining the Church of God, he became the light, the teacher, and the model of the faithful people.

Cyprian's conversion had already struck the pagans <note>original: "Heyden"</note> as significant; but his promotion to the bishopric made them utterly furious. Cyprian had been their favorite as long as he had participated in the religion of the empire; but once he became a Christian, and even the head of the Christians, everyone raged against him. At that time, the persecution of Decius <note>Emperor Trajan Decius (reigned 249–251 AD) ordered the first systematic, empire-wide persecution of Christians, requiring them to perform sacrifices to Roman gods.</note> was raging. While the people were gathered at the theater, they demanded with vehemence that the new bishop be thrown to the lions. Cyprian, in order not to provoke the pagans even more violently, left the city with Victor, one of his deacons, who shortly thereafter won the martyr's crown <note>A traditional metaphor for being executed for one's faith.</note>, and he administered his church from his place of refuge through letters. He gave the wisest instructions on how to deal with those who had fallen away from the faith <note>Known as the "lapsi," these were Christians who had renounced their faith or performed pagan sacrifices under threat of death.</note> during the persecution; he showed an unshakable steadfastness toward those who [disturbed] the church through divisions—

He formed a high opinion of their religion; indeed, he could not deny his respect even for their persons. Fortunately for him, around this same time he became acquainted with a certain priest named Caecilius, who subsequently became his guide and his light in the knowledge of the truth. It is believed with good reason that this Caecilius is the same one who appears in the dialogue of Minucius Felix <note>Marcus Minucius Felix was one of the earliest Latin Christian apologists; his work *Octavius* is written as a debate between a Christian and a pagan.</note>, and who, defeated by Octavius’s speech, renounced paganism and accepted the Christian religion. Throughout his life, Saint Cyprian expressed the most boundless respect and tender gratitude toward the memory of this man, whom he revered as his true father in Christ Jesus <note>original: "C. J."</note>; for this reason, he added the name Caecilius to the other names he had received from his family <note>The saint’s full name became Thascius Caecilius Cyprianus.</note>.

His companion at baptism was Donatus, his bosom friend, who had vied with him for fame in eloquence <term>eloquence: the art of persuasive public speaking, which was a primary career path for the Roman elite</term>, and now paid homage to the Gospel along with him. These two godly friends congratulated each other on their rebirth in Jesus Christ. Preceding the works of our saint is a beautiful letter to Donatus concerning the transformation that the grace of baptism had wrought in his soul. We will later have the opportunity to extract some passages from this writing, from which one will be able to judge the spirit, the writing style, and the refined taste of the author.

This transformation of which we speak was so great that—to use the words of his first deacon, Pontius, who wrote his biography—he soared to the highest level of Christian perfection before he even had time to receive instruction in <meta>catchword: (it)</meta>

# Cyprian.

He swore eternal chastity to God, sold his estates, distributed the proceeds among the poor, and kept nothing for himself but his gardens located at some distance outside Carthage. From then on <note>original: "ißt," an archaic form of "jetzt" meaning now or from that point forward</note>, he restricted all his studies to the Holy Scriptures and practiced every work of mercy, so that he was the refuge, the support, and the comfort of all who turned to him in their affairs. For this reason, even though he had only just been incorporated into the community of the faithful, all eyes were fixed upon him. He was the object of the admiration and love of both the people and the clergy, who raised him to the priestly dignity and, shortly thereafter, to the bishopric. His humility initially resisted this pious insistence, but the faithful occupied all the doors of his house; and since every path to escape was cut off, he finally had to submit to accepting the pastoral office <term>pastoral office: the role of a bishop, viewed as a "shepherd" (pastor) tending to a flock of believers</term>. And thus, shortly after his entry into the Church of God, he became the light, the teacher, and the model for the believing people.

Even Cyprian’s conversion had greatly struck the pagans <note>original: "Heyden"</note>; but his promotion to the bishopric drove them completely to a frenzy. Cyprian had been their favorite as long as he had participated in the religion of the Empire; but since he had become a Christian—and indeed the very head of the Christians—everyone raged against him. At that time, the persecution of Decius <note>The Decian persecution (c. 250 AD) was the first empire-wide organized effort by Roman authorities to force Christians to sacrifice to the Roman gods.</note> was raging. While the people were assembled in the theater <note>original: "Schauplaße"</note>, the crowd clamored impetuously that the new bishop should be thrown to the lions. Cyprian, in order not to incite the pagans even more violently, left the city with Victor, one of his deacons (who soon after won the martyr's crown <note>original: "Marterkrone," a poetic term for dying for the faith</note>), and governed his church from his place of refuge through letters. He gave the wisest instructions on how to deal with those who had fallen away from the faith during the persecution <term>the lapsed: Christians who had renounced their faith or performed pagan sacrifices under threat of death, also known by the Latin term "lapsi"</term>; he showed unshakable steadfastness toward those who confused the church through schisms;

# Cyprian.

...times; and when, after the death of Decius, the storm of persecution gradually subsided under the reign of Gallus and Volusian, he returned again to Carthage. For when a ghastly plague <note>Known to history as the Plague of Cyprian (c. 250–270 AD), this pandemic caused widespread death and was used by pagans to blame Christians for offending the gods.</note> caused the most terrible devastation in the empire, he provided every possible assistance to the sick, without distinguishing between pagans <note>original: "Heyden"</note> and Christians. To settle the ongoing schism <term>schism: a formal split or division within a religious body, in this case concerning the treatment of Christians who had lapsed during persecution</term> in the African Church, he held several councils; and since under the Proconsul of Africa, Demetrius, the persecution—no matter how much it had lessened—still caused several bloody incidents, he made the most earnest representations to him for the benefit of the Christians. These various incidents gave occasion to the writings he composed at that time about martyrdom, about alms-giving, about the murderous plague, and to a multitude of other treatises and instructive, important letters.

He had already administered his office <note>original: "Spigel," likely an archaic variant or OCR error for "Spiegel" (mirror/model) or "Stuhl" (episcopal see)</note> for more than eight years when the persecution flared up anew under the Emperors Valerian and Gallienus. Because of his health, Saint Cyprian was brought from Curubis to the city of Utica <note>original: "Utina," referring to the ancient city of Oudhna or Utica</note>, where the Proconsul was staying at the time. ### V.

In the speech of Saint Cyprian to Demetrianus <note>original: "Demetrius"</note>, the Proconsul of Africa and a cruel persecutor of the Christians, one discovers such a bold fearlessness that today no one would likely take such liberty against even the lowest person of official authority; yet it also contains such strength and refinement as few writers would be capable of imitating. This speech begins as follows:

<margin><unclear>Pierre</unclear></margin>

> “Often, my Demetrianus, I let it suffice to despise the blasphemies which you have uttered with such heat against the true and only God whom the Christians worship. I always thought it better to let the insane chatter of an ignorant man vanish into the air, as if unnoticed, than to provoke him through answers. This was taught to me by the sacred principles of our divine books. But since you often come to me, more with the intention of offering me a battle of words than to instruct yourself; more to let me hear your blasphemies than to hear my reasons: So I believed it would be wasted effort to maintain further conversation with you from now on. For it means wasting one's time when one holds a torch before the blind, reasons before the deaf, and preaches rules of wisdom to a soul that is without feeling for wisdom. These considerations moved me to <meta>catchword: silence [schweigen]</meta>

...silent, and I resolved to oppose the most patient of creatures with nothing but patience, because my instruction would gain nothing over your unteachableness, nor would my holy intentions overcome your impiety, nor my moderation overcome your irascibility. In the future, it would no longer be seen as the effect of our modesty, but as a consequence of mistrust in the justice of our cause; and one could easily mistake the contempt for your accusations as a silent confession of the vices you charge us with. I shall answer you, according to your own nature, Demetrius <note>Saint Cyprian is addressing Demetrianus, the Proconsul of Africa, though the text uses the shortened name "Demetrius."</note>, and those whom you incessantly incite against us."

After Saint Cyprian has refuted the accusations of the heathens as wisely as he has thoroughly, he turns against the idolaters themselves, and says to them:

> “You complain about infertility and hunger. And what is now the foremost cause of this shortage? Is it the drought, or rather the greed of men? Why does the scarcity grow so immensely? Through the increase in prices and the shameful <term>grain-profiteering</term> <note>original: "Kornkiperey." This refers to the practice of hoarding grain to artificially drive up prices during a shortage.</note>. You complain that the heavens are closed and deny us a fruitful rain. What! Are your granaries not far more closed than the heavens? You raise an outcry that the earth bears nothing, yet do you let the thirsty share in its yields?”

> “You wail about plague and disease. And do the vices not multiply through these very scourges themselves, because inhumanity ignores the dying, and avarice greedily plunders the dead? The terror, which the sight of so much misfortune should instill, nowhere awakens the desire for virtue and innocence; and among an army of the dead and dying, no one reflects on the fact that he himself is mortal. On all sides people run—”

people steal and rob; they no longer feel any shame and consider all caution and restraint unnecessary. Greed shows itself with its visor raised <note>original: "mit zurückgeschlagenem Helme." The common modes of death no longer suffice for you; you incessantly devise new and newer sufferings with an ingenious cruelty. What an insatiable rage to torment! Give an answer: is it a crime to be a Christian, or not? If it is a crime, why do you not condemn us to death immediately after the confession? But if it is none, why do you persecute the innocent?”

## Excerpts,

->from which one can conclude the prudence and wisdom<-
->of the Saint in the administration of his church.<-

->I.<-

Nothing shows us Cyprian’s beautiful soul, his tender heart, and at the same time his wisdom and steadfast courage in the administration of his church better than his discourse concerning those who had fallen away from the faith during the persecution of Decius <note>Decius (reigned 249–251 AD) issued an edict requiring everyone in the Roman Empire to perform a sacrifice to the Roman gods, which triggered a crisis for the Christian community.</note>, and who now wish to be reconciled with the Church once again. But to enable the reader to form a correct judgment regarding the excerpts to be included, we must acquaint them with the various degrees of this unfaithfulness committed against the faith.

One can easily imagine how great the horror and unrest must have been among the Christians when the court announced the outbreak of the persecution. Some, who on the one hand did not want to renounce the faith, but on the other hand feared the martyrdom <note>original: "Marter," referring to the physical suffering or torture endured for one's beliefs.</note>, had money offered to the judges in order not to be summoned before the court; they purchased certificates of safety <note>original: "Freybriefe." These were documents known as *libelli*.</note>, which secured them against official investigation and falsely testified that they had indeed already renounced the faith and sacrificed to the gods. These were called, after the Latin, <term>Libellatici</term> <note>original: "Libellaticier." From the Latin *libellus*, meaning a "little book" or document. These individuals did not actually sacrifice but paid for a document saying they had.</note>, or people who were provided with a certificate of liberty. Others had been led before the judge, where at the beginning they confessed Christ, but lost heart when they were approached with torture and pain. Still others had even bravely endured some time in the midst of the martyrdom: but subsequently, the pain overcame them; they surrendered, and renounced the religion. Finally, some fell at the first question, or perhaps even anticipated all the feared unpleas—

infidelities, performed sacrifices to the gods, and participated in all the superstitions of idolatry.

These fallen Christians were, for the most part, tortured by remorse and desired to be reconciled with the Church once again. To this end, they turned to the confessors and martyrs who lay in chains for the sake of the faith, and entreated them for letters of recommendation <note>These were known as *libelli pacis*, or "letters of peace," through which those suffering for the faith interceded for those who had fallen.</note> to their priests and bishops. I note on this occasion that the name of **Confessors** was given to those who had confessed Jesus before the judges and, for that cause, had been condemned to perpetual imprisonment. **Martyrs**, however, was the name given to those who had not only confessed Jesus with words but had also endured torture and agony for the sake of the faith. Now, there were some martyrs who granted these letters of remission and reconciliation with a kind of light-mindedness, without regard for the diversity of the cases in which the defectors <note>original: "Ueberläufer," referring to those who had "run over" to paganism during the persecution.</note> found themselves; just as there were also priests who were far too willing to allow everyone to be admitted to reconciliation.

Saint Cyprian distinguishes all these different cases with wisdom; and he intends that their diversity should be the guideline for conduct toward these people. One should not immediately receive all the fallen, without distinction, back into the bosom of the Church, but rather test them more or less thoroughly, according to whether their fall had been more or less severe, and whether it was more or less punishable by that measure. — This explanation seemed necessary to us for a better understanding of the whole. Now we come to the discourse itself.

It begins with expressions of joy, admiration, and gratitude for the end of the persecution and the return of peace. First, he presents the shining spectacle of these numerous confessors and martyrs of every age and gender, and from all...

> “Despite all the radiance of the heavenly crowns of our martyrs, regardless of the spiritual glory of the confessors <note>Confessors were those who had maintained their faith under questioning or imprisonment but were not executed.</note>, my soul nevertheless swims in a sea of bitterness. A part of my very vitals <note>original: "Eingeweides." In the ancient world, the "bowels" or "vitals" were considered the seat of deep compassion and familial love.</note> is being torn from my body. The enemy has wrought a terrible devastation through the fall of a great number of our brothers. Amidst this unrest, amidst this struggle of intersecting thoughts that divide my spirit, what should I do? What should I say? Not through words, but through tears alone can I lay bare my grief. For what kind of heart of stone would it have to be, which could remain insensitive to the stirrings of brotherly love, and could look upon the deplorable misfortune and the disfigured remnant of the Christians with a dry eye? Must not sighs take the place of words in this situation? I am completely bowed down by pain, and I take the most sincere part in yours; my strength is not enough to raise me from my dejection. I am the shepherd, and I feel all the wounds of my flock. My heart is chained to yours, and I bear with you the entire burden of your sufferings and your unfaithfulness. I mix my tears and sighs among yours. It seems to me that I have suffered shipwreck with you; my vitals too were pierced by the dagger that struck you, and my soul has felt the blow of persecution just as much as you.”

> “Meanwhile, my brothers, in the present matter we must let ourselves be guided by reason; and I do not think that the darkness of persecution has so completely blinded our brothers that they should lack the insight to recognize what God’s will and command require. Let the cause of our misfortunes only be maturely investigated, and the remedy will soon be discovered. God wished to put His children to the proof. Through the long period of peace, all the laws of church discipline <term>Kirchenzucht: the internal rules and moral standards governing the conduct of church members</term> had slackened; a warning from heaven was needed to startle the slumbering faith. And since we had deserved a far harsher punishment, the all-merciful God so tempered the matter that what has happened must be regarded more as a trial than as a persecution.

Then the Saint shows how far the slackening of zeal had progressed among the Christians. The picture is vivid and striking. Greed, luxury, a taste for amusements, the contempt for church customs and their laws, the sluggish indifference or the bad example of the priests, and among them likely also the bishops—these, says Saint Cyprian, were the causes of the falling away <note>The "falling away" or apostasy refers to Christians renouncing their faith to avoid execution.</note> of so many of the faithful.

Since, however, many of those who had fallen earnestly desired to be received back into the Christian community, they petitioned the martyrs for letters of peace and reconciliation <note>original: "Friedens- und Aussöhnungsbriefe." Historically known as *Libelli pacis*, these were written appeals from those about to die for their faith, asking the Bishop to be lenient toward a specific fallen person.</note>, and believed that they must be immediately reinstated to all the rights of the faithful based on these letters of recommendation. Here, this true shepherd showed all the wisdom and fearlessness of a worthy successor of the Apostles. He divides the fallen into several classes and distinguishes those who lost their courage and steadfastness under torture from those who had purchased certificates of exemption <note>original: "Freyheitsbriefe." Known as *libellatici*, these individuals had not sacrificed to pagan gods but had bribed officials to give them a certificate stating they had complied with the law.</note> so that they would not have to appear before the judges; and these again from others who, at the very first questions, renounced Christian—

That would be a poor doctor who feared to press an abscess. By doing so, the trapped pus would only eat away at its surroundings. One must reveal the wound, one must cut, and through cutting, seek to heal. The patient may well be annoyed by it, complain and cry out; but after the recovery, he will be thankful.”

### III.

Here is further evidence of the fearless steadfastness with which Saint Cyprian watched over the maintenance of church discipline <note>original: "Kirchenzucht"; this refers to the code of conduct and corrective measures used by the early Church to maintain its spiritual integrity.</note>. Bishop Rogatian had written to him, stating that he had been grossly insulted by one of his deacons. He brought the complaint to his Metropolitan Bishop <note>A high-ranking bishop with authority over a provincial group of churches.</note> and, at the same time, sought advice on how he should deal with the guilty party. Saint Cyprian replied to him:

> This deacon must be directed toward penance because of his audacity. Let him learn what he owes to the episcopal dignity, and let him submit to the necessary restitution. If he will not comply, then let him be deposed from his office and placed under a ban <note>original: "Banne"; essentially excommunication or a formal exclusion from the religious community.</note>. And because you mention another Christian who has made common cause with the deacon, you may also punish him or exclude him from the Christian community. Moreover, my advice would be to conduct yourself in such a way that they recognize their own error and make amends, and let you fulfill your duty undisturbed in the future. For it is always better that we show kindness and bear insults with patience than that we avenge them with pastoral authority.

### IV.

In the first centuries of the Church, it was forbidden—and this prohibition remained in force for a long time—to assign a legal guardianship <note>original: "Vormundschaft"; in Roman society, this involved the management of estates and legal affairs for minors, a role the Church felt distracted the clergy from their spiritual mission.</note> to anyone among the clergy. Geminius Victor from the city of Furni had appointed the priest Geminius Faustinus, who we may likely assume was his close cousin, as the guardian of his children. The Saint wrote to the clergy and the citizenry of the city, letting them know how painfully he felt this violation of church discipline. He stated that this was a matter forbidden by the Councils, which did not want persons consecrated to the service of God to be hindered in their holy duties

<meta>This page transitions from the biography of Saint Cyprian to the life of Arnobius. # Arnobius.

Behold here the most remarkable of those illustrious men who left behind the service of idols <note>original: "Götzendienst"; referring to the worship of pagan deities</note> and swore allegiance to the banner of Christ. Arnobius <note>original: "Arnob"; the author uses a shortened version of the Latin name Arnobius</note> is this famous refugee, who taught eloquence <term>eloquence: the art of rhetoric and public speaking, a highly respected profession in Roman society</term> at Sicca, one of the premier cities of Africa. He was equipped with all the knowledge that philosophy, history, poetry, mythology, or the pagan study of the gods could provide; and since he knew Christianity only from the hateful portrayals of idolaters, he had often lashed out soundly at the followers of this religion. Nevertheless, despite all his prejudices and his heated imagination, the heroic virtues he frequently observed in the Christians struck him. This impression grew stronger with each passing day; his aversion turned into high esteem, he changed his way of thinking, and finally desired to be accepted among the believers himself.

The Christians of Sicca judged Arnobius just as the inhabitants of the city of Damascus once judged Saint Paul. His expression of faith was suspicious to them; they regarded him as a rhetorical babbler <note>original: "rhetorischen Schwätzer"; implying someone who uses sophisticated speech to deceive others</note> who was an enemy of Christianity at heart, and they rejected his request. Arnobius guessed the entire reason for their refusal without difficulty, and to put an end to all these doubts at once and provide an undeniable proof of his sincerity, he offered to attack the pagan religion with all the strength of which he was capable: and this he achieved in a great work entitled: *Disputations against the Pagans* <note>original: "Streitreden wider die Heyden"; known in Latin as *Adversus Gentes*</note>.

# Arnobius.

If one examines this book, one clearly discovers from the sublime concept he provides of **Jesus**, and from the holiness of Christian moral teaching, that **Arnobius** <note>original: "Arnob,"</note> has studied the Gospel well; but at the same time, one realizes that he must have known nothing of **Moses**, the prophets, or the other books of the Old Covenant <note>The Old Testament</note>, because he never cites them on his own behalf. Since he occupied himself solely with vividly exposing the ridiculous, tasteless, and absurd nature of the pagan religion, and with contesting the false principles and wretched conclusions behind which the pagans entrenched themselves, he also borrowed all his arguments from reason alone; that is, from an unspoiled, simple, and robust <note>original: "körnigen"; literally "grainy," implying something substantial or solid</note> reason to which one must surrender. He shatters his enemies through the strength of his arguments, through the immense scope of his wide reading, through the testimony of their own most credible and prestigious historians, and by forcing from them a confession of the impossibility of glossing over the revolting abominations of their religion in any way.

The little diligence he had devoted to Holy Scripture, and his prevailing taste for **Platonic philosophy**, are the reasons why he sometimes adopts the ideas of this famous sage <note>Referring to Plato</note> as his own and falls into error, especially when he comes to speak of the origin and nature of the soul, as is evident from his second book. However, one must remember that **Arnobius**, while he was composing his book, was still a pagan <note>Arnobius reportedly wrote his apology while still a candidate for baptism (a catechumen) to prove his sincerity to the bishop</note> and had little contact with Christians. For this reason, all the dogmas of pagan theology are no less thoroughly refuted, and this was actually the entire intention of this great man. He never intended to teach or prove the truths of Christianity, but rather to expose the absurdities of its rival, the pagan religion, and this he achieved with the greatest success; [as...] <meta>The final syllable "wi-" likely continues as "wider" (against) or "wie" (as/how) on the next page.</meta>

## First Book.

### On the Injustice of the Complaints and the Hatred of the Pagans Against Christianity.

We wish to present the content of the first book in the author's own words. "Since I noticed some time ago," he says in the introduction, "that certain supposed sages, blinded by their prejudices, are making a noise in a fanatical tone; [claiming] the gods, because they have seen their temples and altars abandoned since the introduction of Christianity, have given up their tender and beneficial care for the world <note>original: "Unterwelt," literally "underworld," but here referring to the earthly realm as opposed to the heavens</note>, and out of revenge have visited the human race with punishments of every kind; so I have decided to apply my meager insights and talents to the refutation of these slanderous accusations, and to dispel every pretext for hatred against the Christian name."

"My intention in this is to prevent the idolaters from taking their hollow, utterly wretched babble for important arguments, and—should we fail to defend ourselves—from believing that they owe their victory not to our silence, but to the weakness of our cause and the strength of the truth <note>In this context, Arnobius refers to the pagans' perceived "truth" of their own arguments</note>."

The accusation with which they come against us could not be more serious: and if it can be proven that we are the cause of the terrible judgments that devastate our globe and shake this universe,

->You clamor incessantly that, since Christians have existed, all laws of nature have been thrown out of joint.<-

In Arnobius’s <note>Arnobius of Sicca (died c. 330 AD) was an Early Christian apologist who converted from paganism and wrote during the Great Persecution</note> answer to this first complaint, everything is united that philosophy, eloquence, and the most fortunate imagination can bring forth in terms of brilliance, instruction, and persuasion. His spirit soars to the stars and describes the path of the heavenly bodies; he wanders through the earth and considers it according to the physical and moral order; he consults the oldest histories to judge with reason the scourges of the human race—plague, war, drought, and famine—and in the end, it appears that the world still follows its old pace. Your question has nothing to do with the present matter. However, if you simply wish to know what I think about it, I could tell you, and so forth. # Arnobius.

...to penetrate [the mysteries of] God, to master His providence, and to attempt to measure the infinite and incomprehensible wisdom of the Supreme Being with his own dull reason. In all these answers, a great deal of wit and strength prevails.

"It is the Christians," the pagans continued, "who provoke the wrath of the gods." "Softly now, if I may," Arnobius <note>Arnobius often uses a satirical, lawyer-like tone in his writing, reflecting his background as a rhetorician</note> cries out: "this insolence of yours is truly too mad. Has the world been incessantly plagued with punishments in the three hundred years since Christians have existed? How many victories have the Romans won? How much have they expanded the borders of the Empire? How many previously unknown nations have they subjugated? What abundance has frequently prevailed? Even if there were occasional misfortunes—if drought and plagues appeared—what can really be concluded from that? A wise man sees in this nothing but the shifts and changes that have always existed in nature."

"You accuse us," he continues, "of replacing the old religion with a form of worship full of godlessness. Tell us, by your grace, you 'hallowed interpreters of the deity,' who are more godless: those who worship an eternal God, the Creator and Lord of the world, or those who slaughter sacrifices to horned and goat-footed forest-demons <note>referring to satyrs and fauns in Roman mythology</note>, harlots, and animals of every kind?" After he has made the ridiculous and absurd nature of these pagan dogmas quite palpable, he provides the most moving and sublime concept of the true God—the one we recognize through the "light of nature" <note>the philosophical idea that human reason alone can deduce the existence of a creator</note>, and whose image is engraved upon our souls with indelible strokes.

"We do not fault you," said the pagans, "for worshipping the great and all-ruling God; but that you bestow divine honors upon a man who was born like any other, and who finally died on the gallows <note>original: "Galgen"; a derogatory pagan reference to the Cross, which was viewed as a shameful instrument of execution for criminals</note>—that is what is condemned in you."

# Arnobius.

"And did not," Arnobius answers them, "all gods have fathers and mothers?" On this occasion, he reminds them with the utmost detail of the genealogy of their gods and adds: "If you have placed [these beings] in the rank of the gods for the sake of the benefits they are said to have shown to the human race, then surely no one deserves to be worshipped out of gratitude more than Jesus Christ." "This great teacher," he says with delight, "has led me onto the path of wisdom; he has taught me to think worthily of God: In this life, we have everything from Him, and in the coming one, we hope for even more, incomparably, from His goodness. And should I not worship Him, or recognize Him as my God?"

"But you say, He died on the cross." Does a cruel and painful death perhaps diminish virtue and goodness? What do you think of Pythagoras, of Socrates, of Aquilius, and of Regulus <note>Arnobius refers to historical figures who suffered famous, agonizing deaths: Manius Aquillius, a Roman consul executed with molten gold, and Marcus Atilius Regulus, who was reportedly tortured by the Carthaginians</note>, who were driven out of this world through the most terrible tortures? Do you not offer sacrifices to Bacchus, to Hercules, to Itys, and to Romulus, whose fates cannot be unknown to you? <note>These figures from myth and history all met violent ends: Bacchus was said to have been torn apart by Titans, Hercules died by fire, Itys was killed and served as a meal, and Romulus was allegedly murdered by senators</note> Either you are not quite right in your heads for worshipping people who were torn to pieces, or executed by fire and sword, or you cannot find it so very wrong that we worship the crucified Jesus. We worship Him because He is God and man at once; man like us, and God like His heavenly Father. — One can imagine nothing greater, nothing more sublime and more moving than the portrait he paints of Jesus Christ, of His life, miracles, virtues, and benefactions.

When the pagans countered the brilliant and undeniable miracles of Jesus Christ with the myths and petty illusions <note>original: "Blendwerke"</note> with which the common people occupied themselves regarding their gods, Arnobius answered them in a way that they must surely have been ashamed of their comparison.

## Second Book.

### On the Reasons Why Christians Believe in the Life and Miracles of Jesus Christ.

# Book Three.

## On the Nature of the Pagan Gods.

The third book is a treatise on the gods of <term>paganism</term> <note>original: "Heydenthum"</note>. One will hardly find a work where more wit and erudition prevail, or where the biting salt of a clever jest is more ingeniously applied. ## Fourth Book.
### On the Origin of the Gods.

The investigations into the origin of the gods are the content of the fourth book. "Romans," says the author, "you are masters of the world; you build the most magnificent temples to Concord, Honor, Piety, Virtue, and Fortune <note>Arnobius is referring to the Roman practice of personifying abstract qualities as deities, known as *indigitamenta*.</note>. We cannot, no matter how much effort we exert, find anything divine in them; we see nothing more than the peace-loving, pious, virtuous, honored, and happy man. We pass the same judgment on their opposites—Discord, Injustice, Impiety, and Unbelief: these are nothing more than words by which we reveal our judgment regarding a person's character <note>original: "Sinnesart eines Menschen." Arnobius argues that virtues are human qualities, not external supernatural beings.</note>.

# Arnobius.

...tearing down theaters where such horrors daily offend the ears and eyes.

You burn our books; you tear down the churches where we are instilled with gentleness, honor, decency, love, and magnanimity toward our fellow human beings; where we pray to God for the authorities and princes, for our friends and enemies. And yet, since you hold the power in your hands, you treat us as godless villains because we abhor your own godlessness.

# Fifth Book.

## On the Origin of Pagan Ceremonies and Mysteries.

In this book, there is a list of facts which, in the minds of the **Pagans** <note>original: "Heyden," referring to practitioners of traditional Roman polytheism</note>, are the holiest and most sublime things, and upon which their divine worship, ceremonies, and the greatest festivities of the religion of the empire are based. The whole of it is very entertaining and extremely important. Arnobius refers to the authority of the most credible writers, all of whom he cites, and unhesitatingly makes the most biting and humbling remarks about the Pagans, whose stupid gullibility regarding their religion he mocks. He begins with the alleged instruction that the nymph **Egeria** <note>Egeria was a legendary nymph or goddess said to have been the counselor and wife of Numa Pompilius</note> is said to have given to the second Roman king, **Numa**.

Numa, he says, was somewhat at a loss for a reliable means to deflect lightning. He turned to the goddess Egeria for good advice. She told the king in strict confidence: There were two gods in the neighborhood, **Faunus and Picus** <note>Ancient Italian nature deities associated with prophecy and the woods</note>, who possessed this secret. They occasionally came to a spring that she named for him. He must place two large vessels of wine there: they would inevitably

# Arnobius.

...the gods, if they were wise, would prefer the juice of the vine <note>i.e., wine</note> to water, get drunk, and fall asleep. In this state, one would have to surprise them, bind them, and upon their awakening, compel them to reveal the secret. **Numa** obeyed exactly. The two deities enjoyed the drink, became intoxicated, fell asleep, were bound, and under the "torture" of their bonds taught **Numa** the means to lure **Jupiter** down from heaven. The father of the gods did indeed come, and in the end, after a long exchange of words, the clever **Numa** wheedled the secret out of the incautious **Jupiter** regarding what kind of sacrifice could deflect lightning. **Arnobius** seasons the entire passage with the sharpest and most witty salt <note>A classical metaphor for biting satire or "Attic wit"</note>.

Next follows a long-winded history of the mother of the gods, **Cybele**, which we shall, however, summarize briefly. **Arnobius** recounts her birth, her love affairs, the debaucheries and follies she committed, and the shameful deeds of her **Attis** <note>original: "Atys"</note> and his priests, who were called **Salians** or **Gauls** <note>original: "Salier oder Gallier"; Arnobius refers here to the "Galli," the eunuch priests of Cybele</note>. The pagans may well say that these stories are nothing but fairy tales; yet **Arnobius** refers to one of the most famous teachers of the pagan religion, **Timotheus**, and a thousand others who have written in exactly this same vein. Against the pagans themselves, he cites the mysteries of the "Good Goddess," where precisely those things are reenacted which the historians recount.

This would be the place, says **Arnobius**, to speak of all the other mysteries of paganism, the secrets of which are known only to a small number of those called the **Initiates**. But the vast scope of the material does not allow us to do so—or rather, to speak more plainly, we are reluctant to touch upon certain of these mysteries for fear of staining our own hearts by a more detailed account of them. As a result of this prudent choice, he contents himself with merely listing their names. Who can [bear] the incest of **Jupiter** with his mother...

The Eleusinian mysteries <note>The secret religious rites of ancient Greece dedicated to the goddesses Demeter and Persephone</note> were far too famous for no mention to be made of them in this book. Arnobius’s cautious regard for propriety does not prevent him from exposing all the horrors <note>original: "Gräuel"</note> therein: and because they were good for nothing but training all people, without distinction of age, sex, or status, for vice or debauchery, the author, in the heat of his zeal, turns to the heathens and speaks: "Behold, of this sort are the religious customs to which you wish to force us with fire and swords, and through the most inhuman tortures. These gods you force upon us; gods whom you yourselves would be ashamed to resemble, and you would be angry with your children or relatives if any among them wished to imitate them."

You pretend, indeed, that these stories—which are not exactly edifying in themselves—are nothing more than symbols <note>original: "Sinnbilder"</note> which contain great truths. But why then must these great truths be wrapped in such a filthy covering? Are your gods treated any less poorly because of it? And how do you prove to us that your writers, when they scribbled this foul material, were thinking of these symbols? Even if it is sometimes possible to extract a symbolic meaning from some of these deeds, secrets, and ceremonies, it is not possible to find the slightest trace of a metaphorical sense in a multitude of others. This entire fragment is written with uncommon fire and exposes the horrors of paganism with the most vivid certainty.

Arnobius.

...even the name bestowed upon them is venerable; this you must yourselves admit. Are you not therefore blameworthy, since you so abominably desecrate the names of your deities, using them to designate the frenzy of war, riotous excesses, wine, and even the most base and contemptible things? All these things already have their own names; what obsession drives you to bestow the names of the gods upon them? You are but men, and yet you would find yourselves insulted by such a misuse. Why then do you so dishonor your gods?

## Book Six

### Concerning the Temples and Statues of the Gods

Valuable investigations into the temples and images <note>original: "Göttuen," likely a transcription error for "Götzen" (idols) or "Göttinnen" (goddesses)</note>, or statues of the gods, constitute the contents of the sixth book. The manner in which Arnobius <note>Arnobius of Sicca (died c. 330 AD) was an early Christian convert and author of *Adversus Nationes*, an apology written to prove the sincerity of his conversion.</note> speaks in this and largely also in the other books always refers to the concept that the heathens <term>heathens: here referring to practitioners of traditional Roman and Greek religion</term> formed of their deities. According to the principles of their religion, they did not recognize God under the image of a unique, purely spiritual, and omnipresent being; rather, their gods, with their presumed divinity, had inherited the entire lot of frail humanity, in both good and evil aspects. I believed I owed my readers this remark so that they might be better able, by means of it, to place themselves into the spirit of the writer.

What purpose do you have, then, Arnobius asks the pagans, when you erect temples to your gods? Viewed with physical eyes, they are magnificent; but how small they become when held against the majesty and greatness of the gods? You are merely building houses for them. For do you not say yourselves: See where Apollo, where Mars, where Jupiter dwells; we go there in order to...

The beautiful temple of Capitoline Jupiter was the burial place of *Olus Vulcentanus*; his head was found there, and the place was called the *Capitolium* <note>original: "Caput Oli" — meaning "Head of Olus." "This is certainly saying something," speaks **Arnob.** <note>Abbreviation for Arnobius of Sicca (c. 255–330 AD), a Christian apologist who wrote against the pagan traditions he once followed.</note> "But do you know for certain that the gods take possession of the statues after this solemn ceremony? Does it happen voluntarily, or through the irresistible power of the consecration? Do they arrive to stay there forever, or do they stay only when and as long as they wish?" **Arnobius** sets out all the consequences of his questions perfectly well and continues: "There are statues which are exceedingly small, hardly the size of marmots <note>original: "Murmelthierchen" — a small alpine rodent; Arnobius uses this comparison to mock the idea of a vast god inhabiting a tiny figurine.</note>. It will be hard for the good gods if they must squeeze themselves into these tiny containers. You have statues of Jupiter, Vulcan, and Apollo by the thousands; they must surely divide themselves to dwell in all these statues at one and the same time. But if these deities dwell in the statues, why do you then fasten them with iron hooks and bands? Why such a numerous guard around..."

# Seventh Book.

## Concerning the Sacrifices and Ceremonies of the Pagan Religion.

Arnobius <note>original: "Arnob" — referring to Arnobius of Sicca (died c. 330 AD), a North African convert to Christianity who wrote "Adversus Gentes" (Against the Pagans) to prove his new faith.</note> concludes his great work against the pagan religion by examining their sacrifices and ceremonies. Regarding the first establishment of sacrifices, he does not consult revelation <note>meaning he does not rely on the Bible or Christian scripture to argue his point.</note>. Instead, he treats the matter philosophically, focusing entirely on the concept that the pagans held of their own gods. It is enough for him to rebuke all that is extravagant and tasteless in these sacred rituals; and it must be admitted that he has used these advantages quite masterfully.

He establishes as a foundational truth that the divine nature is self-sufficient and requires nothing outside of itself for its own happiness; and then he asks the pagans on what grounds they brought sacrifices to their gods, and what benefit these sacrifices yielded to those deities.

Will it perhaps be said that these sacrifices serve as food for the gods, and that they find pleasure in them? But in these sacrifices I see only fragrances which vanish, blood which the dogs lick up, the entrails of animals and the fat over the embers, and I perceive therein only a pestilential stench. And where in all this is there anything suitable for a deity, who must be incorporeal <note>without a physical body</note>, spiritual, and immortal? As for the pleasure of the gods, can they truly find any in this? Do they perhaps take their great delight in the wretched groaning of these poor animals under the priest's knife, in the streaming blood, or in the final convulsions of the dying limbs? We ourselves, despite all our wildness, turn away from this spectacle; and yet! Gods, whose distinguishing characteristics...

<summary>In this opening to the seventh book, Arnobius argues that sacrifice is logically incompatible with the nature of a perfect, immortal deity who lacks nothing. He mocks the idea that gods could be nourished by the physical remains or the suffering of slaughtered animals.</summary>

---

(*) Arnobius's reasons against pagan sacrifices cannot be applied to the sacrifices of the Jews, which were offered in the Old Covenant to the true God, even by His own command. For these are personal proofs against the heathens—which in the language of the schools are called <term>argumenta ad hominem</term> <note>Latin: "arguments to the man." This refers to a logical tactic where the speaker uses the opponent’s own beliefs and logic against them, rather than arguing from a universal truth.</note>—whereby one uses the situation, the various relationships, and the existing opinions of one's opponent to one's own advantage. These proofs were based on the delusion of the pagans that the gods were physically enclosed within statues and were not immeasurable. The Jewish sacrifices, however, were explicitly prescribed and determined through a revelation given to Moses, both regarding the selection of these sacrificial animals and the manner of slaughtering them, as well as the object, the intention, and the ultimate purpose which one must have when offering sacrifices to the true God.

# Arnobius.

...shower them with benefits. First, I could answer you, says Arnobius <note>Arnobius of Sicca was a 4th-century Christian apologist who wrote 'Adversus Nationes' (Against the Heathen) to defend his new faith.</note>, that your demands and your confidence are not so very firmly grounded. For there is an innumerable multitude of people who hold to the doctrine of unavoidable fate <note>original: "unvermeidlichen Geschickes"</note>. And if destiny holds sway, how can your gods bestow benefits that are not possible, or turn away evils which must necessarily occur? Arnobius treats this subject in a quite convincing manner, and continues as follows:

But leaving unavoidable fate aside, I ask you: Do your gods sell their favor? And at what price? Perhaps for so-and-so many jugs or buckets of goat, sheep, or bull blood? If a rich man with a wicked soul has a hundred sacrificial animals burned, while a poor man with a pure conscience cannot even slaughter a single little lamb; which of these two will they hear? And if two enemy nations, each for itself, brought sacrifices in equal number, for which of the two must the gods declare themselves?

The reason why we sacrifice, you say, is the glorification of the gods. So you believe then, Arnobius replies, that the honor and majesty of the gods is capable of increase? You have, in fact, a high concept of them, and they are truly deeply indebted to you. According to your way of thinking, they are enlarged and glorified when you drag sheep, goats, and bulls, bound and gagged, to their altars and slaughter them? If they are such great lovers of blood, then go to it! Slay mules, elephants, dogs, bears, and horses for them.

One honors the gods, you continue, when one sacrifices to them out of gratitude that which serves us as food. That may be very well thought out, repl- <meta>catchword: repl- (likely completing "versetzt," meaning "replied")</meta>

# Arnobius.

Arnobius: but if horses, donkeys, dogs, and pigs possessed reason, recognized our superior dignity, and regarded us as gods, would we consider it a great honor if they were to sacrifice hay, bones, and whatever else they use for fodder to us? Do the immortals gain in glory and reputation if we offer them such materials as sacrifice, which shortly thereafter dissolve into the most disgusting decay? Now **Arnobius** mocks the distinctions among the sacrifices that had to be rendered to the gods according to the differences in their status, rank, and age. Why, he writes, does one sacrifice bulls to this one, lambs to that one, suckling pigs to a third, cows to one, horned he-goats to another, white animals here, black animals there, females in one place, and males in another? Regarding all of this, he makes his own remarks, seasoned with much biting wit <note>original: "mit vielem beißenden Salze versezte Anmerkungen," literally "remarks mixed with much biting salt," a classical metaphor for sharp, clever humor</note>.

He continues with his questions, asking the heathens <note>The term "heathens" or "pagans" refers to the practitioners of the traditional Roman religion that Arnobius had abandoned</note> to explain the mystery of why they slaughtered virginal sacrifices to the virgin Minerva <note>The goddess of wisdom and war</note>, but pregnant animals to Mother Tellus <note>Tellus was the Roman personification of the Earth</note>. If this is done because of a correspondence of virginity between Minerva and her sacrifices, and of fertility between Tellus and her slaughtered beasts, then one ought to slaughter physicians to Aesculapius <note>The god of medicine</note>, blacksmiths' apprentices to Vulcan <note>The god of fire and metalworking</note>, orators to Mercury <note>The messenger god associated with eloquence and trade</note>, and musicians to Apollo <note>The god of music and the arts</note>. But if one finds this suggestion ridiculous, then the reasoning that prompted it must be even more ridiculous. He also jests about the gods themselves, depicting them as gluttons and lovers of delicacies, and about the priests, who act as their chief kitchen-overseers and stewards, choosing the portions of the sacrifice to be set before the gods and determining how they should be seasoned and prepared according to each one's taste.

### Arnobius.

...employ <note>The sentence starts mid-thought from the previous page, likely referring to the methods or arguments Arnobius uses.</note>, whereby the gods of paganism play a very silly role. We will not pursue these investigations in more detail, and refer our readers to the author himself.

Now the turn comes to the great festivals of paganism: the baths of the Mother of all Gods <note>original: "Mutter aller Götter"; referring to the goddess Cybele and the ritual washing of her statue, the *Lavatio*.</note>, the festivities of Jupiter, Aesculapius’s grape harvest, Ceres’s ceremonial bed <note>likely referring to the *Lectisternium*, a ritual banquet where images of gods were placed on couches.</note>, the games of the goddess Flora, and the Great Goddess. None of these improper and ridiculous ceremonies escapes our Arnobius, and he challenges the pagans to give him reasons for the introduction of these various festivities and amusements, which are covered with the cloak of religion.

Because the pagans claimed they hold these festivals and give these games in honor of their gods, Arnobius says to them: What conception are we to form of all these deities? Of the Mother of the Gods, who must use baths; of a Jupiter, who arranges drinking bouts and provides banquets; of an Aesculapius who holds a grape harvest; of a Ceres who wallows in soft down feathers? — "See," you say, "that makes the gods favorable to us." Jupiter will surely have great joy when you represent on the public stage how he makes poor Amphitruo a cuckold <note>Referring to the myth where Jupiter disguises himself as the general Amphitruo to seduce his wife, Alcmene.</note>. How very much will Cybele, Venus, and Flora be indebted to you when you track the sad fate of Atys and Adonis, and the shameful excesses of that last-named harlot <note>Arnobius, like many early Christian writers, identifies Flora as a deified prostitute to mock her festival, the *Floralia*.</note>. Do you honor the gods in this way? You say that this pleases them, that it delights them, that it softens their anger. If that is so, then one can form no better concept of them than of all that rabble which brings these outrages and villainies onto the stage.

All enlightened critics, and all people of firm and refined taste, have unanimously called Lactantius the Christian Cicero; and it must be freely confessed that never has a praise been more accurate, never more deserved. Reading his books, one truly feels the same pleasure that the writings of the Roman orator and philosopher grant us. In both, there prevails the same purity of language, the same harmony in the phrasing, the same fertility in argumentation, and the same keenness of mind; the similarity in writing style is so striking that when he quotes the Roman orator <note>Referring to Cicero.</note>, one has difficulty distinguishing whether Lactantius or Cicero is speaking.

This great man called himself **Lucius Caelius Lactantius Firmianus**, names which appear at the beginning of all editions of his works. The place of his birth cannot be stated with certainty. Some believe he was a native of **Fermium**, a city in **Italy** in the **March of Ancona** <note>original: Ankonermark; a historical border region in central Italy, now the Marche region.</note>, now called **Fermo**, which is where his name **Firmianus** would originate. Others consider him an African, because at an early age he was placed as a student under the supervision of the famous **Arnobius**, to be trained by him in eloquence and the fine arts. His progress under such a great master can be inferred from what **Jerome** <note>original: Hieronymus; a contemporary priest and scholar famous for translating the Bible into Latin.</note> reports—namely, that while still very young, he composed a short philosophical treatise which, following **Plato's** example, he titled the **Symposium** <note>original: Gastmahl; literally "the Banquet."</note>. # Lactantius.

All enlightened critics, and all people of firm and refined taste, have unanimously called Lactantius the "Christian Cicero"; and it must be freely confessed that never has praise been more accurate, never more deserved. Reading his books, one truly feels the same pleasure that the writings of the Roman orator and philosopher <note>Referring to Marcus Tullius Cicero (106–43 BC), whose prose was the gold standard for Latin literature.</note> grant us. One can judge his immeasurable erudition <term>erudition</term><note>Great knowledge or learning, particularly from books.</note> by the immense number of Greek and Latin authors he cites, both in the field of the fine arts as well as in philosophy and history. The great fame he enjoyed was the reason why **Nicomedia** <note>A city in modern-day Turkey that served as a capital of the Roman Empire under Diocletian.</note>, the residence of the emperors at that time, desired him as a teacher of eloquence. But this city was entirely Greek, and because he did not find as many students as he wished—and moreover, since the persecution <note>Referring to the Great Persecution of Christians initiated by Diocletian in 303 AD.</note> was then raging at its most intense—Lactantius left his teaching chair and subsequently worked solely in defense of the holy faith.

Around this time, he conceived his beautiful work, the *Divine Institutes* <note>original: "göttlichen Unterrichtes"; his main work, *Divinae Institutiones*.</note>. He was moved to this labor by the writings that certain pagans had published at the time against the Christian religion. One can see from his fifth book what he thinks of these works and their authors. He was just occupied with this important labor when **Constantine the Great** chose him as the tutor for his eldest prince, the unfortunate **Crispus**. We have no certain records as to the success with which Lactantius managed the education of this young prince, who subsequently became the victim of the slanders of his stepmother **Fausta** <note>The text says "Faustina," but historically this refers to Fausta, the wife of Constantine, who was involved in the downfall of Crispus.</note>.

He dedicated his work to Emperor Constantine, to which prince he offers the most magnificent praise in the first book. From various anecdotes he mentions, one becomes aware that he took it in hand and revised it several times. Finally, he also made an epitome <term>epitome</term><note>A summary or condensed version of a larger work.</note> of this work, of which only a portion has survived to us. He also wrote a philosophical treatise, *On the Wrath of God* <note>original: "von dem Zorne Gottes"; Latin: *De Ira Dei*.</note>...

### Lactantius’s Divine Institutes.

## On False Religion.

# Lactantius.

...carried away from it. And since he is dealing with the Pagans <term>Heyden</term><note>original: *Heyden*—referring to non-Christians or followers of polytheistic Greco-Roman religions.</note>, he first raises the question: Is the world ruled by a single God, or by more gods?

The unity of God cannot be proven more clearly, correctly, or movingly than Lactantius does here. These proofs are now more than fifteen hundred years old, and yet they would still be quite new to the greater part of today’s rationalizers <term>Vernünftler</term><note>A term used to describe those who over-rely on human reason or speculate excessively, often applied to Enlightenment skeptics.</note> and philosophers. They can be summarized roughly into these four points:

1. The concept we form of the Deity leads us to an infinitely perfect being; consequently, there is, and can be, no more than one God.

2. The Deity is eternal: therefore, it is necessarily unique, and incapable of dividing or sharing itself.

3. The creation of the world can only be the work of a single being; and the same holds true for the administration of the world.

4. Multiple ruling beings in this world would be the same as multiple souls in one human body. All the absurd consequences of the second case are perfectly applicable to the first.

To these reasons, which are perfectly well articulated, he adds those proofs drawn from the unanimous agreement of all nations of the world, and from both the oldest poets and philosophers. To this is added the testimony of the prophets, whose authority is based on the complete fulfillment of all their prophecies, and of the Sibyls <note>Prophetic women of the ancient world whose oracles were often cited by early Christian writers to prove that even the pagan world had premonitions of Christ.</note>, whose existence, as he says, can be denied by no one except the ignorant or suspicious. And then he concludes with Plato's beautiful thought, that the glory and omnipotence of this Creator and Ruler of the world can be understood as little as it can be worthily spoken of.

->Lactantius.<-

After these vivid proofs of the unity of God <note>original: *Gotes*—an archaic spelling of *Gottes*.</note>, he investigates the origin of polytheism <term>Vielgötterey</term>. He proves from the most undeniable records that all the gods of paganism <term>Heydenthumes</term> were human beings whose births, life events, and deaths are known from history. The pride of powerful and violent men, and the base flattery of the common people, gave rise to this veneration of mortal men, who in the course of time were even regarded as gods. As ignorance and the corruption of the heart continued to spread further, men ventured to deify everything that brought pleasure, without regard for decency, morals, or reason. The history of the gods, as he cites it from the oldest and most credible writers, guarantees the truth of everything he asserts. We will not engage in any further detailed analysis, because we have sufficiently dealt with these subjects in the report we gave of the work of Arnobius <note>Arnobius of Sicca (d. 330 AD), a Christian apologist and the teacher of Lactantius; both wrote famous works defending Christianity against paganism.</note>. These two writers process one and the same material, yet with the remarkable difference that both stimulate and satisfy the reader's curiosity in equal measure, even though their approach is entirely different.

->Lactantius.<-

...was clinging <note>The previous page ends with the beginning of a sentence describing the "wretched blindness" of those clinging to earthly or false things.</note>. I find no greater pleasure, sublime Prince <note>Lactantius dedicated this work to Emperor Constantine the Great (reigned 306–337 AD), the first Roman emperor to convert to Christianity.</note>, than when I can summon the spirit of these false gods from their dark abode, make the abyss <term>Abgrund</term> of this godless worship comprehensible, and spread the knowledge of the Supreme Being. In my opinion, this is the greatest service that one can render to the straying human race: leading it away from the miserable path upon which it slides toward ruin, and awakening self-knowledge <term>Selbsterkenntniß</term> among one’s brothers, so that they do not, according to the teaching of some philosophers, consider themselves useless, contemptible beings who owe their existence to blind chance <term>Ungefähr</term>.

A damnable, abominable doctrine, which opens doors and bars to all vices; for once man thinks there is no God watching over us, but rather that everything ends with this life, he will soon hear nothing more than the voice of his passions. He will, as long as he lives, plunge from one debauchery into another, until finally the snare of death covers him unawares. They do not believe they have a rational soul: if they would listen to it, they would recognize the Creator by its voice, love virtue, leave idolatry <term>Götzendienst</term>, loathe debauchery, value themselves, and recognize that there is something greater about man than he seems to us to be. They would see that one cannot save this rational soul in any other way than by rendering the due worship to our Creator and Father, and renouncing damnable idolatry.

Afterwards he shows: 1. That our innermost consciousness constantly presents to us the knowledge of a single God, which the pagans <term>Heyden</term> experience just as well as we ourselves. 2. That man, as Ovid <note>Publius Ovidius Naso (43 BC – 17 AD); the famous Roman poet whose works often touched on the creation of the world.</note> so correctly noted, carries his face and eyes toward heaven <note>original: *Himmel an trägt*; a reference to a famous passage in Ovid's *Metamorphoses*: "While other animals look downwards at the ground, He gave to man a face uplifted, and commanded him to look at the sky."</note>, to remind him of his origin and his destiny, while other animals, with necks bent downwards, look toward the earth, to which all their inclinations and desires are restricted.

## Book Three.

### On False Wisdom.

In the introduction to this third book, Lactantius wishes for himself a small portion of that eloquence which once distinguished the Roman mayor <note>A reference to Marcus Tullius Cicero (106–43 BCE), the famous Roman orator and statesman who served as Consul—the highest office in the Roman Republic—which the author here likens to a "mayor."</note>, so that the truth—this truth already so powerful in itself—might be further supported by the charms and the power of eloquence to more forcefully combat general errors, and especially the daydreams of those people who pass themselves off as philosophers; and that truth, showing herself in all her strength and grace, might win a decisive victory. Two reasons, he says, justify me in this wish. People, who are so easily led astray by lies when they are cloaked in the charming garment of a beautiful style of writing, will surely grow to love the truth much more easily if it is adorned in the same manner; and we hope to beat and defeat the philosophers without much effort if we turn against these people the very weapons in which they place all their confidence.

Our writer does justice to the philosophers and admits that there were some among them...

...possessed <note>The text continues from the previous page: "...those who possessed the same [talents]..."</note>, who had many and distinguished talents: but they did not arrive at the knowledge of truth, because they sought it neither in that place, nor with that intention, where and how it must be sought. The philosophers may well have been learned people; but we cannot accept them as interpreters of truth, because they never approached Him who is the source of that very truth.

To uncover the vanity and inadequacy of human philosophy, the author enters into specific details which are as exquisite and critical as they are entertaining. In the beginning, he says, the love and search for truth was called philosophy. If one is still searching for it, then one must surely not yet have found it. And how could one have come into its possession? Then he examines the various schools <note>German: *Sekten*, referring to the philosophical sects or traditions of antiquity.</note> of philosophers—the Pythagoreans, Academics, Platonists, Stoics, and Epicureans; he presents their opinions, shows that one always contradicts the other, and concludes in the end that none has hit upon the truth. Then it is the turn of the physicists <note>In this context, "physicists" refers to natural philosophers (physiologoi) who sought to explain the physical world and its origins through reason rather than theology.</note>, who, proud of a few experiences and proofs, pretend that one can boldly decide upon everything. And this, he says, would be the "philosophy of the people" <note>Likely referring to a common-sense or accessible wisdom based on divine revelation rather than abstract speculation.</note>, with which the <term>Weltweisheit</term> <note>German for "worldly wisdom" or "secular philosophy."</note> of the learned should not presume to compete.

If one passes from speculative philosophy to moral philosophy, one finds on the part of the philosophers just the same...

# Lactantius.

...the same errors. We do not need to go through every point of this part of philosophy: let us hold only to the principal question around which all others revolve, and to which everything in morality must relate:
->Wherein consists the highest happiness?<-

He cites the various opinions on this and says: Epicurus places the highest happiness in the pleasure of our soul—an ambiguous expression, as will be seen later; Aristippus in the pleasure of the body; Calliphon in honorable pleasure; Diodorus in the absence of pain; the Peripatetics <note>Followers of Aristotle’s school of philosophy, so named because they allegedly conducted their lessons while walking around (*peripatētikos*).</note> in the goods of the body and the soul; Herillus in learning; Zeno in a life lived according to nature; and Aristotle in rectitude and virtue.

Lactantius <note>Lucius Caelius Firmianus Lactantius (c. 250 – c. 325 AD), an early Christian author and advisor to Constantine the Great, often called the "Christian Cicero" for his elegant style.</note> evaluates all these different opinions and, with the most admirable accuracy, uncovers the appalling impropriety of some and the inadequacy of others. One finds here all the acuity of a deep-seated metaphysics, all the salt <note>A reference to "Attic salt" (*sal Atticum*), meaning refined wit or sharp critical insight.</note> of a critic who believes he must spare nothing, placed among the most important observations for a person seeking the truth, and moreover, all the grace of gentle eloquence. Even Cicero and Seneca, who said so much that is beautiful regarding happiness and virtue, appear upon the stage; and Lactantius, as he lets them step forward, shows how far even these great spirits have wandered, how blinded they were that they did not ascend to the primary source of truth. This entire fragment, which fills three whole chapters, is extremely important, written in a manner charming to those curious for knowledge, and deserves to be recommended most highly for reading to those who love beautiful passages.

Thus far Lactantius has presented the horror and the errors of the philosophical systems concerning the highest happiness of man; now he tells us what...

# Lactantius.

reason and religion teach about this subject. Everything that contributes to the decision of this great question is derived from infallible principles through the most concise conclusions, and is executed in a manner corresponding to the dignity of God and most honorable for human nature.

At the beginning, he establishes that whatever one intends to name as the highest good <note>original: *summum bonum*, the ultimate goal or end toward which all human actions should be directed.</note> and the ultimate purpose of man must be of such a nature that it belongs to him alone, resides in his soul, and is the consequence of knowledge and the fruit of virtue. By this, he annihilates all philosophical systems and proves that all the "good men" in this field were blind.

Next, he shows that one can find the highest good in and through religion alone, and that among all beings here below, man alone is capable of religion and, through religion, of union with God. He shows that none of those advantages which flatter the senses and passions and are transitory can be the highest good, because the wicked can share them with the good—indeed, even irrational animals can share them with man. Even virtue itself, he says at the end, cannot be the highest good because it often suffers, and consequently is only the means to reach perfect happiness. And from all this, he concludes that the highest happiness consists in immortality as the reward for virtue. The principles of religion therefore acquaint us with the ultimate purpose for which we were created, and virtue with the means to reach this goal, which consists in a blessed immortality.

He concludes his judgment of philosophy by enumerating all the variations, doubts, contradictions, and errors into which the greatest men—among them Cicero <note>Marcus Tullius Cicero (106–43 BC), Roman statesman and orator whose Latin style Lactantius famously emulated.</note> and Seneca <note>Lucius Annaeus Seneca (c. 4 BC – 65 AD), a Stoic philosopher whose ethical writings were often admired by early Christians.</note>—have fallen, and says at the end: One must not reproach me...

# Lactantius.

...make me banish philosophy, since I place in its stead true wisdom, through which God himself has deigned to enlighten us.

Having previously judged philosophy itself, Lactantius now judges the philosophers. First, he takes up Epicurus. This philosopher knew how to disguise himself skillfully by stating that the "pleasure of the soul" was the highest good. He deceived the world through the ambiguity of this expression. But since he allows for neither Providence <note>original: *Vorsicht*; in this context, it refers to Divine Providence or the idea that God oversees the universe.</note> nor the immortality of the soul, he has opened the gate to all disorders and excesses of every kind. Horrible is the picture Lactantius paints of the consequences that necessarily flow from these abominable doctrines. In the most ingenious way, he mocks Epicurus's extravagant system of atoms, which he borrowed from Democritus, and Democritus in turn from Leucippus <note>Leucippus was the earliest Greek philosopher to propose the theory of atomism, later expanded by Democritus and Epicurus.</note>.

After Epicurus, Pythagoras appears with his comical system of the transmigration of souls, where a spirit, once its lodging is revoked, must move into another—perhaps the body of a pig, a donkey, or a bull—according to the judgment of Rhadamanthus <note>In Greek mythology, Rhadamanthus is one of the judges of the dead in the underworld.</note>. Plato also appears with his daydreams of the "community of women," which he wanted to see introduced in the phantom of his *Republic* <note>Lactantius is critiquing Plato's suggestion in *The Republic* that among the guardian class, wives and children should be held in common to ensure total loyalty to the state.</note>. And thus he examines even more philosophers, whose absurd voices clearly betray how far they were removed from genuine wisdom.

In the end, Lactantius says he has proven as far as possible how much the philosophers have deviated from the truth, and how poorly off one would be if one were to listen to them in the hope of finding the truth. My entire intention, he writes, was to show that genuine knowledge is to be found nowhere but in that religion which Jesus established; and the only means to arrive at true wisdom and bliss...

## Book Four.

### On True Wisdom.

True wisdom is inseparable from true religion. Now, true religion consists in the worship which one pays to the true God, who is at once our Father and our Lord and Master. Plato and Cicero <note>Lactantius frequently cites these two as the highest representatives of Greek and Roman thought, respectively.</note> sensed this truth; but they did not recognize it fundamentally so as to be able to draw the necessary conclusions from it. But if this one God is our Father, then we are indeed his children, whose duty it is to love him; and because he is our Lord, we must honor and fear him. Authentic wisdom consists in the knowledge of these truths, and the practice of what these truths prescribe constitutes true religion.

Consequently, it is impossible for idolatry <note>original: *Götzendienst*</note> to be a true religion; it is impossible to possess true wisdom through this kind of religious worship. For the forgetting of the only God—this Father and Lord of all mankind—is the reason why they have lost sight of the highest Majesty and the virtues by which he must be honored. This forgetting of the only God introduced those frail, fantastic deities seen in the temples and devised that religion which displays nothing but debauchery and wickedness. Through whom and how, then, was true religion and true wisdom revealed to us? This we must now investigate.

Lactantius confesses that he feels very well the entire weight and difficulty of his undertaking. Meanwhile—

...virtue and truth, a proposition he pursues in a most convincing manner. Then he demonstrates the cause of the jealousy and the hatred of the Jews toward Jesus, and their incomprehensible blindness. He concludes this victorious response by showing that everything that occurred at the death of this God-man <note>German: *Gottmensch*. A theological term referring to Jesus Christ as being simultaneously fully divine and fully human.</note> is found recorded stroke by stroke in the books of the Prophets, which the Jews themselves held in their hands and read daily without understanding them. One can say that it is impossible to give a more learned, clearer, or more convincing interpretation of Jesus’ suffering, which more correctly matches the prophecies of the Prophets to subsequent events.

After he had dealt in the same way with the burial, the resurrection, and the return of Jesus to his Father, he brings his disciples onto the stage, who, equipped with a truly divine power, proclaim the new religion to the world and introduce it in all places. The first proof which the author puts forward is based on the fact that every lawgiver who wishes to train humanity in virtue must himself practice what he commands, because all his laws would be fruitless if he did not support what he teaches with words through examples. Secondly, it was necessary that the teacher who was to instruct humanity in the perfection of virtue come from heaven and be clothed in a human body. Thirdly, this teacher had to be simultaneously God and man, in order to provide examples as a man and to provide authority <note>German: *Gewalt*. In this theological context, it refers to the divine power and sovereign right to establish moral laws.</note> as God.
