# Book Five.
## On Justice.

Just as true wisdom orders the mindset of man, so must justice order all the stirrings and desires of his heart: through this, he becomes righteous in the eyes of God, and worthy of the Highest Being. The relationship of man to God, and to his fellow men, imposes duties upon him, and the faithful fulfillment of these duties is called justice, which Lactantius treats in his fifth book.

The introduction is a masterpiece of eloquence and the best method of presenting evidence. Therein, the author gives an account of the reasons that moved him to write. My intention, he says, is to enlighten the pagans <term>Heyden: practitioners of the traditional Roman polytheistic religions</term>, to strengthen the believers in their religion, and alongside this, the sweet comfort of fighting for such a beautiful cause. To these first motives, he adds two others. First, he says, although the cause of the Christians had been quite well defended by some writers, they had been satisfied to present the truth quite simply, without decorating it with the finery of eloquence and erudition, which he felt was necessary to give it a better reception through this innocent trick <note>Lactantius, often called the "Christian Cicero," believed that the intellectual elite of Rome looked down on Christianity because its early writings lacked the sophisticated rhetorical style of classical Latin literature.</note>. Secondly, some pagan writers had recently exerted every effort to mistreat and dishonor this holy religion with their pens.

After this introduction, the author immediately takes up his subject and explains what justice is. At the beginning, he reminds his readers of the Golden Age <note>original: "goldne Weltalter"—referring to the mythical "Aetas Aurea" or the reign of Saturn, a time of primordial peace and justice in Roman mythology.</note>, of which the poets give us the most charming paint—

Just as true wisdom guides a person’s way of thinking, so must justice regulate all the impulses and desires of his heart: through this, he becomes righteous in the eyes of God and worthy of the Highest Being. The relationship of man to God and to his fellow humans imposes duties upon him, and the faithful fulfillment of these duties is called justice, which Lactantius <note>Lucius Caecilius Firmianus Lactantius (c. 250 – c. 325) was an early Christian advisor to Emperor Constantine I, known as the "Christian Cicero" for his elegant Latin style.</note> discusses in his fifth book.

But can people with such dispositions find a taste for true justice? Should we wonder at the cruelties they practice against righteous souls? -># Lactantius.<-

...proved his proposition through several examples, and among others, by the following.

Justice, he says, forbids us from taking someone's life, as well as from seizing another’s property. Consequently, what will a just man do who, during a shipwreck, sees someone who has fortunately obtained a plank to which he clings to escape death? Let us assume the just man has the advantage of strength; will he swim over, push the weaker man from the plank, seize it for himself, and save his own life at the expense of the other? If he does so, he is an unjust villain; if he does not, he is a fool. — This same case occurs when, during a flight after a lost battle, a soldier on foot takes a horse from a wounded rider and thus escapes death. And what would one have to say about a conqueror? And what figure would the Romans themselves cut? From this it follows, Carneades concludes, that wisdom and justice do not get along well together, and justice is nothing more than a folly.

These traits are taken from Cicero’s dialogues *On the Republic* <note>original: *de re publica*. This famous work by Cicero explores the ideal state and the nature of justice; much of it was preserved only through citations by later authors like Lactantius.</note>. In them, Furius speaks for self-interest against justice, and Laelius <note>Gaius Laelius was a Roman statesman and a close friend of Scipio Aemilianus; in Cicero's dialogues, he often represents the voice of traditional Roman virtue and Stoic philosophy.</note> defends the cause of justice against personal advantage. Yet his reasons do not suffice to refute Furius: but what Laelius was unable to do, Lactantius accomplishes with delightful strength and eloquence.

The pagans, he says, lacked the light from above; they had only a very weak, uncertain, and wavering concept of immortality; indeed, most of them believed nothing of it at all and restricted themselves entirely to the present. # Book Seven.
## Concerning the Blessed Life.

With a feeling of the most heartfelt bliss and contentment, Lactantius begins this seventh book of his *Institutions* <note>original: "Unterweisungen" — a reference to the *Divinae Institutiones* (Divine Institutes), the author's most famous work written to defend Christian belief to educated Romans.</note>. "How desirable! How magnificent!" he says; "We have laid the foundation, and a strong foundation it is, well-able to support so great a building; indeed, we have not only laid the foundation but have raised the building itself up to the gables: it requires only the roof and the decorations." But what would be the use of having uncovered errors, unmasked false wisdom, demonstrated the superstition of idolatry, and revealed the bright-shimmering radiance of true wisdom, justice, and genuine virtues, if we did not finally arrive at that most blessed life which must be the reward of virtue? Our Father and God has reserved this for us: with this blessed life we wish to conclude our instruction.

In the beginning, he treats at length God's ultimate purpose in creating the world and, preeminently, human beings within it. He shows how the philosophers' teachings on this subject do not correspond at all to the wisdom and holiness of the Creator; he brings together all the observations and conclusions that this investigation offered him and says: It is indeed a comforting truth that God created this world for us; that we are in it to worship His greatness; and that the service we render Him through laborious virtues is rewarded with immortality. # Lactantius

...reaps the reward of those virtues, without which man would be worse off than the irrational beasts <note>original: "unvernünftige Vieh." This reflects the classical philosophical view that humans are distinguished from animals by the possession of reason and a moral compass.</note>.

3. The distinction between vice and virtue, which is grounded in nature, is a striking proof of the immortality for which we strive. The fruit of vice and passion is brief and fleeting, like all earthly things. This is evident in the passions of desire, ambition, and physical pleasure. Once the desires of the passions are fulfilled, the enjoyment is followed by disgust and boredom. Virtue does not seek or expect its reward here: it seeks merit alone; eternal reward alone is its focus. It perseveres steadfastly even unto death: for only after death does it come into possession of its reward. Through death, everything comes to an end for vice, and for virtue, everything finds its beginning.

One should observe the works which depend upon the body and the hand, and those which come from the soul, and one will immediately conclude that the soul must be immortal; if one examines our desires, one will draw this very same conclusion. All works of human hands perish; time destroys and annihilates them: but the works of the spirit are immortal. Consequently, the same must hold true for their productive causes. As far as desires are concerned, those of the body relate to the needs of the body: but the desires of the soul take their flight toward eternity. For this reason, the soul despises present goods—even life itself—to ensure the eternal ones. These thoughts and reflections are taken from *Cicero* <note>Marcus Tullius Cicero was a Roman philosopher whose works on the nature of the gods and moral duties heavily influenced early Christian thinkers like Lactantius.</note>.

There are other reasons concerning this subject which will certainly have their effect and make an impression. One can look these up in *Lactantius* himself.

<meta>This page continues a discussion on the early Christian apologist Lactantius, specifically focusing on his rebuttals to Epicurean philosophy regarding the soul's immortality.</meta>

->Lactantius. 303<-

After citing proofs, he answers Lucretius’ <note>Titus Lucretius Carus (c. 99–55 BC), a Roman poet and philosopher known for "On the Nature of Things," which argued for a materialist worldview.</note> objections, which the anti-Christian philosophers of our century have so often repeated, and to which we have sufficiently responded in our *Philosophical Dictionary of Religion*; we refer our readers there.

1. The soul, says Lucretius, is born with the body; so it also dies with the body.

The body, Lactantius answers, consists as a whole of various physical parts; one sees, smells, and feels it. These united parts can separate; this composite being can be dissolved. But the soul can neither be seen nor touched; one admits no parts to it; it is therefore not subject to dissolution in the same way as the body. The Lord created it directly and united it with the body after its formation: but it is not shaped like the body: it is not subject to death because it is not subject to dissolution.

2. One sees that the soul is weak in childhood, becomes stronger with the years, and decreases again in old age.

One must clearly distinguish the soul from the understanding. The soul is the substance which, through its union with the body, animates and enlivens it. The understanding is the power of the soul to think, to comprehend, to conclude; a power and ability which works according to the measure of the disposition and the condition of the auxiliary organs <note>The author uses "Hilfsglieder" to refer to the physical senses or brain functions that the mind uses to interact with the world.</note>. The soul was called by the Latins <term>Anima or Animus</term> <note>original: "Anima oder Animus"</note>, and by the Greeks <term>Psyche</term> <note>original: "$\Psi\upsilon\chi\eta$"</note>; the understanding, however, was called by the former <term>Mens</term> <note>original: "Mens"</note>, and by the latter <term>Nous</term> <note>original: "$N\upsilon\varsigma$"</note>. If the auxiliary organs are weak or disordered, the activity of the understanding is hindered: but the soul does not therefore cease,

3. The soul suffers through the illness of the body and recovers along with the body: should it not then be mortal just like the body?

Illnesses manifest themselves in the intellect, not directly in the soul. — Epicurus’ <note>Epicurus (341–270 BC) was a Greek philosopher who taught that the soul was made of atoms and perished with the body.</note> remaining objections do not deserve mention.

After Lactantius has refuted the materialists and strengthened the case for the immortality of the soul, he treats the general resurrection, the final judgment, and the happiness of righteous souls after their union with their God and Father. Finally, he also mentions the opinion of many church writers of the first centuries who allowed for the <term>thousand-year reign of Christ</term> <note>Also known as Millenarianism or Chiliasm, this was a common belief in the early Church that Christ would reign on Earth for 1,000 years before the end of the world.</note> before the world's end, writing before the Church had formally spoken on the matter, and following their example, he declares himself not unclearly in favor of this opinion. He concludes his beautiful work with the most touching expressions of gratitude toward God and our divine Savior, who came to enlighten us, to instruct us, and to show us that path which leads unfailingly to heaven, where we shall reign with Him eternally.

### I.

The most accurate concept of the truly philosophical spirit is found in the introduction to the first book of the *Divine Institutes* <note>The *Divine Institutes* (Latin: *Divinae Institutiones*) was Lactantius's most important work, intended as a systematic defense of Christian doctrine against pagan philosophers.</note>. In it, one discovers a modest writer who accepts only the most honorable and certain principles, traces their ultimate consequences, seeks nothing but truth, and directs everything toward virtue, which alone leads to genuine happiness. He expresses himself with these words:

> “From time to time, people of extraordinary mind have been seen who restricted all their industry to true philosophy alone; they not only renounced public office but also neglected their private business and searched for truth with their whole soul, convinced that gathering all divine and human knowledge graces a rational being infinitely more than accumulating wealth or chasing after honor. They look with contempt upon the frail and earthly advantages which are created for this fleeting life alone and make man neither more just nor more virtuous. Because of these sentiments, they also deserved to attain the knowledge of truth, which was the sole object of their desires and their restless effort; just as some, with this intent, have left their possessions and renounced all pleasure to devote themselves with entirely undisturbed freedom to virtue, which they held to be the highest good. However, they did not achieve the goal at which they aimed; all their efforts were frustrated because the truth—that is, the wisdom and the intentions of the Creator—is impenetrable to the human gaze; and there would be no difference between God and man if man's limited spirit could fathom the secrets of the Uncreated.”

most of all as the teachers of virtue. It is indeed more essential for a human being to act uprightly than to speak well. We shall deal with this religion and with entirely divine subjects in this work. Several famous orators, after they had long been the admiration of the people, threw themselves into the arms of philosophy and viewed this new occupation of the mind as an honorable rest after their labors. These good people conducted investigations in areas where no discoveries were to be made. This was not rest, but rather an ungrateful and far more laborious work than that which they had renounced. May I not, without contradiction, count myself more fortunate—do I not act more reasonably—if I choose a kind of philosophy in which one can express oneself about everything without difficulty, where everything is heard with pleasure, grasped with ease, and may be accepted with honor? This philosophy, which I announce, is divine wisdom, which is entirely truth and virtue.

## II.

->A beautiful passage on the manner in which one should<-
->judge divine pronouncements and the opinions<-
->of philosophers.<-

Since Holy Scripture tells us that all the over-refined speculations <note>original: "Grübleyen," referring to excessive or circular intellectual brooding</note> of philosophers are nothing but foolishness: this statement must be illuminated through the presentation of the matter itself and through logical reasoning. This is done for fear that people might be deceived by that grand word, "philosophy," or blinded by the tinsel-glitter of eloquence, and thus find themselves more inclined to believe in human delusions than in the word of God. These pronouncements of divine truth are simple and certain; and it was not fitting for God to speak otherwise. For when the Lord reveals himself to man, he does not support his words with logical proofs, as if one were permitted to doubt his revelations. He spoke as he had to speak, as the highest, unlimited judge, who delivers the verdict without occupying himself long with proofs: in short; God spoke as God.

His gods lived in comfort and cared little for how things go down here among men.

Epicurus’s entire system of doctrine <note>referencing Book III, Chapter 18 of Lactantius's *Divine Institutes*</note> refers to the proposition that man exists in the world solely for the purpose of enjoying all the goods and pleasures that present themselves. But would anyone who adopts this principle have much desire to avoid vice and debauchery? For if the soul is mortal, what better can one do than to accumulate wealth and procure pleasures of every kind? But what is to be done in the event that money and wealth are lacking? One must seize every possible means—deception, cunning, and force (it all counts the same)—and rob others of what they possess: and because the gods do not involve themselves with the affairs of this world, one may indeed plunder and murder, provided one knows how to cleverly avoid the gallows.

Doing evil, when one finds advantage in it and has nothing to fear, is what "sound philosophy" advises in this adventurous system, because the gods are not offended by the actions of men: and doing good is a folly, because the gods take no notice of it. Enjoy quickly, for as long and as much as we can; the moments dart swiftly by; and soon we are no more. Let us therefore lose no day, indeed no hour, and wastefully use every tiny bit of time for the enjoyment of pleasure <term>Wohllust: while often meaning "lust," in this 18th-century context it refers more broadly to sensory gratification and luxury</term>: for every minute is stolen from our lives which we do not dedicate to such sweet labor.

Epicurus does not say all of this in such explicit words; but it flows from his entire system of doctrine. For since he adopts as a principle that a wise man, a philosopher, does everything solely for his own sake, he can achieve nothing thereby except his own advantage. Consequently, he who adopts these abominable principles will be careful not to do anyone a service, because in that case, he would have to work for the benefit of others. He will never recoil from a crime, however gruesome it may be, as long as he finds it to his account <note>meaning: profitable or advantageous</note>. If the leader of a band of robbers wanted to give his accomplices courage for some villainous deed, he wou—

These were carried away by their natural ferocity; those sought to win the favor of the Emperors through ingenious cruelty, and to climb to the sublime and lucrative positions of honor along this bloody path: some seemed possessed by fits of the blackest rage, and beside themselves, like that governor <term>Landpfleger: a regional administrator or prefect in the Roman provincial system</term> of Phrygia who, while the Christians were gathered in their church, ordered fire to be set and had them all burned alive together. One can say of him: the more cruel he was, the more leniently he proceeded. For he is always the cruelest executioner who puts on a display of false mercy and knows how to moderate the most horrific tortures so that they do not kill, but rather grant him the pleasure of tormenting his victim for a very long time. How ingenious they are in inventing exquisite pains to achieve their aim! They use these cruel artifices not only to be able to boast that they have murdered no innocent person, but also because they wish to avoid the gossip that they themselves were defeated, and they begrudge the Christians the crown of their virtues. In the devilish inventions of new ways to torment and torture, they have no other intention than to conquer your steadfastness. They view all of this as a competition between themselves and the Christians. I myself have heard how several of these executioners boasted of their moderation in this regard.

-># Lactantius.<-

In Bithynia <note>A Roman province in modern-day Turkey.</note>, I saw a governor who was intoxicated with joy when a Christian—after the most horrific torture, which he had steadfastly endured for two full years—finally seemed to succumb to the cruel trial. Had he won a new province for the Empire, he would not have felt a more heartfelt pleasure. They persecute us, therefore, with the sole intention of overpowering our faith; they torment us with the most vivid and sensitive pains, while they fear nothing so much as that we might give up our spirit under the torture. Their unfathomable inhumanity goes so far that they have the wounds of those who have hung on the rack carefully dressed, in order to enable them to endure new pains, and to be a match for new struggles and new cruelties with renewed strength.

The great man <note>Referring to Lactantius (c. 250 – c. 325 AD), an early Christian author and advisor to Constantine I.</note> was himself an eyewitness to all these horrors. In truth, this is a weighty response to everything the enemies of religion write to diminish the number and the honor of our martyrs <term>Blutzeugen: literally "blood-witnesses," a traditional term for those who died for their faith</term>.

## VII.

### Origin of the Errors of the Philosophers, some of
### whom have thought very beautifully and correctly
### about the first principles of natural law.

The philosophers seek the path that leads to truth (Book IV, Chapter 8), and they do not find it for the reason that they seek it on this earth. I compare them with those who sail about on the open sea at random without a steersman and without the help of charts. Although we walk upon the earth, we must possess the same means as the sailors, who, if they do not constantly direct their eyes toward heaven, cannot hold their course securely. Whoever always [seeks] his way in the present life without dan... <note>The sentence is interrupted at the end of the page; "Gef" likely begins "Gefahr" (danger) or "Gefährte" (companion/guide).</note>

<margin>*) Book III of *On the Republic* <note>original: "L. III. de Republ."</note></margin>
Driven by a tender love, we wish therefore to submit ourselves to this law of the Lord, this holy, heavenly law, which Cicero <note>Marcus Tullius Cicero (106–43 BC), the Roman orator and philosopher whom Lactantius greatly admired for his prose style and moral insights.</note> presents to us with these more-than-human expressions:

> “There is a true law, which consists of right reason <note>original: *gesunde Vernunft*</note>, is perfectly in accord with nature, is immutable and eternal, and is engraved upon every soul with inextinguishable traits. This law urges us toward our duties through its commands and discourages us from evil through its prohibitions. One can raise no objection against this law; no statute can overrule it, nor can it be completely repealed. It requires no interpreter; it is valid for now and for all time to come. This law is unique, eternal, and unchangeable, embracing all ages and all peoples; and God Himself, the Creator and Lord of all mankind, has given it. Just as He will punish its transgressions, so will He reward its observance. Those who violate this law are their own enemies; they degrade the humanity within themselves and will thereby draw upon themselves the greatest punishments, even should they not have to experience the other plagues mentioned by so many writers.”

And if this man had treated the individual circumstances of this law with the same insight, I would consider him not merely a philosopher, but a true prophet.

## VIII.

### Absurd Opinions of the Philosophers Regarding the Origin of Society.

The philosophers have devised various reasons which might have moved men to gather into communities and to build cities (Book VI, Chapter 10). Some said that men had emerged from the earth and led a wandering life in the fields and in the woods, where leaves and moss were their beds and a rocky cleft was their dwelling, without right or law <term>Recht und Gesetz: refers to the distinction between "jus" (natural right/justice) and "lex" (written statute)</term>, because all language was still lacking; in which state they often became the prey of wild animals that tore them apart. Those who had been attacked or wounded, or had seen their kind snatched away by these animals, these philosophers continue, noticed the danger, turned to other men, and begged for their assistance, as they revealed their desire and need to them through signs and cries. In the beginning, they formed one sound and then another, gave each thing its name, and so the crude foundations of a language gradually developed among men, in order to communicate their thoughts to one another. Through this union, they initially saw themselves secured against the attacks of dangerous animals, and—

### Lactantius

...to be able to rest without fear even during the night, they came upon the idea of building cities, in order to thwart the nightly prowling of fierce predatory beasts through no other weapons than ramparts and walls.

What a contemptible vermin of men <note>The author is using a polemical tone common in early Christian writing to disparage Epicurean or Materialist philosophers who sought naturalistic rather than divine origins for humanity.</note> who have concocted such absurdities, and were foolish enough to pass down the memory of their silly opinions to posterity! Human beings, these philosophers say, discovered in animals the "call of nature," which urged these creatures to unite, to avoid dangers, to use caution, and to choose the most suitable places for their dwellings. And our "highly-wise" philosophers believed that humans, despite all their reason, would never have learned what to flee or fear without the example of animals; nor would they have taken clever measures for their safety, nor ever known how to gather into a society or form a language, if the wild beasts had not done them the "favor" of devouring them.

Other philosophers have considered these notions to be the dreams of an overstrained imagination; (and in truth, only a man in the throes of a high fever could babble such silly nonsense) and said that humans joined together in a society because they are social by nature and enemies of a solitary life. There is, in fact, no great difference between these two <term>schools of thought</term> <note>original: "Lehrgebäuden"</note>. While each takes its own particular path, in the end, they both arrive at the same destination. One cannot say that these systems are absolutely impossible, as no obvious contradiction hangs over them; yet they are both false. For humans did not emerge from the womb of the earth in the manner of those...

### Conclusion

What will a person feel and think who has carefully read through this little work! Will he not see with heartfelt joy and admiration how the divine religion of Jesus Christ <note>original: "J. C."</note> was, even in its earliest times, presented, explained, and developed with such elegance and insight? How it was proven with such strength and clarity, and so triumphantly defended against everything that unbelief, <term>freethinking</term> <note>original: "Freydenkerey." In this context, it refers to Deism or the Enlightenment critique of organized religion.</note>, and wickedness have spewed out against it in this century? And what a pleasure to have become acquainted with so many great men, some of whom he previously did not even know by name! Now he perceives in them such an astonishing variety of knowledge and talents alongside the most sublime virtues; he receives from their mouths the principles of a hitherto unknown philosophy, which listens to nothing but reason, loves the truth, and teaches virtue; which soars to the heavens, even to the Godhead, and is so worthy of the Godhead! But what astonishment must—

### Lactantius

...overcome when he sees that these men, renowned for their wisdom and virtue, were offspring of **Paganism**, that is, members of a society where one abandoned oneself to all disorders, vices, and excesses without shame. This was because such behaviors had been introduced, approved, and—as it were—deified by the religion one professed, the education one received, the examples one witnessed, and the principles one heard. And now, one sees the brightly shimmering light emerging from the thickest darkness, and the purest and most divine sentiments coming forth from the infectious pool of all vices.

Will not the reader, like Saint Paul once did, compare such a striking transformation of the greatest men of their times with the work of God's omnipotence at the creation of the world, and cry out with this Apostle: *God, at whose command light arises from the darkness, has enlightened the hearts of these extraordinary men, so that they might enlighten others with the bright <term>knowledge of God</term> <note>original: "Wissenschaft Gottes." In the 18th century, "Wissenschaft" referred to a systematic body of knowledge or learning, often used here to mean "theology" or "divine wisdom."</note> through the Lord Jesus.* \*)

With what delight will he finally learn to realize which are the true philosophy, the true philosophers, and those teachers who deserve to be heard and respected. But what will he think of that class of people who, in our day, set themselves up as teachers of the human race, hoping to justify all their errors through the name of a "philosopher," who mock the believers and cause such terrible devastation in the Christian community? What a vast distance, what a horrifying contrast, when one holds the one against the other!

In these philosophers of the first three hundred years <note>The author refers to the Early Church Fathers and Christian apologists of the first three centuries AD, who lived under the Roman Empire before the Edict of Milan.</note>, one sees people who, since they were born in the center of all superstition and all excesses...

# Lactantius

...themselves, opened their eyes to the rays of reason, and their ears to the voice of conscience, recognized the misfortune of their birth <note>The author refers to being born into "Paganism" as a misfortune that these early thinkers had to overcome.</note>, sought truth and virtue with a sincere soul, surrendered themselves to them with a kind of **holy enthusiasm**, and with great courage renounced the corruption of the heart and the superstition in which they were entangled by birth and religion. But what are today’s philosophers? People who—since they do not dare to publicly abjure the sublime religion in which they had the good fortune to be born—abjure it secretly in their deeds. They do this by contesting, with all their inherent malice, the divine truths and the heavenly principles that constitute the entire <term>doctrine of faith and morals</term> <note>original: "Glaubens- und Sittenlehre." This refers to the systematic teachings of the Church regarding what to believe (faith) and how to act (morals).</note> of this religion, and setting out to reintroduce among us, in their place, pride and debauchery, which were formerly the shame of **Paganism**.

In the former, one discovers great souls who sacrifice their talents, their peace, their blood, and their lives to make themselves useful to the human race, to enlighten it, and to uncover before its eyes the injustice and indecency, the dangers and unhappy consequences of **idolatry** and the pagan religion. And the latter are enemies of the Divinity, of virtue, and of religion; they use their intellect and their talents to the misfortune of mankind, so that they might blaspheme the Divinity, mock and slander virtue, and degrade religion. They do this sometimes through the falsest and most hateful accusations, which they sell as the most indubitable facts; sometimes by highlighting the abuse that powerful villains have made of religion; and sometimes through fallacies, through which they seek to shake its foundations, its certainty, and its truth.

The first group finds nothing more sublime and beautiful than virtue; they present us with the most charming and touching...

# Lactantius

...present the finest portraits of [virtue], seeking to spread a taste for it; they speak of it like people who are thoroughly moved, enchanted, and convinced of the merits of virtue; who feel their own happiness and wish so dearly to share it with others. One sees clearly that they speak the **language of the heart**. To be sure, they do not conceal the effort that virtue requires; but this effort vanishes when one hears the magnificent colors with which they depict the reward of virtue, which consists partly in the peace and serenity of the heart during this life, and partly in the delight that the virtuous person will taste in eternal union with God. Only men of unfeigned virtue can speak this language.

The others, in order to place **vice** upon the throne, behave exactly like the honorable man when he wishes to win a heart for virtue. They sketch portraits of debauchery, pride, ambition, and greed that could not be more charming or seductive; they also teach the trick of silencing conscience and reason, should they happen to raise their voices. They say that the passions are nature's most precious gift, and that what nature advises is always innocent; they claim that one has the passions to thank for beautiful and great souls; that men without passions are useless for anything, incapable of any noble impulse, and disinclined toward any praiseworthy deed. This is the instruction that these eulogists of vice give to an inexperienced, fiery youth, who is so easily seduced due to a lack of reflection. They then take revenge in a manner worthy of them, through blasphemies and crudeness, with which they overwhelm their critics, whom they treat just as insolently as they often deal with God and the Saints.

I will say nothing of the difference between these two types of philosophers in respect to genius and talent. One can judge this from what has appeared in this little work and in others which we have published for the protection of religion. But the judgment would turn out far more thorough and certain if one were not satisfied with the **little streams** <note>original: "kleinen Bächen"</note> which we have shown, and with the short extracts we have presented, but went all the way to the **source**; that is, making oneself acquainted with the works of these learned defenders of religion themselves.
